#6255. Protein fibers linked to Alzheimer’s are also found in semen, but why are they there?

Amyloid fibers in semen bind RNA, carry it into sperm and reach the embryo, a route that may one day deliver gene therapies.

Amyloid proteins are widely associated with Alzheimer’s disease, but similar protein fibers found elsewhere in the body may serve important biological functions.

New research suggests that amyloid fibers in seminal fluid could play a role in transferring genetic information from fathers to their offspring.

The discovery offers a fresh perspective on how biological information beyond DNA may influence the next generation.

Scientists knew that seminal fluid carries small pieces of RNA, and that RNA in sperm can shape how an embryo develops.

How RNA naturally moves from seminal fluid into sperm cells has remained unclear. The findings raise new questions about the role of amyloid fibers in reproductive biology.

Anthony Fitzpatrick, who runs a lab at the Zuckerman Institute at Columbia University, led the work. He studies amyloid in the brain, where it’s a sign of Alzheimer’s and other diseases that destroy nerve cells.

The delivery experiments used lab-made fibers and added RNA, so whether the body’s own fibers do this during an ordinary conception is still untested.

“This is wild biology,” Fitzpatrick said.

“Amyloids are most often thought of as a hallmark of Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s and other neurodegenerative diseases in the brain, but they also have functional roles throughout the body, and keep turning up in unexpected places.”

The project began with a virus. In 2007, researchers found that amyloid fibers in semen help HIV get into cells.

Fitzpatrick wondered whether the fibers could do the same for something the body makes itself.

RNA plays important roles in regulating gene activity and producing proteins. Seminal fluid contains an abundance of small RNA fragments.

Earlier studies had tied those fragments to the next generation.

Male mice fed a high-fat diet carry a different mix of small RNA in their sperm, and their offspring show metabolic changes.

The researchers examined the relationship between RNA and amyloid fibers, finding that RNA influences how these protein structures form.

The team also confirmed the presence of naturally occurring amyloid fibers in human seminal fluid.

The small RNAs attached to the fibers were mostly fragments of transfer RNA, a type of RNA that helps assemble proteins.

One of those fragment types had already been reported, in earlier work, to pass from sperm into embryos.

The findings highlight how much remains to be learned about the biological functions of amyloid fibers outside the brain.

Using advanced microscopy, the researchers observed amyloid fibers inside sperm cells. The observations provided evidence that these protein structures can interact with reproductive cells.

Study first author William Mallen, who conducted the work as a doctoral student in Fitzpatrick’s lab, is now a medical student at the University of Vermont.

“Seeing those amyloid fibers inside sperm cells was just so extraordinary to me,” said Mallen.

“There were hints of this happening earlier in our other experiments, but actually seeing this just totally blew us away.”

Laboratory experiments involving mouse embryos provided further evidence of a potential connection between amyloid fibers and early development.

However, whether naturally occurring amyloid fibers perform a similar function during reproduction remains uncertain.

Several important questions remain unanswered. The researchers have not established whether naturally occurring amyloid fibers influence gene activity in developing embryos.

Changes a father passes on without altering his DNA are called epigenetic.

“There are metabolic disorders such as insulin resistance that recent papers have shown can be passed down the paternal line in mice, and it’s thought RNA is how,” Mallen said.

“By learning how disorders based on epigenetics work, we can come closer to how to possibly treat or prevent them.”

The authors’ next steps are to work out how a fiber gets into a sperm cell and where the RNA goes once inside.

After that comes a test of whether RNA on natural semen fibers changes gene activity in embryos. Until then, the delivery route is a laboratory result.

The full study was published in the journal Molecular Cell.

#6254. ‘Political malpractice’: Calls grow to delay Senate GOP leadership elections

Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., walks through the Ohio Clock Corridor this summer. Now he’s pushing to delay leadership elections for his conference, urging a discussion of last week’s larger than expected losses. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

After last week’s midterm elections saw them lose at least seven Senate seats and the majority, some Republicans are pushing for a reckoning, saying the conference should stop and think about its future.

“After the stunning defeat [we] just can’t continue on business as usual. That kind of defeat demands change,” Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., said on Monday evening.

Asked if he himself would want to run for Senate minority leader, the Wisconsin Republican responded with a question of his own: “That’s part of our problem. Who’d want the job? Would you want it?”

Though no hopeful had emerged as of Monday afternoon — at least publicly — to challenge current Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., for the top GOP post, the frustration was palpable as Republican senators returned to D.C. and grappled with the election results. Calls grew throughout the day to delay the conference’s leadership elections planned for Tuesday morning.

“Well, I mean, I’m open to hearing what the arguments are for that,” Thune told reporters Monday when asked about the possibility of postponing the leadership votes. “I don’t know if that solves anything, but like I said, it’s going to be a decision that’s ultimately made by Republican senators. We’ll hear them out.”

Johnson told reporters on Monday that if the election is held, he would “leave the room” and walk out. Either way, he seemed certain to at least get a “fulsome” discussion of the topic, as he requested in a letter he sent to Republican Conference Chair Tom Cotton, R-Ark. Four other Republican senators signed on to the letter, hitting the threshold to call a conference meeting under internal GOP rules.

Also signed by Sens. Mike Lee of Utah, Ted Budd of North Carolina, Rick Scott of Florida, and John Kennedy of Louisiana, the letter obtained by CQ Roll Call cites last week’s “stunning defeat” and reads in part: “Holding leadership elections without engaging in a robust discussion and evaluation of how those running for leadership intend to lead would be political malpractice.”

Kennedy said Monday evening that he was asking to postpone the leadership elections because “we need time to talk to each other.”

“We’re like a shop owner who’s losing his customers. It’s not the customer’s job to fix that. It’s the shop owner’s job, and I’m not looking for blame-shifting. I’m looking for self-examination,” he said, adding that he wouldn’t consider running for minority leader himself.

In the letter, the group asked that at the time the leadership elections were set to begin, 9 a.m. on Tuesday, they instead “have a fulsome conference discussion and delay holding leadership elections until we all have a chance to hear from leadership candidates as to what type of collaborative conference governing model we should adopt and what our strategy will be to counter the emboldened Democrats.”

Thune echoed that wording Monday as he spoke to reporters, saying, “I do think that we need to have a very fulsome, robust conversation about where we go from here, and then we’ll see what the consensus of the conference is.”

But Sen. Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., who serves as chair of the Senate Republican Policy Committee, said she has seen such requests launched in the past and didn’t think it would do much to affect the ultimate outcome. “I think Sen. Thune will be reelected,” she said.

And several Senate GOP aides said that they suspected a “robust” conversation wouldn’t do much to delay the plans and that leadership elections were still expected to take place Tuesday. They noted similar efforts from some of those same senators in previous years to sow discord in the ranks.

That includes Scott, who unsuccessfully challenged Thune in 2024 and then-GOP leader Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., in 2022. But Scott told Fox News over the weekend, “I don’t want to run again. I’ve run twice.”

Republicans “failed. We had a horrible night,” Scott said. “Instead of having an [leadership] election, the first thing you do is you say, ‘OK, what are we going to change? We have to change something.’”

Lee floated the idea of waiting until after the uncalled Senate races in Mississippi and Alaska are officially resolved.

An online pressure campaign was building in some of the same MAGA corners of the internet that have pushed to pass a sweeping voter ID bill, known as the SAVE America Act, that has stalled in the Senate. On Monday morning, influencer Scott Presler in an X post urged constituents to call their senators while praising the lawmakers who have already pushed for the leadership elections to be postponed. “Where is everyone else?” he wrote.

Sens. Jim Banks of Indiana and Dave McCormick of Pennsylvania also called for a delay, though they did not appear on Johnson’s letter.

“A week ago, we had the worst election results in decades,” McCormick said in a post on X, calling Tuesday “too soon” to vote for leaders. “I know it’s been practice to go straight to leadership elections in recent years, but we should not rush it.”

Banks similarly said Tuesday was “too soon,” posting on social media, “Our conference needs to sit down and have a frank conversation about where we fell short, what we stand for, and what we’re going to do for the working families who sent us here.”

One senator speaking out in Thune’s defense was Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, who competed with Thune for the top spot in 2024 but on Monday said the leader isn’t to blame for the midterm results.

“I think the president needs to look in the mirror and look at the flawed candidates that he endorsed, and the kind of environment that we’re in,” said Cornyn, who is still smarting from losing his primary to a challenger backed by President Donald Trump.

Cornyn’s loss means he has no say in the coming conference leadership elections. But he said, “I think Thune’s a good man, and did as well as he could against a president and an environment that was pretty hostile.”

#6253. This scientist proves which problems computers can’t solve quickly

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

MIT computer scientist Dor Minzer uses math to prove when there’s no computational shortcut. He now guides graduate students through the kinds of problems that drew him to the field.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Dor Minzer remembers sitting in an undergraduate computation class at Tel Aviv University. He was intrigued by his professor and soon found himself pulled into a new world: the mystifying intersection of math and computation, first laid out by Alan Turing during World War II. Working with the professor, Minzer became deeply interested in the limitations of what computers can and can’t do.

“My part is actually to prove not only do I not know how to do it, but I can prove that it’s impossible,” Minzer says. “You have to really be curious.”

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Minzer’s hard work has paid off. In 2018, he proved a theoretical computer science problem called the 2-to-2 games conjecture. It asks whether computers can efficiently distinguish games where almost all rules can be satisfied from those where almost none can be satisfied, when the rules have a strict structure.

In September, Minzer and his two graduate students at MIT posted a 95-page milestone paper on the unique games conjecture, which builds off the 2-to-2 conjecture. The paper wasn’t quite ready, but they published to get ahead of a press release from OpenAI, describing its proof for the same problem, slated for only days later. It’s a situation that many mathematicians have found themselves in this year as AI companies flood the field with findings at lightning speed.

Minzer says it’s critical to remember that math, and all the research and contemplation behind it, is very human. “It’s a human activity,” he says. “Research is sort of a living organism, a living body.”

Minzer teaches his own students now. Some days, he talks to his class and gets the sense that nobody is paying attention. But other days, he gets a few students that participate. They have ideas, they’re excited, and they remind him of his own days as a graduate student.

“I feel like now I feel like I’m passing the torch,” he says. “Before you have a Ph.D. adviser, you’re like a new person in a dark room. There are infinite places to go. Your Ph.D. adviser is the person that holds your hand and says, ‘Okay, let’s walk here.’”

#6252. Drones could help protect wildlife, but photographs may miss serious health problems

Drones help scientists monitor wildlife, but measuring animals directly can reveal health problems that aerial images may miss.

A sleeping seal on a beach can now be measured from nose to tail by a drone hovering overhead.

Changes in the seal’s length and width can be tracked from one flight to the next. Whether those changes reflect fat or muscle cannot be read from the images alone.

That limitation is examined in a review published in Science. Drone measurements, the authors conclude, should be checked against weights and other hands-on data.

The review was led by Michelle Shero, an associate scientist at the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution (WHOI).

Her co-authors are based at Oregon State University, the University of Maryland Center for Environmental Science (UMCES) and other institutions.

No new experiment was carried out for the paper. Existing methods were compared using more than a decade of Weddell seal measurements from Antarctica.

“Integrating traditional methods – weighing and handling animals on the ground – with emerging, non-invasive toolsets such as drone imagery means that we can now really tailor the scope of how we look at wildlife health,” said Shero.

In many field studies, an animal’s condition is judged by comparing its weight with its length. An animal that is heavy for its length is assumed to carry more fat. The same logic is used for people in the body mass index, or BMI.

In a 2010 analysis of wood mice, Algerian mice and shrews, such scores suggested age and sex differences in condition.

The same analysis traced those differences to adult body size and to size gaps between males and females.

The Weddell seal records were examined in the same way. They cover 328 weigh-ins of 236 seals, and the scores were found to track body weight closely.

Fat was measured on 318 of those occasions with a heavy-water method. A dose was given to each seal and traced through its body water.

Percent body fat was predicted poorly by the scores. Weight-for-length values were mostly a measure of how large each seal was.

A statistical issue was also raised. Scores are usually calculated relative to a population’s own average. In a population where all animals are in poor condition, about half would still be scored above average.

In older ecological studies, weight changes were often assumed to consist entirely of fat. Changes in muscle and organs, the lean tissue, received less attention.

Hooded seal mothers nurse their pups for three to four days. No other mammal is known to have a shorter nursing period.

During that time, 21% of a mother’s fat is lost, along with 6% of her lean tissue.

Weddell and elephant seal mothers nurse for four to six weeks. Over that period, about 55% to 60% of their fat stores are used.

Between 15% and 25% of their lean tissue is lost as well.

Lean tissue is broken down from working muscles and organs. In mammals, heavy losses have been linked to fatigue, slow wound healing, disease and pregnancy loss.

Per gram, about six times more energy is stored in fat than in lean tissue. Muscles and organs, however, cost 10 to 45 times more to maintain.

Energy needs can therefore fall when muscle is lost. Prey requirements would be overestimated if every lost pound were treated as fat, the authors wrote.

Weddell seal mothers return to sea to feed after their pups are weaned. Over the first month, nearly all of the regained weight is lean tissue.

About 1 to 2 pounds (0.5 to 1 kg) of it is added per day.

Fat gains were recorded only in the females with the largest overall weight gains.

A single photo or weigh-in from that month could therefore be misread. Body weight would be rising while the share of fat in the body was falling.

Dive records are subject to a similar error. Seals drift without swimming during some dives, and lean tissue is denser than fat.

Faster sinking during these drifts is commonly read as a sign of poor feeding. Muscle gained after successful feeding would produce the same pattern.

Young seals are easily misjudged too, said Jennifer Burns, a professor at UMCES and a co-author of the review.

“Based on external appearance alone, seal pups don’t seem to grow much between the time they are weaned and their first birthday,” said Burns.

“However, physiological measurements reveal many internal changes: yearlings are much leaner than weaned pups, and their muscles have developed to support effective underwater foraging.

“Without information on mass, age, and body composition, it would be possible to conclude that seals don’t develop much over their first year of life, when really they are directing energy toward maturation rather than structural growth.”

None of these concerns make drones less valuable as a research tool.

A single overhead photo of a surfacing whale gives its length. Its width can also be measured at many points along the body, especially around the middle.

Drones can also be flown in a circle around resting animals. The angled photos are combined into a 3D model of each animal.

This approach was tested on gray seals on land. Adult females’ weights were estimated to within about 8 pounds (3.8 kg) on average.

Pup weights were off by about 9 pounds (4.1 kg), close to a tenth of a pup’s body weight.

Body shape has a large effect on these models. Assuming that an animal’s body has a circular cross section can lead to an overestimate of its volume by more than 25%.

When the body is modeled as an oval, the error drops below 3%.

Aerial photos have already been used to track long-term change. Images from crewed planes and drones showed that North Atlantic right whales have been getting shorter.

Oregon State researchers have reported a similar decline in gray whales off the Pacific Northwest.

The most convincing examples in the review pair outside measurements with measurements from inside the body.

African and Asian elephants were scored from photos of their ribs, hips and backbones. Those scores were compared with ultrasound measurements of fat and with blood fat levels.

Once confirmed, the scores showed that elephants in zoos were more likely than wild elephants to be overweight.

For sperm whales, one research team combined drone measurements with historical whaling records. Tags recorded how fast the whales drifted during dives.

The team estimated that each extra cubic meter (about 35 cubic feet) of body added about 6.3% more fat. Counting all of the added size as blubber would have produced an estimate of 12.5% to 14.4%.

Drones are also flown through whale spouts to collect exhaled breath. The breath can contain DNA, hormones and microbes.

Hormones can also be measured in whiskers, feathers, baleen or dung.

KC Bierlich, an assistant professor at Oregon State’s Marine Mammal Institute, also co-authored the review.

“Pairing additional internal biomarkers, such as endocrine state, with external appearance, can also provide key insight into an individual’s health state,” said Bierlich.

A whale may look average in photos, he said. Stress from human activity or its surroundings may still be keeping it from gaining weight.

“Pregnant females often require greater mass gain in a feeding season to support the high energetic costs of gestation, which often overlaps with periods of migration and fasting.”

“As such, failure to gain additional mass, particularly for pregnant females, may negatively influence reproduction and, in turn, have negative consequences to the population.”

The authors recommend choosing research methods based on the animal, the research question and the level of detail needed.

The researchers evaluated body condition scores using data from a single seal species. Few studies have compared body condition scores with actual fat measurements in marine mammals.

Researchers often avoid catching sick or very thin animals because handling them is risky. This means their data may favor healthier animals.

Drones avoid this problem but require a licensed pilot, low wind speeds and dry weather.

Shero sees an important role for physiologists, the scientists who study how bodies function. They can test new tools against real measurements, a step known as ground truthing.

“From gaining an in-depth understanding of shifts in an animal’s metabolism to capturing indices of condition at unprecedented scales across whole populations, and everything in between, it’s here that physiologists can really help to ground truth and guide efforts as people begin reaching for new technologies to study species that are protected or otherwise less accessible,” said Shero.

In the framework the authors lay out, drones would screen whole populations for animals whose size is changing.

Follow-up sampling on the ground would then show whether fat or muscle explains the change.

The Weddell seal data used in the review have been made publicly available.

The full study was published in the journal Science.

#6250. How much time in nature does it really take to improve mental health?

A review of decades of research suggests that even modest weekly exposure to green spaces is associated with meaningful mental health benefits.

People are often told to spend more time outdoors when they feel stressed or overwhelmed. But how much time is enough to make a difference? And does going out once a week really help?

A new analysis of decades of research suggests that people may need less time in nature than they think.

Just one visit to a green space or one hour spent there each week was associated with half of the maximum mental health benefit estimated by the researchers.

Spending more time outdoors was linked to greater benefits, but the difference became smaller with each additional hour.

The research was led by Bin Jiang, director of the Division of Landscape Architecture at the University of Hong Kong (HKU).

His team examined studies that observed people in their everyday lives. The findings reflect patterns across different groups of people rather than a routine that everyone needs to follow.

Life in a crowded city can be stressful. Finding somewhere to sit among trees or take a walk away from traffic is not always easy.

According to 2022 figures from the World Health Organization cited by the researchers, depression and anxiety disorders affect more than 550 million people worldwide.

By 2050, around 70% of the world’s population is expected to live in cities.

Meanwhile, the amount of urban land covered by buildings and paved surfaces has increased more than fivefold in recent decades.

As cities grow, there is less room for greenery. Knowing how much contact with nature can benefit people could help city planners decide where and how to provide green spaces.

The researchers approached the question much as scientists would when studying the effects of medicine.

They wanted to know whether the benefits of nature changed depending on how much of it people experienced.

Living near greenery is one part of the picture. How often people visit natural places, how long they stay and how far they have to travel also matter.

Scientists have long suggested that natural surroundings can help people recover from stress and give an overworked mind some rest.

However, much of the existing research has focused on the amount of greenery around people’s homes. Less attention has been paid to how people actually use those spaces.

The team initially identified 92,430 research records.

After narrowing down the selection, the researchers examined how different amounts of nature exposure were linked to depression, anxiety, stress and mood.

There was not enough information to draw firm conclusions about distance. Instead, the researchers focused on the number of visits people made and how much time they spent in green spaces each week.

Would someone who spends four hours in a park feel four times better than someone who spends just one?

Some earlier studies assumed that the benefits increased steadily with time. Others suggested there might be an ideal amount of exposure, beyond which the benefits would begin to decline.

Neither explanation fit the combined data as well as an S-shaped curve. This type of curve has been used in medicine for nearly a century.

The pattern showed that much of the benefit appeared with relatively little exposure to nature. As people spent more time outdoors, the additional benefits gradually became smaller.

There were clues to this in earlier research. Some studies linked a single weekly visit to lower levels of depression, while others reported improvements after brief sessions lasting around 10 minutes.

Other findings suggested that benefits began to level off at around 200 to 300 minutes a week.

In medicine, researchers often calculate how much of a drug is needed to achieve half of its maximum effect. Jiang and his colleagues applied the same idea to time spent in nature.

Their model suggested that one weekly visit or one hour in a green space was enough to reach 50% of the estimated maximum benefit.

Around four visits or four hours a week brought that figure to 90%. Reaching 99% required about six visits or eight hours a week.

In other words, the difference between spending no time in nature and spending an hour there may be greater than the difference between spending seven and eight hours outdoors.

There are a few important details to keep in mind. The researchers calculated the number of visits and the hours spent outdoors separately.

The hours refer to the total time spent in nature over an entire week. Also, reaching 50% of the estimated maximum benefit does not mean that someone’s depression or anxiety symptoms will decrease by 50%.

What interested Jiang, who also founded the Urban Environments and Human Health Lab at HKU’s Faculty of Architecture, was how similar the results were across different studies.

“The most striking aspect for me is the theoretical value of these findings, which suggest that the dose-response curves in most reviewed studies follow a remarkably consistent pattern,” said Jiang.

“This indicates the potential existence of an objective scientific law.”

“For public health, the findings suggest nature is not merely an object for aesthetic appreciation but a free, accessible ‘medicine’ for mental health, where the dosage matters.”

Chris Webster, chair professor of urban planning and development economics at HKU, was particularly interested in how little time people might need to spend outdoors.

“It is surprising neither that nature exposure helps mental health nor that there is a dose-response curve,” Webster said.

“What was intriguing to find in this study was a consistent pattern across historical results, and the relatively small dose required to achieve measurable benefits.”

For someone living with depression, even getting out of the house can feel like a difficult task. Spending several hours outdoors every week might not seem realistic.

That is why the findings interested Gunter Schumann, a professor at Fudan University, Charité in Berlin and the University of Cambridge.

“From a psychiatric perspective, the most relevant finding is that the steepest gains occur at low doses; one hour or one visit per week already achieves half of the modelled maximum response,” Schumann said.

“This threshold is highly realistic for individuals experiencing low mood or reduced energy. Derived from a synthesis of observational studies, these benchmarks reflect population averages that complement rather than replace clinical treatment.”

“Crucially, they offer an achievable starting point for clinicians and patients, while demonstrating that green space access is a modifiable determinant of mental health actionable through urban planning.”

The researchers believe cities could do more to make outdoor spaces inviting.

Something as simple as a shaded bench, a well-maintained footpath or healthy plants could give people more reasons to visit a park regularly.

They also suggested that cities should pay attention to how often residents use green spaces, rather than simply measuring how much greenery exists.

For individuals, getting more time in nature could mean taking a weekly park walk or choosing a tree-lined route to work.

How close does a park need to be for people to benefit from it?

Previous studies have suggested that having a green space within a 15- to 20-minute walk from home may be helpful. However, the researchers did not find enough comparable data to determine an ideal distance.

The studies also measured mental health and contact with nature in different ways.

Most importantly, they were observational, which means they cannot prove that spending time in nature directly improves mental health.

The quality of a park, what people do during their visits and their personal circumstances could all influence how much they benefit. These are questions that future studies will need to explore.

Jiali Li, the study’s first author and an HKU PhD graduate, explained why the team wanted to put a number on nature exposure.

“We wanted to turn the broad advice from ‘spend more time in nature’ into something people can use in everyday life,” Li said.

“Our findings suggest that even modest weekly contact with green spaces is associated with meaningful mental health benefits, while additional gains become smaller at higher levels of contact.”

“My advice is to start with a routine you can sustain, such as a weekly park walk, and adjust it to your needs and circumstances. These benchmarks offer an achievable starting point, rather than a fixed prescription for everyone.”

Not everyone has the time or energy to spend an entire afternoon outdoors. But according to the findings, even setting aside an hour each week could be a worthwhile place to start.

The study is published in the Journal of Environmental Psychology.

#6249. New Congress will still be filled with losers

The Capitol Dome is illuminated before dawn on Oct. 13. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call)

OPINION — Once again, the next Congress is going to be filled with losers.

This is not a personal judgment about their character or personality, but a simple recognition that many members have lost races before getting elected. And the incoming class is no different.

I’ve written many versions of this column for more than a decade, and yet the lesson always seems to get lost, no pun intended. Parties routinely attack candidates who enter a race with losses on their record. And, of course, it happened this cycle as well.

“We beat him once. We’ll beat him again,” National Republican Senatorial Committee Chairman Tim Scott declared when Democratic former Sen. Sherrod Brown announced his challenge to appointed GOP Sen. Jon Husted in the summer of 2025.

“Ohioans gladly sent him packing last year, and they’ll not hesitate to toss him aside again,” said a Republican strategist.

Brown lost reelection to Republican Bernie Moreno in 2024 but came back to defeat Husted for the state’s other Senate seat. And Brown is far from the only candidate to avenge a loss with an electoral victory last week.

The fact of the matter is that losing a race doesn’t have to be the end of a political career. Losses can lay the foundation for future success by building name ID or a fundraising network. Or sometimes it takes a change in the political environment or change in circumstances, such as running for an open seat instead of challenging an incumbent.

In addition to Brown, there are more than a dozen losers coming into the next Congress:

In some instances, though, the losses are piling up.

Republican Rep. John James of Michigan now has three statewide losses on his record. He lost Senate contests in 2018 (taking 46 percent of the vote) and 2020 (48 percent) and came up short in his bid for governor this year (44 percent).

Republican former Sen. John E. Sununu of New Hampshire, who lost reelection in 2008 to Democrat Jeanne Shaheen, fell in his comeback attempt for the open seat last week.

But they could take heart from another repeat loser. Charlie Crist, a former Florida governor and congressman, has had a handful of high-profile losses over the years, including for Senate and two gubernatorial comeback bids. He was just elected mayor of St. Petersburg.

So even though I know it’s a futile request, let’s have a bipartisan agreement not to attack candidates for past losses, because losing doesn’t mean they can’t later pull off a win.

Scientists reported that an AI-designed protein can activate broken insulin receptors in lab mice, hinting at a potential new treatment for some forms of severe insulin resistance.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A protein designed with the help of artificial intelligence (AI) has successfully switched on faulty insulin receptors in lab mice even when insulin itself couldn't.

The findings hint at a new way to treat certain rare, life-threatening genetic disorders that cause insulin resistance, in which the body's cells don't respond well to the blood-sugar-controlling hormone.

In a study published Wednesday (Nov. 25) in the journal Science Translational Medicine, researchers found that the AI-designed protein, called RF-409, lowered blood sugar and reduced damage to the pancreas in mice with a genetic form of severe insulin resistance. This, in turn, prevented dangerous weight loss that typically comes with the condition.

When blood sugar rises, the pancreas releases insulin, a hormone that binds to proteins called insulin receptors on the surface of cells. This changes the receptors' shape, triggering a series of chemical signals that ultimately help bring blood sugar levels back down.

But mutations in the gene that encodes the insulin receptor can disrupt this process. More than 150 such mutations have been linked to inherited forms of insulin resistance. In one of the most severe forms, called Donohue syndrome, children can experience dangerously high blood sugar after eating, and unusually low blood sugar between meals, as well as poor growth. Most children with the condition die before their first birthday.

"Some [of these] patients produce extremely high levels of insulin, but their receptors cannot respond properly," study co-author Eunhee Choi, a cell biologist at Columbia University, told Live Science. "Simply giving more insulin may not solve the problem."

That's why Choi and her colleagues explored whether they could activate the receptor in another way.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

In 2025, the researchers used computational tools, including AlphaFold2, an AI program that predicts protein structures and how they fit together, to develop proteins that activate insulin receptors in a different way than insulin does. In that previous study, one of those proteins, RF-409, lowered blood sugar in both healthy mice and mice with obesity. In the new research, the team wanted to see whether RF-409 could also activate defective insulin receptors.

First, they ran experiments with laboratory-grown mouse and rat cells and with healthy mice, both with working insulin receptors. This confirmed that RF-409 largely mimicked insulin's effects on cellular signaling and metabolism. In the mice, RF-409 had a nearly 60-fold longer half-life in the bloodstream than insulin, meaning the protein stays in circulation much longer before breaking down.

"Both these features make [the finding] more than just an elegant trick," said Dr. Rajiv Agarwal, a nephrologist at Indiana University School of Medicine who was not involved in the study. Unlike a protein that mimics only some of insulin's effects, RF-409 reproduces most of its normal signaling, "which matters in children who need growth as well as glucose control," he added.

Insulin (orange) plugs into the insulin receptor (blue) to change its shape and trigger signals inside cells. The new protein activates the receptor in a different way.

To test how RF-409 works with defective receptors, the researchers focused on a mutation previously identified in patients with Donohue syndrome; this genetic mutation alters a key part of the receptor's structure, preventing insulin from binding to it. Computer models suggested that RF-409 could bypass the affected region and hold the receptor in the shape needed to transmit signals inside cells.

The researchers genetically engineered mice to carry this mutation. Compared with mice that retained a functioning copy of the insulin receptor gene, these mice had, on average, roughly 2.5 times higher blood sugar and 10 times higher fasting insulin levels (the amount of insulin in blood after a period without food).

When injected with insulin, mice with defective receptors showed no substantial drop in blood sugar. Treatment with RF-409, however, lowered mice's blood sugar by roughly 60% within two hours.

"It is like designing a new key to open a defective lock," said Kalaiarasan Ponnusamy, a computational biologist at SRM Institute of Science and Technology in India who was not involved in the study. "From a computational protein-design perspective, this is a major advance because it demonstrates that entirely new proteins can be engineered to restore receptor function without correcting the underlying genetic mutation."

After 14 days of continuous treatment, five mice given RF-409 had lower blood sugar, maintained their body weight and retained more abdominal fat than five mice given a saline solution, for comparison. The treated mice also showed less pancreatic damage.

"Extending this approach to other disease-causing receptor mutations is a realistic possibility, provided the receptor retains its ability to transmit signals," Ponnusamy said. Some mutations, for instance, prevent insulin receptors from reaching the cell surface or transmitting signals inside cells at all. That means the technique demonstrated in the study is unlikely to work against such mutations.

Identifying which mutations can be treated in this way is now a priority for Choi. The team also plans to investigate how RF-409 affects different tissues in the body and whether it remains safe and effective over longer periods of treatment, she said.

Although Agarwal foresees several hurdles in bringing RF-409 into clinical use; for instance, the immune system's reaction to the protein will have to be carefully studied, and in general, it's challenging to run trials with infants with rare disorders. That said, he remains hopeful that it could help patients whose diseases have no treatments to treat the underlying cause.

"This is the first approach I have seen that addresses the actual defect rather than working around it," he said.

#6247. Antarctica’s ozone hole has grown to one of its largest sizes in nearly 50 years

Satellite observations reveal an unusually large ozone hole above Antarctica in 2026, despite the long-term recovery of Earth’s protective ozone layer.

Today’s Image of the Day reveals the immense scale of the Antarctic ozone hole in 2026.

Earth’s natural shield against harmful ultraviolet radiation has experienced one of its most dramatic seasonal changes in decades.

Satellite observations show that the Antarctic ozone hole expanded to 10.5 million square miles (27.3 million square kilometers) by September 20, 2026.

The depleted region covered an area considerably larger than Antarctica itself.

The hole was approximately 31 percent larger than the average for that time of year over the past two decades.

The findings, released by the European Space Agency (ESA) on November 26, mark a striking contrast to 2025, when Antarctica experienced one of its smallest ozone holes in recent decades.

However, the dramatic expansion does not necessarily mean that efforts to restore the ozone layer are failing.

High above Earth’s surface, a relatively thin concentration of ozone helps make life on our planet possible.

Ozone molecules consist of three oxygen atoms. Most atmospheric ozone resides in the stratosphere, where it absorbs much of the Sun’s harmful ultraviolet radiation before it reaches the ground.

Without this protection, living organisms would face greater exposure to radiation capable of damaging DNA.

Excessive ultraviolet exposure can increase the risk of skin cancer and cataracts in humans, while also harming plants and marine life.

The Antarctic ozone hole is not an actual opening in the atmosphere. Instead, it represents an extensive region where ozone concentrations have fallen to unusually low levels.

Scientists use a measurement known as the Dobson unit to quantify the amount of ozone in a column of atmosphere.

Regions with readings below 220 Dobson units are considered part of the ozone hole.

The atmosphere above Antarctica undergoes a remarkable transformation during the Southern Hemisphere winter.

As the continent enters months of darkness, temperatures high in the atmosphere plummet.

A powerful circulation of winds, known as the polar vortex, isolates extremely cold air over the region.

Under these conditions, unusual clouds can form in the stratosphere.

Chemical reactions on the surfaces of their particles convert chlorine compounds into forms that can readily destroy ozone once sunlight returns.

As spring approaches and Antarctica emerges from darkness, sunlight triggers reactions that rapidly break apart ozone molecules.

The strength and duration of the polar vortex can significantly influence how much ozone disappears during this period.

In 2026, an exceptionally persistent vortex maintained the cold atmospheric conditions associated with ozone destruction, contributing to the unusually extensive hole.

Although the Antarctic ozone hole covered an enormous geographical area this year, satellite measurements revealed another important detail.

The severity of the ozone depletion remained relatively close to average, even as the affected region spread much farther than usual.

Scientists must therefore look beyond the boundaries of the hole to understand what is happening in the atmosphere.

The duration of ozone depletion, the concentrations of remaining ozone and the movement of surrounding air all provide valuable information about the health of Earth’s protective layer.

A particularly large ozone hole in a single year does not necessarily indicate a reversal of the broader recovery trend.

The latest observations draw on measurements from Copernicus Sentinel-5P, a satellite launched in 2017 to investigate the composition of Earth’s atmosphere.

Its instrument, known as Tropomi, analyzes light interacting with different atmospheric gases.

Each gas leaves a distinctive spectral signature, allowing researchers to map its distribution.

From orbit, the satellite can monitor atmospheric changes across vast and remote regions that would be difficult to survey using instruments on the ground.

Such observations are particularly valuable over Antarctica, where extreme weather, geographic isolation and prolonged periods of darkness complicate scientific fieldwork.

When combined with decades of previous measurements, satellite data help researchers separate temporary atmospheric fluctuations from lasting environmental changes.

The discovery of severe ozone depletion over Antarctica in the 1980s prompted an unprecedented international response to an environmental crisis.

In 1987, nations adopted the Montreal Protocol, an agreement to phase out chemicals responsible for destroying atmospheric ozone.

Among them were chlorofluorocarbons, which were once commonly used in refrigerators, air conditioners and aerosol products.

Although atmospheric concentrations of ozone-depleting substances have declined, many of these chemicals remain in the atmosphere for decades.

The latest scientific assessments indicate that Antarctic ozone levels continue to recover and could return to their 1980 levels during the 2060s.

That recovery will not follow a smooth or predictable path. Natural variations in atmospheric circulation and temperature can produce dramatically different conditions from one year to the next.

Today’s image offers a reminder of both the vulnerability and resilience of Earth’s atmosphere.

Nearly four decades after the world came together to protect the ozone layer, satellites continue to document a recovery that will span generations.

Image Credit: ESA / Copernicus Sentinel-5P

#6246. Astronomer Isabel Angelo hunts for odd signals in telescope data

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

A comet or a newborn star might explain an odd signal in telescope data. Astrophysicist Isabel Angelo is looking for signals that defy those familiar explanations.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Isabel Angelo spends her days searching the cosmos for exoplanets and signs of extraterrestrial intelligence. But Angelo’s head isn’t in the stars. It’s buried under mountains of 0s and 1s — data from space telescopes old and new.

To piece together a fuller picture of what’s out there (alien megastructures around nearby stars, perhaps?), Angelo and her colleagues at the SETI Institute in Mountain View, Calif., are turning to machine learning models. These tools are analyzing the troves of telescope data for anomalies — things that look “weird” in space that we don’t know how to explain yet.

Most of the space weirdos will probably turn out to be total normies — a comet, a newborn star or a star surrounded by lots of gas and dust. “These are things that I would expect [the models] to find,” Angelo says. “But the goal is to find something that’s not even in any of these categories.”

In the meantime, Angelo keeps her whimsy and wonder for space alive by remembering historic moments, like the reveal of the first portrait of a black hole in 2019. The scientists “put all of these telescopes all over the Earth. They wait for the Earth to rotate. They do all this math to construct this one image,” Angelo says. “I can’t believe how creative and innovative we have to be to learn about space. It’s such a specific and really fun challenge.”

#6244. Quitting smoking with e-cigarettes may depend on one overlooked factor

A large clinical trial reveals how e-cigarettes and brief behavioral counseling can improve the chances of successfully quitting smoking.

Smoking cessation programs often combine nicotine replacement products or e-cigarettes with behavioral counseling.

However, counseling costs money, isn’t always available, and may not appeal to everyone who wants to quit smoking.

A trial of 1,170 adults in Britain examined how effective e-cigarettes could be without behavioral counseling.

Dr. Katie Myers Smith and her colleagues at Queen Mary University of London provided one group with e-cigarette starter kits but no behavioral counseling.

Six months later, 11.3% of that group had stopped smoking, against 6.4% of the group that got automated quit-smoking emails.

Reported smoking abstinence was verified using a carbon monoxide breath test.

Adding five short phone calls over four weeks nearly doubled the quit rate among e-cigarette recipients, to 21.1%.

Everyone in the trial smoked daily and wanted help stopping, and anyone already vaping weekly was excluded.

They smoked 19 cigarettes a day on average and were 48 years old on average. Most had tried to quit with something before.

One group was signed up to the NHS SmokeFree email program on the morning of their quit date, which sends stop-smoking advice and daily motivation for 28 days.

A second group was mailed a refillable e-cigarette with nicotine e-liquid in tobacco and strawberry flavors, spare coils, and a leaflet on how to buy more.

The third group got that same pack plus a call on the quit date and weekly calls for four weeks, matching what a British stop-smoking service normally offers.

The starter supplies were expected to last about two weeks, after which people bought their own.

At six months, 21.1% of the group with the calls had stopped smoking, against 11.3% of the group with the e-cigarette alone.

The trial was built around those two comparisons, and both differences were statistically significant.

In an interview with Earth.com, Dr. Myers Smith emphasized the impact of adding behavioral support to the e-cigarette intervention.

“What surprised us most was how much difference a few short phone calls made. Five calls over four weeks nearly doubled quit rates,” she said.

“Providing support through remote approaches is practical, low-cost and acceptable to many smokers, and it has important real-world implications, particularly for reaching groups who may be less likely to engage with face-to-face services.”

The calls may not have made vaping work better. More people in that group were using their e-cigarette early in the attempt, when quitting either takes hold or doesn’t, and the authors read the gap that way.

Participants in the email group were asked not to vape, and by six months about a quarter of them had. Among those in that group who quit, 68% were using an e-cigarette at six months.

That crossover makes the headline comparison a cautious one. The authors also ran the numbers with everyone who used a treatment outside their assigned group set aside.

On that reading the email group’s quit rate fell to 2.7%, roughly a quarter of the rate from the pack alone.

Dr. Myers Smith noted that the findings should not diminish the importance of existing stop-smoking services.

“Firstly, it is important to emphasize that stop-smoking services remain essential. However, our findings suggest that specialist counseling does not need to be provided to every smoker in order to achieve positive outcomes,” she told Earth.com.

“Simply offering an e-cigarette can help smokers quit when support is unavailable or unwanted, while engagement with behavioral support can further increase the likelihood of success.”

The same group had already put e-cigarettes up against patches and gum in an earlier trial, with counseling included throughout.

The new trial examined how effective e-cigarettes could be without behavioral counseling.

The gaps were still there at a year. Validated quit rates were 16.8% with the calls, 9.0% with the e-cigarette alone, and 5.4% with the emails.

Most of the people who stopped smoking were still vaping a year on.

Peter Hajek, the study’s senior author, said ex-smokers can keep using an e-cigarette for as long as they need to feel sure they won’t go back to smoking.

Smoking fell even among people who didn’t quit. Those still smoking at six months had cut back by 6.4 cigarettes a day in the email group, 8.2 with the e-cigarette, and 9.6 with the calls.

Serious adverse events were reported by 8.1% of the email group, 10.8% of the e-cigarette group and 10.7% of the group with calls.

Four people died during the trial, two in each e-cigarette group, one of pneumonia and three of causes the trial could not establish.

The breath test behind every quit rate here picks up smoking over roughly the past 24 hours, so somebody who smoked three days earlier could pass it.

True abstinence in the e-cigarette groups may have been lower than the figures say, and the authors said so themselves.

Being handed a vape inside a trial is also not the same as buying one.

Most people now believe e-cigarettes are as dangerous as cigarettes, the authors said, so uptake outside a study could be lower.

The e-liquids came in flavors, which limits what the trial says about countries that have banned them. Staff collecting the follow-up data knew which group each person was in.

The trial also measured smoking, not health. Vaping is not risk-free.

Previous research has linked nicotine exposure to blood vessel damage and e-cigarette use to an increased risk of heart failure.

What happens after year one to the people who swapped and kept vaping is the part no one followed.

The benefits of stopping smoking show up at any age, and this trial’s own evidence runs out at twelve months.

Britain is already handing out free vaping starter kits through its swap to stop scheme.

The authors pointed to these results as support for not making counseling a condition of it.

A longer follow-up is what would show whether the people it reaches stay off cigarettes.

The full study was published in the journal NEJM Evidence.

A study claims that ancient "supervolcanoes" hidden under Antarctica may have provided the nutrients that led to an explosion of complex life millions of years later. But not everyone agrees.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Scientists have found the remnants of supermountains in the seabed around Antarctica. They say these ancient peaks may have provided the nutrients that led to an explosion of complex life millions of years later. However, others are more skeptical about these conclusions.

About 600 million years ago, landmasses in the Southern Hemisphere collided to form the supercontinent Gondwana, which included what is now South America, Africa, Arabia, Madagascar, India, Australia and Antarctica. At that time, there was multicellular life, but it was very primitive.

Previous research suggested that the continental collision created massive Himalaya-like mountains in what is now Antarctica. Now, in a new study, published online Sept. 12 in the journal Earth and Planetary Science Letters, scientists say they've found the sediment that accumulated in the oceans when the Gondwanan mountains eroded over millennia.

"The results suggest that the assembly of Gondwana involved multiple major continental collisions, producing an extensive network of mountain belts comparable in scale to the modern Himalayas and Tibetan Plateau," Nathan Daczko, a petrologist at Macquarie University in Australia who was not involved in the research, told Live Science in an email.

"The study highlights just how much geological history remains hidden beneath Antarctica."

Most of Antarctica is trapped beneath an ice sheet, so it is difficult to understand its evolutionary history.

To address this, the team drilled into the seabed at 12 locations around Antarctica, extracting soil samples. They were looking for ancient crystals called detrital zircon. Zircon is a mineral that grows in rocks and is strong enough to remain chemically intact when the rock erodes.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"We can date it very, very precisely, and from the geochemistry, and especially the trace elements, we can determine where the zircon came from," Ian Campbell, a geochemist at the Australian National University and a co-author of the study, told Live Science.

They dated 1,712 zircon grains extracted from marine sediments and compared the abundance of zircons in Antarctica with a global zircon database, across different time scales.

"We have used the zircon record to show that the mountains that formed during the amalgamation of Gondwana were the largest and most extensive in the history of the Earth, and they included some very high mountains like the Himalayas today," Campbell said.

Alan Collins, an earth scientist at the University of Adelaide in Australia, said that he was surprised by the scale of the erosion from these rocks. "It beautifully supports ideas that the mountains that formed as the supercontinent Gondwana amalgamated were amongst the largest on Earth through deep time," he told Live Science in an email.

The formation of Gondwama produced one-fifth of the world's zircons, and the creation of the supercontinent Pangaea around 320 million years ago produced 14%, the study found.

Elias Rugen, a geochemist at the University of Southampton in the U.K. who wasn't involved in the research, was surprised by the "abundance of zircons associated with Gondwana's assembly in the Antarctica samples." "It is remarkable how much information about Antarctica's geological past can be recovered from these tiny minerals, particularly when so much of the continent remains hidden beneath ice," he said.

However, he cautioned against estimating the range's height from the zircon data. "It is really difficult to infer a mountain's height from data like this," he said.

An illustration of what the Pangea supercontinent would have looked like.

The formation and erosion of the Gondwana supermountains had consequences for the rest of the planet and the life on it, the authors said.

"In order to get life, you need nutrients," Campbell said. "At that time, most of the life was in the oceans, so you need to get nutrients into the ocean."

Today, the world's biggest ongoing erosion event is the Himalayas. This massive mountain range is eroding, and sending sediment down rivers and into the ocean. This deep-sea sediment deposit is called the Bengal Fan and is Earth's largest such deposit.

In a similar way, Gondwana's massive mountains also "sent lots of nutrients into the ocean," Campbell said, which "significantly advanced the evolution of life" on Earth.

Soon after the formation of Gondwana, the planet entered the Cambrian period. This era, which lasted from about 541 million to 485 million years ago, saw a dramatic diversification of life on Earth, known as the Cambrian explosion. The period saw the rise of creatures such as chordates (animals with a dorsal nerve, including humans) and arthropods (the ancestors of insects and crustaceans).

The study's authors drew a link between Gondwana's supermountains and this rapid evolution of complex life. While the supermountains don't explain the Cambrian Explosion directly, they "provide the opportunity for it to happen," Campbell said. The paper suggests that these nutrients fed organisms that formed the base of the animal food web.

However, Daczko and Rugen are skeptical. "The methods used in this study cannot directly demonstrate that this particular mountain belt was directly responsible for the rise in oxygen or the Cambrian Explosion," Rugen said. "However, the evidence for a Gondwanan supermountain belt that would inevitably have had a substantial impact on Earth's biogeochemical cycles is growing."

Daczko said he would frame the link between the Gondwana's supermountains and the Cambrian explosion as "an exciting hypothesis rather than an established causal relationship."

However, the study did show that there was much more to discover under the ice in Antarctica.

"The most exciting aspect is the possibility that some of the largest mountain systems in Earth's history are effectively hidden beneath the East Antarctic ice sheet," Daczko said. "Antarctica potentially holds some of the most important remaining evidence for understanding the tectonic and environmental evolution of our planet."

#6242. Motion under the ocean explains the depth of the world’s deepest spot

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

A tight bend in the subducting Pacific plate may help explain Challenger Deep

The ROV Jason/Medea (Jason shown here during a 2021 dive at the East Pacific Rise) can descend up to 6,500 meters below the ocean surface. In a new study, it helped researchers discover volcanic deposits in the Mariana Trench.

D. Fornari, WHOI-SSSG, MISO Facility, NDSF Jason Team, NSF

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Challenger Deep is the deepest valley in the deepest trench in the ocean, plunging to roughly 11,000 meters below sea level.

Now, scientists have a new clue about how it got to be so … well, deep.

Challenger Deep is found within the Mariana Trench, a crescent-shaped gouge in the seafloor east of the Philippines in the Pacific Ocean. The trench is the scene of a slo-mo tectonic collision called a subduction zone: The Pacific plate is diving beneath the Mariana plate, bending downward as it sinks into the mantle, forming a steep trench on the ocean floor.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

All subduction zones are deep, but “it’s interesting why this is the deepest spot in the Earth’s ocean,” says geoscientist Robert Stern, an emeritus professor at the University of Texas at Dallas and a visiting researcher at the University of California, Los Angeles.

He and colleagues employed a remotely operated robot called ROV Jason/Medea to descend to more than 6,000 meters and explore the Mariana Trench seafloor around the edges of Challenger Deep. The rocks turned out to contain pyroclastic deposits, evidence of an erstwhile explosive volcanic eruption. Those deposits included platelike blocks that could indicate eruption pulses, and lobe-shaped rocks where the volcanic flows ended and quickly cooled.

These are the deepest pyroclastic deposits found on Earth, the scientists report November 23 in Frontiers in Earth Science.

How explosive an eruption is at Earth’s surface depends on the chemical makeup of the magma. When the molten rock contains a high proportion of volatile gases, including water vapor, those gases suddenly expand when the magma reaches the surface, producing a violent explosion.

Such explosive volcanism shouldn’t be possible in the deep sea; the pressure is too high for any escaping gases to expand, Stern says. Along with that mystery, the volcanic deposits were found unusually close to the trench, compared with what would be expected for a subduction zone.

Stern and his colleagues developed a hypothesis that incorporates these disparate pieces of evidence: The extreme depth of Challenger Deep, they say, may be at least partially due to an especially sharp bend in the Pacific Plate as it sinks into the mantle.

That tighter bend would explain why volcanism is happening closer to the subduction zone than usual. The classic subduction zone scenario is that the sinking plate heats up and melts partially as it descends; the magma rises through the overhanging plate and erupts, forming volcanic island arcs several hundred kilometers from the collision zone. Here, the volcanic deposits were just a hundred kilometers or so from the trench — which makes sense if the plate is dipping more steeply.

As for the pyroclastics, “we can’t answer if the eruptions were really explosive,” Stern says. But at those pressures, any gases such as water vapor contained in the magma wouldn’t be able to explosively expand as they would at the surface.

Instead, the pyroclastic rocks might have formed through a new version of deep-sea eruption, one in which water emerging from the magma is initially in a supercritical fluid state. That would minimize any explosive expansion during the eruption and could also produce fragmented, dense deposits like those seen by Jason/Medea.

The discovery of deep-sea pyroclastics is “surprising and unprecedented,” says William Chadwick, a geologist at Oregon State University in Newport. Challenger Deep may be the only place on Earth “with the ingredients to produce explosive volcanism in the super-deep ocean,” he says. “Imagining this happening is … pretty mind-boggling.”

A lot more work remains to be done to evaluate all of these new ideas, Stern says. “But a lot of things are now coming together.”

#6241. What keeps a woman’s egg cells viable for decades? Scientists uncover a clue to reproductive aging

Scientists have identified a protein in mouse egg cells that protects chromosome stability, offering new clues to age-related infertility.

Women are born with virtually all the egg cells they will ever have. Some of these cells remain in a suspended state for more than 40 years, gradually becoming more vulnerable to age-related damage.

But new research suggests they are far from dormant.

In mice, researchers have found a protein that works inside the egg the whole time, keeping the glue that holds each chromosome pair together from falling off too soon.

Take that protein away, and young mouse eggs start making the chromosome mistakes normally seen in old ones. Put it back, even late, and some of those mistakes stop.

Dr. Kei-ichiro Ishiguro, a professor at Chiba University in Japan, led the work with colleagues at Kumamoto University and the RIKEN Center for Biosystems Dynamics Research.

The protein is new to science, and the researchers named it OMC1.

In an interview with Earth.com, Dr. Ishiguro explained how the discovery challenges conventional thinking about the long resting period of egg cells.

“I think one of the most fascinating aspects of this discovery is that eggs are not simply waiting passively for decades,” he said.

“They appear to possess specialized molecular mechanisms that actively protect the integrity of their chromosomes throughout reproductive life.”

Before a baby girl is born, her future eggs copy their chromosomes and lock the copies together with a protein complex.

Biologists call that glue cohesin, and in eggs the key piece of it is a protein named REC8.

Then the eggs stop, mid-division, and stay stopped until ovulation. In mice that pause lasts months. In women it lasts decades.

The chromosome cohesion established before birth must be maintained throughout this long pause.

Over the years, however, cohesin gradually separates from chromosomes, increasing the risk of premature chromosome separation and abnormal chromosome numbers in egg cells.

The National Human Genome Research Institute calls that aneuploidy. It is a major cause of miscarriage and of conditions such as Down syndrome, and it grows more common as mothers age.

The team reasoned that any protector of egg chromosomes should be made only in eggs.

So they compared gene activity in fetal mouse eggs with gene activity in young male germ cells going through the same stage of division.

Of about 12,000 genes active in the eggs, 1,800 were switched on only in females.

One of them had been filed in a public database as a stretch of DNA that made no protein at all. It did make one.

The researchers named it oocyte-specific meiotic chromosome protein 1, OMC1 for short, and traced where it went.

OMC1 appeared on egg chromosomes a couple of days before birth, right where REC8 sits.

It stayed there through the whole pause and into the final divisions of the adult egg, and it did not show up in male germ cells.

Mice engineered without OMC1 looked healthy at first. Their ovaries held a seemingly normal supply of eggs, and young females had litters. But their eggs carried less REC8 on their chromosomes.

Litter sizes fell faster than in normal mice, and almost no pups were born after the mothers passed 30 weeks of age.

When the team fertilized eggs from 8-week-old mice in a dish, 80% of normal embryos reached the blastocyst stage, an early stage of embryonic development that precedes implantation in the uterus.

In contrast, only 35% of embryos from eggs lacking OMC1 reached the blastocyst stage.

Inside those young eggs, the two copies of each chromosome were coming apart ahead of schedule, the same defect that builds up in naturally aged eggs.

By 35 weeks, chromosome pairs in the OMC1-free eggs were separating even earlier, during the first division.

“What surprised us most was that restoring OMC1 in mouse oocytes could substantially suppress premature chromosome separation, even after the oocytes had already developed without OMC1,” Dr. Ishiguro told Earth.com.

The team injected the genetic instructions for OMC1 into adult eggs that had grown up without it, just as those eggs resumed dividing.

More REC8 stayed on the chromosomes, and fewer eggs showed early separation. The fix was partial, which the researchers took to mean OMC1 does part of its job during the long pause and part at the end.

Dr. Ishiguro cautioned against interpreting these findings as evidence that egg aging can be reversed.

“Importantly, this does not mean that we can reverse egg aging or restore chromosome cohesion that has already been completely lost,” he said.

“Rather, our findings demonstrate that protecting the remaining cohesion machinery can improve chromosome stability.”

Humans carry a version of the same gene, called CCDC201.

A 2024 genetic study found that women carrying two copies of a variant that cuts the protein short reach menopause earlier, have fewer children, and have their last child younger.

“Interestingly, the human counterpart of OMC1, called CCDC201, has already been genetically linked to primary ovarian insufficiency (POI), a condition associated with premature loss of ovarian function,” Dr. Ishiguro told Earth.com.

The team built the mouse equivalent of that broken human version. It couldn’t attach to chromosomes, and it couldn’t rescue eggs lacking OMC1.

The experiments were conducted entirely in mice, whose egg cells remain in a suspended state for months rather than decades.

No human egg cells were examined, and the researchers have not established whether OMC1 performs the same protective function in humans.

“An important next step is to understand whether OMC1 performs the same protective function in human oocytes,” Dr. Ishiguro told Earth.com.

He also hopes to determine exactly how OMC1 maintains chromosome stability and whether variations in the protein help explain why some women remain fertile longer than others.

“Although our findings are still at the basic research stage, understanding how OMC1 protects chromosomes may eventually open new avenues for preserving egg quality and developing treatments for age-related infertility.”

For now, whether this chromosome-protecting protein plays a similar role in human reproductive aging remains unknown.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Aging.

Scientists have discovered the earliest-known quasar lurking in the ancient universe — and it's growing at a slower rate than scientists believed possible.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A Euclid space telescope image of the newfound quasar (red dot in the center), which is further away than any known active galactic nucleus found yet.

Astronomers have just discovered the earliest-known quasar — and it's 40 million years older than the previous record holder. The finding, which observed the object at just 630 million years after the Big Bang, could help researchers to better understand how black holes developed in the early universe.

"Finding quasars at ever-increasing distances, at the edge of the observable universe, teaches us something about how the black holes in their centres grew," study co-author Julien Wolf, a researcher at the Max Planck Institute for Astronomy, said in a statement. "The closer to the Big Bang we find them, the faster their black holes must have grown or the more massive they must have been at birth — or both."

The object — estimated to have the mass of 360 million suns — was described in a new study published Tuesday (Nov. 24) in the journal Astronomy and Astrophysics.

A quasar, short for "quasi-stellar radio source," is an incredibly bright core at the center of some galaxies — a region known as the active galactic nucleus (AGN). They form when supermassive black holes, which lurk at the hearts of most galaxies, start to binge on nearby matter. Once enough swirling material accumulates around these black holes, it heats up and glows intensely before falling into the object. What sets quasars apart from other AGNs is their sheer luminosity; they can be brighter than all the stars in a galaxy combined.

Quasars were much more common early in the universe than they are today. They are thought to have peaked in number about 10 billion years ago. Observing them can give scientists important clues as to how galaxies evolve — and how their supermassive black holes develop.

The quasar was discovered during the Euclid Wide Survey's scan of the sky — marked here in light yellow. Dark yellow patches show the target areas of Euclid's Deep Survey, which will repeatedly view smaller parts of the sky.

Because it takes time for light to travel, observing celestial objects that are very far away is tantamount to peering back in time. We see galaxies very near to Earth as they were only a few thousand years ago; conversely, we see galaxies very far away from us as they were billions of years ago, because their light is only now reaching our telescopes. The older the galaxy, the more red its light becomes as it stretches across the universe — a phenomenon called "redshift."

Using data from NASA's James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) and the European Space Agency's Euclid Wide Survey, the researchers behind the new study identified a quasar with a redshift of 8.13 — the first such object ever found with a redshift beyond 8. This makes it the oldest quasar yet observed, at approximately 13.1 billion years old. For reference, the universe itself is thought to be 13.8 billion years old.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The scientists named the object Dún Aonghasa, after a prehistoric cliff fort on the Atlantic-facing edge of Inis Mór, an island off the coast of Ireland. The name is meant to reflect the quasar's position at the very edge of our current observational frontier for the cosmos.

According to the researchers, Dún Aonghasa also appears to be growing more slowly than astronomers previously thought possible, given its size. This suggests that its supermassive black hole may have gone through a massive growth spurt, followed by a period of much slower growth in the distant past. The discovery could put new constraints on black hole growth models, which are already being challenged by previous JWST detections of supermassive monsters that seem to have grown too big for their early place in cosmic history.

Future observations from Euclid and JWST could help researchers test this hypothesis and see if it holds for other ancient quasars, the researchers said.
