#6238. ‘Mitt & Ted’ recounts how a political odd couple changed U.S. health care

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The Big Dig podcast host Ian Coss explores how Mitt Romney and Ted Kennedy worked together to reform American health care laws

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

In 1973, U.S. Senator Ted Kennedy often visited the cancer ward at Boston Children’s Hospital, where his eldest son was battling osteosarcoma. Kennedy witnessed other parents on the ward make impossible decisions regarding their child’s care when insurance didn’t cover it. Their stories lit a fire within the senator that burned bright for the rest of his life.

Kennedy spent decades fighting for health care reform, representing his home state of Massachusetts. He even teamed up with a former political rival from across the aisle: Mitt Romney. The story of this unexpected alliance is recounted in Mitt & Ted, the newest season of the GBH News podcast The Big Dig. Over eight episodes, journalist and host Ian Coss explores how their work laid the foundation for the Affordable Care Act, one of the most significant and divisive health care reforms in U.S. history.

We first meet Romney as a young upstart Republican challenger vying to flip Kennedy’s Senate seat in 1994. The race seemed close until a legendary debate. Romney had Kennedy on the defensive until the sitting senator pivoted to the issue near and dear to his heart: health care.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

“Kennedy is the elder statesman, in command of the issue,” Coss says. “Romney is like an eager student trying to pass the test.” Using his deep knowledge, Kennedy buries the less experienced Romney. In the election, Kennedy then beat Romney by a landslide, even when many Democrats were ousted by Republican challengers that same year. But the loss may have motivated Romney to keep going.

Several years later, Romney unexpectedly became a champion of health care reform as the newly elected governor of Massachusetts. The state’s health care system was facing the potential loss of about a billion dollars in federal funding, threatening hospitals that served vulnerable populations. Romney’s administration created Romneycare, which was supported by three features: individual and employer mandates, affordable options for low-income people, and a health care exchange where people could compare plans from different providers.

With Senator Kennedy’s help, the groundbreaking law passed in 2006 and expanded health insurance coverage to 98 percent of Massachusetts’ population.

Romneycare gained national attention and kicked off years-long efforts to replicate it on the federal level. Finally, in 2010, President Obama signed the Affordable Care Act, or ACA. Modeled on Romneycare, the law (colloquially called Obamacare) adapted the reforms made in Massachusetts for all 50 states, a challenge since many states had larger shares of uninsured people than Massachusetts had even before Romneycare.

The Democrats in Congress also sought to include a government insurance plan in the reform, similar to Medicaid but available to more people. Republicans were wary of the ACA generally, but a government-provided insurance option was a line they wouldn’t cross. The ACA eventually passed without the public option, but by then the political winds had shifted. If there ever was a chance to secure bipartisan support for the law, it was gone by the time Democrats were willing to compromise on the public option. And as soon as the ACA became law, Republicans started fighting it.

The podcast traces an impressive number of political twists and turns on this health care reform journey. Though I got turned around a few times, I never fully lost the plot thanks to Coss’ well-placed reminders and takeaways.

Beyond the story of Romney and Kennedy, the podcast gives voice to many more people who made the ACA a reality: government workers who went from foes to allies who enlisted unlikely help from the conservative Heritage Foundation; longtime friends in the Massachusetts state legislature who were driven apart by the reform; a father who struggled to afford health care and how he advocated for reform with his church. I teared up more than once listening to the human stories behind these policy changes.

Overall, Mitt & Ted gave me new appreciation for why passing a reform is so difficult, despite how life-changing and life-saving access to health care can be. The series points to moments when stars aligned to make reform possible and suggests that more of those opportunities lie ahead.

“The work of American health care remains very much unfinished,” Coss says. “When the perfect alignment of frustration and opportunity arrives again, that might be what determines whether our leaders actually work together.”

Researchers knew that cholesterol and blood pressure are important for estimating stroke risk, but a new study suggests these should be measured far earlier in life.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Cardiovascular disease has long been linked to risk factors like high blood pressure and cholesterol — but a new study suggests that these factors, combined with proteins in the blood, could help forecast people's risk of heart attack and stroke decades in advance.

The new study, published Monday (Nov. 23) in the journal JAMA Network Open, took a broad view of the factors that spike the risk of stroke or heart attack. The researchers found that warning signs for these conditions can be seen in patients' health data up to 30 years before they happen.

The researchers say their work shows that some understudied biomarkers — measurable signals in the blood — could be useful tools in anticipating later conditions.

"We did know that there are some well-established risk factors that are related to heart disease, for example, blood pressure, cholesterol," said study co-author Dorien Kimenai, an epidemiologist at the University of Edinburgh. But "nobody really has looked at the patterns of these risk factors prior to when these people are getting cardiovascular events — not systematically."

For the new study, the scientists tracked data patterns from a diverse group of nearly 114,000 healthy people over 34 years. Their data spanned four long-term health studies conducted in the U.S., U.K., and Norway. At the end of the study period, the researchers divided data from participants who were still healthy at that juncture from those who had experienced heart attacks or strokes and either died or survived the events.

But even at the study's outset, these two groups' blood pressure and cholesterol data showed a clear divergence.

"We did see that, even three decades before, already, that these patterns were different," said Kimenai. That suggests, she added, that the difference between the two groups likely began even earlier than that.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The team also divided their participants by sex and age, finding that men and women experienced different trajectories in their cardiovascular disease risk over time. Women, on average, started with lower blood pressure than men in middle age, but that switched later in life.

"It shows that the age effect is as important as the sex differences," Kimenai said. In short, both factors need to be taken into account.

Dr. Sintip Pattanakuhar, a clinician scientist at the University of Strathclyde in Scotland who was not involved in the study, said that while these risk factors can't be modified in the way blood pressure or cholesterol can, age and sex could be incorporated into personalized screening programs for cardiovascular risk.

During a stroke, the brain's blood supply is blocked or a blood vessel bleeds inside the organ. This reduces the blood and oxygen supply in certain parts of the brain, driving tissue damage and death.

The team also looked at the trajectories of biomarker proteins that circulate in the bloodstream and are linked to cardiovascular disease. These include cardiac troponin and N-terminal pro B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP), which are released by damaged heart muscle tissue and used to diagnose a heart attack. They also included C-reactive protein, a liver-borne molecule that signals rising inflammation in the body.

Differences in cardiac troponin and C-reactive protein were visible in people who would go on to have a heart attack or stroke up to 30 years before they happened. For NT-proBNP, the differences emerged about 10 years before.

That said, Kimenai cautioned that the biomarker data came from fewer participants than the full study cohort, so these results bear further confirmation.

Dr. Deepak Bhatt, director of the Mount Sinai Fuster Heart Hospital in New York, said the study's blood pressure and cholesterol data confirmed what cardiologists had long suspected about these risk factors: that these modifiable factors predict cardiovascular disease. Bhatt, who was not involved in the study, added that the biomarker data in this study built on other studies that have also shown that cardiovascular events can be predicted years before they happen.

"What this adds is that it's actually predicting events decades before," he said.

The study's clearest message was that people should get their cardiovascular risk factors checked early, Kimenai said.

"When you're 40 years old, get your risk assessments and your blood pressure measured," she said. "Because these are the things you can change. If you've then been identified as having hypertension, then you can get those drugs that are very effective and safe and efficient to alter the pattern."

However, while the value of checking blood pressure and cholesterol is well established, Kimenai and Bhatt agreed that the clinical value of the biomarker data was less clear at this stage. Bhatt said that he might advise a patient with high blood pressure to start medication and cut out salt, for example, but the way forward for someone with an elevated biomarker reading is less clear for now.

"Ideally, more work will be done" to see whether panels of biomarkers, perhaps combined with tools that measure genetic risk, could flag patients at very high risk of having heart attacks and strokes and should be treated differently than a patient with lower risk, Bhatt suggested. "That's sort of the missing piece of the Holy Grail of prevention."

#6232. The notion of ‘positive masculinity’ is dividing the male studies field

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Researchers’ debate shapes how mental health experts advise men

Does “positive masculinity” exist or reinforce sexist gender norms? Researchers grappling with that question say the answer will help determine how doctors and therapists treat men.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Ryon McDermott set out seven years ago to create a new scale measuring masculinity. McDermott, along with other researchers studying male psyches, was tired of the field’s long-standing assertion that the manlier the man, the worse his outcomes. It was high time to measure masculinity in a positive light.

For almost half a century, the many social science scales that measure gender or masculinity have consistently shown that rigid fealty to Western masculine norms — such as prioritizing work, power-seeking and status — link with poor mental and physical health. Endorsement of such norms also correlates with misogynistic beliefs and violent behaviors, including sexual violence, studies have shown.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

But giving men a talking-to about their many defects rarely lands well. Nor does that negative focus help men thrive. But what approach would help? “We don’t really have a definition of men’s health. If we don’t know what we are going towards, how can we even do this [research]?” says Matt Englar-Carlson, a counseling expert at California State University, Fullerton.

What traits, the researchers wondered, define a healthy man? And could a healthy reframing of manhood improve men’s outcomes, such as by getting them to the doctor or lowering their high rates of social isolation, depression and even death by suicide?

Those questions would cleave the field, though as fights go, this one has been downright nice. McDermott, a psychologist of masculinity at the University of South Alabama in Mobile, would ultimately question positive masculinity’s very existence. Meanwhile, his friends and collaborators at Movember — a nonprofit research organization based in Richmond, Australia that encourages mustache-growing in November to spark conversations around men’s health issues — are poised for a 2027 launch of the Healthy Manhood Index. That scale uses a positive framing and is designed to gauge men’s strengths, while illuminating areas for improvement.

The first gender measurement scale emerged almost a century ago. It positioned femininity and masculinity at opposite poles, with researchers assuming that the most gender-conforming men and women were the healthiest.

That thinking has since unraveled. As women began smashing gender barriers, by doing everything from donning pants to entering the workforce, penalties for women acting more masculine largely disappeared.

Inspired by the feminist movement, researchers began studying the masculine psyche. Yet they largely framed masculinity as a barrier to health. The Male Role Norms Inventory, one of the most popular masculinity scales in use today, exemplifies that focus. Individuals rank statements like: “A man must stand on his own two feet and never depend on other people to help him do things.”

The higher the score on that and more than 60 similar statements appearing in popular masculinity scales used over the past 50 or so years, the worse men’s outcomes, McDermott and his colleagues at Movember reported in July in Men and Masculinities. “Manlier” men often struggle with depression and substance use and engage in sexual aggression. They also tend to avoid asking for help or taking precautionary health measures, such as wearing a mask during the COVID-19 pandemic.

But almost 80 percent of the statements used frame masculinity as a problem to be solved, the team found. That deficit lens biases the findings, argues coauthor and social psychologist Peter Fisher of the Movember Institute of Men’s Health, the organization’s research arm. “If the only tools you have available to you are looking for deficits, you will find deficits,” says Fisher, who is based in Santa Monica, Calif.

That negative framing has also seeped into public discourse, so much so that some people now intuitively link “masculinity” with the word “toxic.”

Yet those most macho of men are the outliers, the small percentage who score highest on masculinity scales, Englar-Carlson says. He suspects that what really matters for health is flexibility around when to behave in certain ways. Stoicism, a typically masculine-coded trait, can be calming in emergencies but scary when a man experiences a mental health crisis and refuses help.

Englar-Carlson and psychologist Mark Kiselica, of Penn State University, Harrisburg, developed the Positive Psychology Positive Masculinity, or PPPM, paradigm in 2010. Public health experts, therapists and others should focus on men’s strengths not deficits, they argued.

The ideas in PPPM are what McDermott began trying to turn into a masculinity scale a few years later. But his efforts sent him into a tailspin.

He and his colleagues began by identifying positive traits that people linked more with men than women. The team generated a list of 79 possible positive male attributes based on findings from focus groups and studies of positive masculinity and positive psychology, such as “having a good sense of humor,” “serving country or community” and “having passion for one’s work.” More than 1,000 individuals then rated those attributes on a scale from 1 for “strongly disagree” to 7 for “strongly agree” along three dimensions: positive, typically expected of men and typically expected of women.

Roughly 40 percent of the attributes, particularly those pertaining to protective behaviors and assertiveness, were seen as both positive and expected more of men than of women, McDermott and his colleagues reported in 2019 in Psychology of Men & Masculinities.

But the study also showed that both men and women scored above the midpoint on almost all the allegedly male attributes. That could mean the supposedly gendered attributes had little to do with gender. And for many measures, such as patience and having good hygiene, women scored higher than men. Could that mean that the study’s list was rebranding attributes from feminism as masculine? The idea didn’t sit well with McDermott.

Then, the team’s research took a dark turn. The researchers had respondents fill out both their new masculinity survey and a scale measuring sexist beliefs. That revealed that the more strongly respondents endorsed masculine ideals, the more likely they were to endorse sexist beliefs, the team’s unpublished work shows. Think about a statement like, “A good man should be strong,” McDermott says. For many people, that translates to “a good woman should be weak.”

“I’ve looked at this across three different samples [of people], and I find the same results each time,” McDermott says. “Whenever you define masculinity, you are inherently defining it against femininity.”

Most attributes are neither male nor female, but human, McDermott has come to believe. And gendering those universal traits merely reinforces sexist stereotypes. The work has left him gutted. “I really thought that there was such thing as positive masculinity,” he says. “But now I believe that it can never truly be positive.”

Fisher is well aware of McDermott’s journey. “He’s been trying to create a positive masculinity scale, or isolate the positive characteristics of masculinity, for a while,” Fisher says. “And he’s been struggling.”

Perhaps McDermott has set too high a bar, Fisher says. Rather than trying to identify and measure masculinity through beliefs, he says, why not focus on men’s actions?

So for the past several years, Fisher and colleagues have been doing just that. They have organized numerous focus groups and tested survey statements with some 12,000 individuals across six countries. Besides addressing the lack of age and cultural diversity used to create most masculinity scales currently in use, Fisher and his team hope that their scale will provide men with a blueprint for what constitutes healthy behavior.

Below are qualities Movember Institute of Men’s Health researchers are evaluating to develop a new masculinity scale. The items are preliminary and may not appear in the final version. The rows show counterproductive behaviors that result from pressures facing men, healthy responses and possible wording for survey statements the men would then rate.

All the statements in the Healthy Manhood Index start with “I” plus a verb, such as “I do,” “I talk” or “I check in,” Fisher says. For instance, men often feel pressure to restrict their emotions, so the healthy response would be for men to open up emotionally. The index might have men rate a statement like: “I share difficult things I’m going through with people I trust.” Crucially, the higher the score on the index, the healthier the man.

Fisher’s goal is to move men toward healthy behaviors without alienating them. “We just want to meet men where they are,” he says.

A debate that could easily become acrimonious has remained almost cloyingly friendly. McDermott refers to Fisher as “brilliant.” Fisher credits McDermott for “letting the data change his mind.”

Researchers in the field recognize that they share the same goals, says psychological researcher Michael Addis of Clark University in Worcester, Mass. They want men to be healthier and to treat others, including women and seemingly less masculine men, with respect. “The question is how do we do that? We either sell them on a new masculinity, or we say ‘…. masculinity is always going to be in some ways a box,’” he says.

Though discussions around how to frame masculinity can feel wonky, the stakes are real, Addis and psychiatrist and behavioral scientist Ethan Hoffmann of Stanford University wrote in 2024 in Psychology of Men & Masculinities.

Consider suicide. Men who strongly endorsed masculine norms were less likely than others to seek help for depression and more likely to die by suicide, researchers reported in 2025 in Psychiatry International.

Theoretically, public health campaigns aimed at men can help. But what form should they take? A positive masculinity campaign may recast a statement like, “real men never ask for help” to “real men know when it’s time to ask for help,” Addis and Hoffman write. But a campaign that rejects gender labels may roll out statements like: “Real men aren’t real: It’s a fiction that could cost you your life.”

Such postgender messaging may feel too abstract for the average guy, Fisher says. Convincing a 65-year-old man to stay on top of his prostate cancer appointments is hard enough without trying to shift his worldview.

McDermott counters that positive masculinity “makes the sex role stuff continue,” enshrining the idea that gender roles and hierarchies constitute a necessary organizing principle for societies.

Reconciliation may be possible, Addis says. Policy makers and public health experts could first rope men in with a more positive masculine approach. Then over time, they could help men question and relinquish gender norms. “I call it dancing with the devil,” or temporarily adopting the gendered approach as a means to a desired end, he says.

However the debate unfurls, researchers are writing their own script on how to fight like real men — or real people. “There’s a lot of men in the psychology of men [field] who have worked really hard to not let our egos get in the way of good work,” Addis says. “It’s sort of like practice what you preach.”

If you or someone you care about may be at risk of suicide, the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline offers free, 24/7 support, information and local resources from trained counselors. Call or text 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org.

#6230. The Sky Today on Thursday, November 26: Thanksgiving turkey in the sky

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

Celebrate Thanksgiving with a celestial turkey: The famous Orion Nebula (M42) is also playfully known as the Turkey Nebula because it looks to some like a turkey, particularly in deep astrophotos. But whether you’re a photographer or not, this bright deep-sky treat is easy to enjoy tonight while dinner digests.

By about 9 P.M. local time, Orion the Hunter has risen above the eastern horizon, his recognizable three-star belt standing in a vertical line. The lowest star in that line is Alnitak (Zeta [ζ] Orionis), and the Orion Nebula lies just 3.7° south-southwest of this star, to its lower right on the sky this evening. You might be able to spot its glow without optical aid, although the bright Moon nearby may make that difficult. Binoculars or any telescope will easily show it.

At 4th magnitude and spanning some 85’ by 60’, the Orion Nebula is a huge and bright star-forming region that sits roughly 1,350 light-years from Earth. In the brightest portion of the nebula lies a small grouping of young stars called the Trapezium Cluster. Take your time with this gorgeous sight, scanning around the region to pick out detail in the nebulosity. And if you are an astrophotographer, consider turning the view into a Thanksgiving memory to share for years to come.

Live Science spoke with astrophysicist Erin Macdonald about her role as a science adviser for 'Star Trek' and other Hollywood movies.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

From gravitational waves to time travel, science has always been at the heart of "Star Trek". While the franchise has never shied away from imagining the impossible, much of its appeal comes from making strange situations seem believable.

That's where the role of a science adviser comes in. It's not necessarily about making sure everything is scientifically accurate, but understanding the science well enough to know where creative liberties can be taken and how to make them come alive on screen.

Erin Macdonald knows this balance all-too-well. After studying general relativity and gravitational waves for her doctorate and spending years working at Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory (LIGO), Macdonald shifted gears and became a science advisor for six "Star Trek" series, including the "Discovery" franchise, as well as a variety of other television and film projects. Live Science spoke with Macdonald about how she brings the world of "Star Trek" to life, and her job's biggest pitfalls.

Erin Macdonald is an award-winning writer, science communicator, producer, and science advisor. She is most well-known for her advising work on 'Star Trek' and has played her own character across multiple iterations of the franchise. As a science communicator she has also appeared on NPR, BBC, CBS, and StarTalk Live.

KHC: How did you end up getting into the field of science advising?

EM: After I got my Ph.D. and did a little bit of research, I realized academia and that world just weren't really for me. So I went into engineering, but I really missed teaching and being able to engage with students. I was trying to find more opportunities to do public science communication. I'm a big sci-fi nerd, so I started going to sci-fi conventions and giving solo panels and workshops that were basically, "Here's the physics behind faster-than-light travel," and "Here's all the physics in 'Star Trek'."

This article is part of a series called "Science Behind the Camera" which focuses on the role of science advisors. From helping to create engaging stories to set design and script rewrites, these experts shape some of the most compelling narratives on screen.

Through that particular talk and just life happening, I met a lot of people on the convention circuit. I decided I wanted to go to L.A. I learned that science advising was a job, so I moved out there, still working as an engineer.

CBS and "Star Trek" got wind of my talks, and they invited me to give presentations at their official licensed "Star Trek" events. That's how I got on their radar. A couple of years later, we were in a world where there were a lot of 'Star Trek' shows being produced, and they were looking for a science adviser for "Star Trek: Discovery". [Editor's Note: "Star Trek: Discovery" ran for five seasons (65 episodes) from Sept. 2017, to May 2024 on CBS] That went well, and they brought me on as an in-house science adviser.

KHC: You've now advised on how many shows?

EM: Well, six "Star Trek" shows, but I'm starting to lose track of the films and other shows I've been called into for either one-off things or bigger jobs. It's been a great experience.

I think a lot of being successful in L.A. and Hollywood is that every job is an audition for your next job. You work on one show, everyone goes their separate ways and works on new shows, and if they know someone they might want to bring in, they'll give you a call. I've been very lucky in that regard.

KHC: What does the day-to-day look like for a science adviser?

EM: All the jobs I've done are different. When I get pulled in to talk to someone about a new project, it could be almost anything.

The biggest role, and the one I enjoy the most, is being brought in when a show is just getting off the ground and the writers' room is being established. They'll bring me in to sit in that writers' room and help contribute to the ideas and stories as they're being developed. If questions come up in real time, I can help answer them. That's the most ideal scenario for being a science adviser because you can get ahead of any issues as plots are starting to be developed.

A lot of the time, when you're doing something wild like that, I'll just say, "Great, don't explain it. Do your thing. Try not to science it."

But it can also look like being handed production scripts. Basically, they've gone through the whole process, they're nearing the point where they're going to start filming, and they're like, "Hey, can you check this for us?"

That can be a blessing and a curse because it's a little less work, but then you can't course-correct as much if there are big plot problems. You have to find a way to work with the story and try to get the science as accurate as possible. In that scenario, it can end up being, "Don't explain it. Take these lines out. You're getting yourself in trouble. Leave everything else."

The last kind of job, and one I've had a lot of colleagues do, is set design. They'll be brought in when they're building sets or doing post-production and want to make sure what's on screen looks science-y.

The best example I can give is someone writing all the equations on "The Big Bang Theory". All those whiteboards you see? That's a scientist coming in to write all of that.

Science advisors may help with set design, such as writing the equations on the whiteboards in CBS's popular show "The Big Bang Theory."

I worked on a show called "Good American Family" on Hulu. It's not a science show at all, but they had a kid who was really interested in physics. I went in and wrote all the equations and talked to the actor about how to say the things he was going to be saying.

The process can vary greatly. Even within "Star Trek", my relationship has been different from show to show. That's an exciting part of it, but I think people can see that it's a very varied position.

KHC: Out of all your 7 years of experience in science advising, is there a particular scene, moment, or script you're especially proud of?

EM: There are certainly ones that are really close to my heart. I'll give a couple of examples.

One was the season two finale of "Star Trek: Lower Decks." I wasn't brought in until season two, At the end, the showrunner was basically like, "Hey, I have this vision, but we need to build the 'Star Trek' science around it."

He just had a scene in his mind and wanted to build the story. We came up with this great story about an asteroid belt with a lot of charged particles that disrupted the [protective] shields. There was a lot of good technobabble in there, too. It was really fun. Watching that episode, it just feels like a really authentic "Star Trek" episode because of all the science in it. I'm really proud that I was able to contribute to that.

If you spend your time just criticizing the science in films and TV, this is not the job for you.

Another one that stands out to me is the musical episode of "Star Trek: Strange New Worlds". That was one of the first times the show was taking one of these big swings. The show is kind of known for doing all these big swings now, but that was one of the first. A lot of the time, when you're doing something wild like that, I'll just say, "Great, don't explain it. Do your thing. Try not to science it."

But they pushed back on me and said, "No, no, no. We need a science explanation."

We really worked together and came up with a detailed science explanation. What I'm really proud of is that they created that ready room scene [Editor's note: a ready room scene is a dramatic sequence set usually in a command office before a major battle or mission] where Spock explains everything that's happening. It's probably one of the longest ready room scenes we've had in "Star Trek". It's like, "And then this, and then this, and this is why, and this is why, and this is why, and this is what we need to do."

It's goofy, but there was a lot of science put into that episode, which was a really fun process.

KHC: I would be remiss if I didn't bring up the creation of Dr. Erin. How did that character come about, and how have you felt about the impact of the character?

EM: It's really funny. The character of Dr. Erin has now shown up in multiple series, video games, and comic books, which delights me.

Macdonald's influence as a science adviser resulted in the creation of the character Dr. Erin, based on Macdonald herself.

The origin of it started on "Star Trek: Prodigy". It was a "Star Trek" show aimed at children. They wanted me to come in not just to help make sure the science was right, but also to do more traditional science communication and help create a character who was a kid who wanted to be a scientist and talk about what that process is like. That's the character of Rok-Tahk, and she's adorable.

As they were reaching the end of season one, the kids were going to Starfleet Academy, and the showrunners were like, "She has to meet Dr. Erin. She is who she is because of Erin." That was just one of the greatest honors. It was a quick, one-line mention, not even named in the episode.

KHC: Is there anything you wish you could change from your perspective?

EM: Yeah, there are a few that haunt me a little bit.

There are some shows where I was really involved, we meshed well together, and I helped with the story. There are very few things I would change. But then there are other shows where I'm just given the script at the 11th hour. Plot-wise, would I have suggested something different? Yes. But it was too late to course-correct.

One really good example was in "Star Trek: Discovery". They had an episode where they were trying to ride gravitational waves out of a nebula, as one does. They had that ready room explainer moment, and they were showing the gravitational waves as literal sine waves, like the ocean waves you think of. I was working with the visual effects team, and I pushed back. I said, "Really, these are compression waves." You could still make an argument that they were going to ride them out, but it's more like how sound waves move. They're compression waves.

To their credit, they animated that and put it in the scene. But as people were watching it, they felt that the way we were talking about it versus what we were seeing just wasn't working. It was pulling people out of the scene, so they had to revert back.

It was funny because when that aired, I had three or four former gravitational wave colleagues who were like, "Erin, you had one job."

Gravitational waves are compression waves, like sound waves, as opposed to sine waves.

Another quick example was an episode in season one of "Strange New Worlds" where Spock says, "We're being pulled into the black hole."

That's one of those moments where it's technically not correct. You fall into black holes. It's a very public misconception that I try to fight back against a lot. Black holes aren't hoovering things up. It's just deep gravity. But in the context of the scene, Spock is being very condescending and talking down to La'an, so he's simplifying the language for the public. I can sort of get away with that.

KHC: Is there anything else you think our readers should know about science advising?

EM: I meet a lot of people who, delicately or not, say, "I could do your job. I'd be a great science adviser." I think what's made me successful in science advising is that I take a very "yes, and" attitude.

I'm a fan first and foremost. If you spend your time just criticizing the science in films and TV, this is not the job for you. You need to work with the stories you're given, and you need to understand the mission.

There's a quick anecdote. I worked on another film called "Space Cadet," which is a stoner comedy on Amazon, and they were having a really hard time finding a science adviser because everyone was trashing the script. It's ridiculous, goofy, and fun. They were like, "Look, we just want someone who makes sure the NASA people know what NASA people would say. That's it."

The job isn't for everyone. Storytelling comes first.

Editor's note: This interview has been edited and shortened for length and clarity.

#6228. How to make friends at freshman orientation

A group of incoming members of Congress and staff arrive on Capitol Hill for new member orientation on Monday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

What happens when more than 100 members-elect descend on Capitol Hill a week after Election Day?

As Rep.-elect Dan Koh, D-Mass., put it, “It really is like high school — but it’s fun high school.”

Trainings and guest speakers aren’t everyone’s idea of a fun time, but Democrats are feeling good about this year’s new member orientation. Giddy, even.

The incoming freshmen will pose for a class photo on the House steps. They’ll test their luck in a lottery to see who lands the best office space. And everywhere they look, they see signs of the blue wave that swept over the country.

“I think — well, I hope — that we will be doing a lot of exceeding expectations in this caucus. The American people deserve it and expect it,” said Rep.-elect Sam Forstag, D-Mont., as he headed to lunch after an orientation session on Monday.

Forstag is the first Democratic congressman from Montana in 30 years, succeeding retiring GOP Rep. Ryan Zinke. A former smokejumper who parachuted into remote forests to put out wildfires, Forstag won by more than 3 points in a district President Donald Trump carried by double digits in 2024.

“I think there’s a lot of folks who didn’t expect us to,” he said of his win. “Nobody knew who we were this past December when I was still working at the smoke jumper base in Missoula.”

Democrats are still digesting their larger-than-expected wins, which saw them flip more than 40 House seats and oust a number of high-profile incumbents, including National Republican Congressional Committee Chairman Richard Hudson, R-N.C.

“It’s like drinking out of a firehose,” said Rep.-elect Rebecca Cooke, D-Wis., who unseated incumbent GOP Rep. Derrick Van Orden in Wisconsin’s 3rd District.

Cooke and her opponent clashed during the campaign over his use of AI-generated ads that she described as deepfakes. Now, they have to work together to make sure the transition goes smoothly.

“The congressman said that he’s willing to be helpful in that transition. I think it’s important that we make sure that the casework is transferred over, that constituent service is a priority, and that nothing falls through the cracks for people,” she said.

The 120th Congress will be full of history-makers, and a record-breaking number of women are set to serve in the House.

“This is a Congress with the most women ever to be a part of this chamber,” Cooke said. “And a lot of [Democrats], frankly, from the Midwest, and so I’m excited to build that sort of power from the Midwest to make sure that our interests are represented.”

The math isn’t lost on Republicans navigating a freshman class where they have fewer peers than they hoped.

“I thought that it would probably go a little bit different. I think a lot of people did, but it is what it is. You work with what we have,” said Rep.-elect Mark Lamb, R-Ariz.

But just like high school, everyone’s trying to make friends. As incoming members filed into the Capitol Visitor Center on Monday morning, Rep.-elect Cait Conley, D-N.Y., introduced herself to Rep.-elect Sydney Gruters, R-Fla.

Meanwhile, Rep.-elect Claire Valdez, D-N.Y., who describes herself as a “proud democratic socialist,” walked by chatting with Del.-elect Robert White, who will become only the third person in the modern era to hold the title of D.C.’s nonvoting delegate.

“I’m sitting next to a teacher right now; I’m sitting next to the mayor of Scranton … good, nice people,” said Rep.-elect Zack Mullock, D-N.J., who said he was surprised by how many “regular people” he was meeting among the incoming class.

Rep.-elect Brad Lander, D-N.Y., who ousted fellow Democrat Dan Goldman in a Brooklyn-based primary before cruising to victory in the general election, was also making friends.

“I was hanging out with Donavan McKinney yesterday in orientation, and I’m just really excited to meet all the amazing people. Micah Lasher, we were hanging out last night. Jacqui Irwin, so we’re just trying to get to know each other,” he said.

After arriving on Sunday with suitcases in hand, the future freshmen got a chance to set foot inside the House chamber later that day. Lander said he’d been there before to see Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, a friend of his, get sworn in four years ago. But Sunday was his first time on the floor itself.

“It’s obviously a lot different when it’s you,” he said.

Koh agreed, saying “everyone in that room, Republican or Democrat, had a lot of reverence for where they were.”

“I think it was just a good reminder about how despite all the division, that’s what we’re going to focus on — trying to figure out how to get things done for the American people,” he said.

Members-elect were trying their best to navigate their new workplace on Monday, many of them donning backpacks as they came to terms with the realities of their new job.

“We just have to get back to class,” said Rep.-elect Ed Gallrein, R-Ky., to a crowd of reporters trying to flag him down as he left orientation to use the restroom.

They’d have Italian food for lunch, after a session in the CVC auditorium where many of the future members typed notes on their laptops.

“They’ve got a packed agenda for us all week, really helping us figure out how to get started. Build our team, set course, understand where the bathrooms are — large and small. We got a lot to learn,” Lander said.

#6227. Nov. 26, 2018: Mars InSight lander touches down

InSight, short for Interior Exploration using Seismic Investigations, Geodesy, and Heat Transport, landed on Mars Nov. 26, 2018, tasked with a simple yet challenging mission: unlock the mysteries of Mars’ interior. Top priorities included uncovering Mars’ internal structure by measuring the thickness of the crust, obtaining the size and density of the core, and sussing out the structure and composition of Mars’ mantle.

In addition to bountiful seismic data, which included more than 1,300 marsquakes, InSight recorded about a year’s worth of weather data at the lander’s location with unprecedented accuracy, according to Bruce Banerdt, the mission’s principal investigator and principal research scientist. The InSight lander also took the first magnetic field measurements on the surface of Mars and measured several properties of the soil around it.

Not everything was a rousing success, however. Most famously, the mission’s “mole” subsurface probe only penetrated about 16 inches (40 centimeters) deep, despite being designed to burrow to a depth of at least 3 feet (10 meters). It turned out that the soil beneath InSight’s struts was unlike any previously encountered on the surface; it simply didn’t cooperate with the instrument’s design. But even that cloud has a silver lining, as it provided scientists with important details about the terrain upon which InSight landed.

InSight’s successful initial two-year mission was extended to run at least through the end of December 2022. But the stationary lander relied on power generated from its two large solar panels, which steadily gathered dust. That dust reduced the panels’ efficiency over time, forcing mission planners to make tough choices regarding power allotment. In May of 2022, engineers placed the craft’s robotic arm into a final resting pose and turned off all its instruments, save one: InSight’s seismometer continued to operate on what little power was available, running about half the time, according to Banerdt. InSight last contacted Earth Dec. 15, 2022, after which two attempts were made to raise the lander. Both failed, and a few days later, NASA officially brought the mission to a close.

Alison Klesman is senior editor of Astronomy magazine. She holds a Ph.D. in astronomy and has studied a variety of topics, from minor planets to supermassive black holes.

#6225. Math’s holy grail, the Riemann hypothesis, appears solved with AI’s help

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The proof apparently settles a 167-year-old question related to prime numbers

The Riemann hypothesis reveals a secret order hidden in the prime numbers.

ROBERT BROOK/Science Photo Library/Getty Images

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

A long-sought pinnacle of mathematics has apparently been reached. In a feat that will go down in mathematics history, a human working with AI appears to have solved the most famous puzzle in math, proving the Riemann hypothesis. The problem has foiled repeated and valiant attempts at solution for more than a century.

Now, mathematicians are working to understand the proof, posted by Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, on November 20. The Riemann hypothesis, if true, reveals the secrets of prime numbers. In a statement on his website, Alpöge said he’d developed the proof alongside Anthropic’s AI tool Claude.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

By the next day, independent mathematicians had confirmed the result. “We have full confidence that Alpöge’s proof of the Riemann hypothesis is correct, and we congratulate him on this achievement,” read a joint statement from Lean Focused Research Organization and Mathlib Initiative.

A proof of the Riemann hypothesis is one of the most sought after achievements in mathematics. “As a mathematical landmark, it really doesn’t get bigger than this. I can’t think of a theorem proven not only in my lifetime, maybe in the history of mathematics that is as important as this,” says mathematician Ken Ono of Axiom Math and the University of Virginia in Charlottesville.

“It’s an historic achievement,” says Bryna Kra, a mathematician at Northwestern University in Evanston, Ill.

Importantly, this was not the work of AI alone, Kra says. First of all, Claude had been trained on the work of thousands of human mathematicians, plus Alpöge was an experienced mathematician himself. He did not just ask for the proof then “push a button and wait,” Kra says.

Over six weeks, he worked back and forth with Claude. As an AI agent, Claude can use outside tools to perform tasks. The precise version of Claude that Alpöge used has not been disclosed, but the AI checked its work using Lean, software that converts mathematical arguments into code in order to confirm that a chain of logic holds up. It also had access to Mathlib, a library of known arguments already converted into Lean.

The result is 250,000 pages of dense, complex math. The world’s mathematicians are still working to translate the proof into a form people can understand. “What’s amazing about this proof is that it involves so many different areas of mathematics,” Ono says. “And I don’t know how a single human being could hold all of the ideas in their mind.”

The Riemann hypothesis, which dates to 1859, is closely linked with prime numbers. Prime numbers seem to be sprinkled randomly along the number line, but the Riemann hypothesis reveals a hidden order. At play is a mathematical enigma called the Riemann zeta function. The zeros of this function — the values that, when plugged into the function, produce a zero — are closely related to prime numbers. The Riemann hypothesis says that certain zeros — of which there are an infinite number — all sit on a particular line on a graph. If that is true, it would reveal how many primes exist below a given number.

Because so much of mathematics involves prime numbers, many other mathematical statements rest on the correctness of the hypothesis. The new proof will have wide implications. “It’s an earthquake throughout mathematics,” Ono says.

Alpöge claims to have solved not only the Riemann hypothesis itself, but a more general form of it, called the generalized Riemann hypothesis, which extends the idea to related functions. Though he guided the AI, Alpöge wrote that “what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater … Claude far outpaced me near the finish line.”

AI has been steadily felling major problems of mathematics, and this is the biggest one yet. But according to cognitive scientist Gary Marcus of New York University, AI’s genius at math will not carry over to more open-ended types of problems in biology, business or robotics. “In short, it’s not at all obvious that whatever Alpöge did has the generality many people are hoping for,” he wrote in a Substack post.

And some mathematicians have pushed back against the dominance of AI, disputing the utility of proofs created with the technology. The Association for Human Mathematics wrote in a November 20 statement on their website that no human being can claim to be responsible for the Riemann hypothesis proof, and that no mathematician can “confirm with full certainty that the proof is correct.”

Kra has been critical of achievements where AI agents worked largely on their own, independent of human intervention. The recent solution, by OpenAI, to a puzzle about the Navier-Stokes equations that describe fluids came about that way. But Alpöge’s approach was different, Kra says. “There is someone to stand behind [the work],” she says. She just hopes that people don’t see this as an end to math. “I think that this is a beginning, this is opening up more questions than it answers. … I think we have to use our imagination and find what’s the next frontier.”

#6224. The closest exoplanets may host magnetic fields

In all the universe, Earth is the only planet known to have life. A big part of the reason life is possible here is our planet’s magnetic field. It acts like a shield, deflecting harmful energy from our Sun as well as cosmic rays from deep space that could otherwise erode Earth’s atmosphere and irradiate the surface, a death sentence for evolving life-forms.

But Earth is far from the only planet we know of. As of this writing, there are more than 6,300 confirmed exoplanets on the roster, with more added by the day. Scientists have discovered stars with as many planets as our own Sun hosts. In other systems, planets as big as Jupiter whip around their sun in only a few days’ time. Astronomers have even discovered planets that orbit multiple stars at once, and they recently caught a glimpse of a possible atmosphere around a rocky, Earth-sized world in its star’s habitable zone. But until 2026, they had no compelling evidence that any terrestrial exoplanets had magnetic fields of their own.

Because of their protective role, magnetic fields have major implications in the search for life beyond Earth. Astronomers have long suspected that part of the reason Mars now appears dead is that its magnetic field fizzled out billions of years ago. This let the solar wind strip the water and other volatile compounds from its atmosphere, leaving it cold and barren.

Beyond the solar system, in 2019 researchers reported “indirect detections of exoplanetary magnetic fields” in four hot Jupiters. Then, a 2021 study found a strong signature of a magnetic field around HAT-P-11 b, a Neptune-like planet. Two years later, a pair of studies detected possible signs of a magnetic field around YZ Ceti b — this time, a rocky, Earth-like planet roughly the same size as, and only a bit less massive than our own. But this find has not yet been confirmed.

In July 2026, a study published in Astronomy & Astrophysics found possible evidence of magnetic fields around two rocky exoplanets. Not just any exoplanets, either — Proxima Centauri b and d, the closest confirmed planets beyond our solar system, orbiting the red dwarf Proxima Centauri 4.2 light-years away.

Proxima b, roughly Earth’s mass and size, orbits every 11.1 days. Proxima d, likely a quarter to a third of our planet’s mass and 70% its size, orbits closer in with a period of 5.1 days. Because Proxima Centauri is smaller and less massive than our Sun, Proxima b is inside the habitable zone, where temperatures allow liquid surface water. A third planet, Proxima c, was tentatively detected in 2019 but is still unconfirmed. Astronomers don’t yet know if any of these worlds host atmospheres.

The new study, led by María Rosa Zapatero Osorio of the Centro de Astrobiología in Madrid, Spain, used 117 separate observations made with the Echelle SPectrograph for Rocky Exoplanets and Stable Spectroscopic Observations (ESPRESSO) instrument on the Very Large Telescope atop Cerro Paranal in Chile. The research followed up on previous studies conducted with ESPRESSO in 2020 and 2022, which focused on confirming the presence of planets around Proxima Centauri. Zapatero Osorio and her collaborators used the data to identify a peculiar correlation between the timing of flares emitted from Proxima Centauri and the orbital periods of its planets.

“We detected low-energy flares occurring with a characteristic period of about 5.1 days,” Zapatero Osorio says. “This is very close to Proxima d’s orbital period.” But flares did not occur during every orbit of Proxima d, so the team ran statistical analyses to determine whether the flares were preferentially occurring at particular phases of the planet’s orbit. They found strong statistical evidence “that the occurrence of the flares is not randomly distributed over the planet’s orbital period,” Zapatero Osorio says. “Instead, a significant number of flares tend to occur at particular times in Proxima d’s orbit.” This is a possible indication that Proxima d could be interacting magnetically with its parent star, which would be likely to happen if the planet has a strong magnetic field of its own.

Using a model adapted from the physics of solar flares, Zapatero Osorio’s team calculated that Proxima d could have a magnetic field anywhere from 8 to 230 gauss in strength, with the best median estimate limited to around 16 gauss. This is about 27 times more powerful than Earth’s magnetic field (0.6 gauss), which protects life on Earth from the worst of the Sun’s energy.

Their model assumes that the star and planet are magnetically connected, Zapatero Osorio says. Each sustains its own magnetic field, and these fields are interconnected. As a result of this connection, stress builds up on the stellar surface. From time to time, this stress is released in the form of low-energy flares, whose period is closely tied to the planet’s orbital period.

Although there was not as strong a correlation between Proxima b’s orbital period and the stellar flares, the team did find that Proxima b could also be interacting with the star, albeit in a lesser capacity. This suggests that although the finding is less sure, Proxima b may also sustain a magnetic field.

There are alternative explanations for the findings. One possibility is that there could be intrinsic, long-lived active regions on Proxima Centauri itself that account for the peculiar timing of the flares. Another explanation is that gravitational interactions between the planets and Proxima Centauri could induce disturbances on the star without requiring a strong planetary magnetosphere, although the team suggests this is less likely. It’s also possible that when Proxima’s stellar wind reaches the planets, it interacts with them in a way that mimics the effects of a planetary magnetic field without requiring one.

Like most red dwarfs, Proxima is a highly active star, regularly belching out intense flares that would be hazardous to any fledgling life-forms on the worlds in close orbit. Because Proxima is so close to Earth and has at least one rocky planet in its habitable zone, it makes a perfect testbed for studying how stellar flares could affect habitability around red dwarfs — the most common stars in the universe.

Astronomers looking for habitable worlds around these stars must contend with the likelihood that any planets would be effectively sterilized by the intense radiation in the flares constantly washing over them. Now, though, there is a glimmer of hope. If Proxima b and d do have magnetic fields, as this research suggests, they could act much like Earth’s own protective magnetic shield, deflecting enough harmful stellar radiation that life might just be able to take hold.

“Earth’s magnetic field plays an important role in protecting life and supporting human progress,” says Zapatero Osorio. “It shields our planet from the solar wind and energetic particles, and it has also played an important role in navigation.”

Unfortunately, Proxima d is so close to its host star that it is likely too hot to sustain life as we know it. Proxima b, however, lies within the habitable zone. “Based on the results of our study, both Proxima d and b may have magnetospheres capable of providing some protection against their host star’s activity,” Zapatero Osorio says.

The importance of this find goes deeper than simply a pair of neighboring planets. In the last few years, evidence has emerged that gas giant exoplanets similar to Jupiter and Saturn host magnetic fields. These are the easiest types of planets to detect and study, but while magnetic fields around such worlds are certainly fascinating, the implications for planetary habitability are limited.

But as the number of known planets continues to swell, so, too, does our sample of Earth-like worlds. And if the two closest rocky planets beyond our solar system do indeed have magnetic fields, then perhaps these features are common. If true, it increases the chances that rocky worlds across the galaxy could be habitable — at least, for life-forms as we understand them. And the more planets capable of hosting life, the more likely it is that we might someday discover we are not alone.

Nick Oakes is a science writer for NASA’s Heliophysics Education Activation Team at Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland.

#6223. Redistricting battle could spill into 2028

Maryland Gov. Wes Moore, here at the Capitol in January, wants to see his state's congressional map redrawn. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

The redistricting fights that underscored this year’s battle for the House could continue into the 2028 election cycle, although lessons from last Tuesday will likely shape those efforts.

House Republicans had hoped that new congressional maps in seven states would help them limit losses in the face of an unfavorable political environment. But nearly a week after the election, the GOP appeared on track to flip just three redrawn seats while losing a host of seats in Texas, Florida, North Carolina, Ohio and Alabama that were reconfigured in their favor.

“The question is whether the results have let some air out of the [redistricting] balloon or not,” said Erik Nisbet, a professor at Northwestern University’s School of Communication.

Republicans may question the utility of redrawing more state maps in the 2028 cycle, while Democrats will need to weigh how to spend their political capital. But the new lines approved over the past year could still prove more favorable for Republicans in future elections.

“This was a wave election, and there’s no guarantee that the Democratic generic ballot would be D+13 — which is the reason why redistricting didn’t work for Republicans — in the next cycle,” Nisbet added.

New maps appear possible, if not likely, in at least a few states. Maryland voters last week approved an amendment that would clear the way for new boundaries ahead of the 2028 elections. Democratic Gov. Wes Moore, who easily won a second term last week, said he hopes to see a new map, citing the threat of President Donald Trump continuing to push for friendlier lines in GOP-led states. Maryland Democrats could draw a map that would favor them in all eight of the state’s House seats, including the Eastern Shore district of Rep. Andy Harris, the state’s lone Republican in Congress.

Advocates for a new map in Wisconsin got a boost last week when Democrats flipped both the state House and state Senate, setting up a Democratic trifecta. Gov.-elect David Crowley said he would sign a bill redrawing the state’s congressional map if legislators sent one to his desk.

Republicans in recent years have had a lopsided edge in the congressional delegation for Wisconsin, a perennial battleground state. But Democrats flipped two House seats last week, with Rebecca Cooke and Mitchell Berman unseating GOP Reps. Derrick Van Orden and Bryan Steil, respectively, bringing the state delegation to an even 4-4.

Democrats could also look to redraw the lines in New York and Virginia. Earlier this year, voters in the commonwealth approved a new map that would have given Democrats up to four pickup opportunities, but the Virginia Supreme Court later struck it down on procedural grounds. Even without the new map, Democrats flipped two House seats in Virginia last week and came within 2 points of flipping a third.

Democrats in New York, meanwhile, took initial steps toward mid-decade redistricting earlier this year, but 2028 is the earliest they could hold elections under a new map.

On the Republican side, several states have been mentioned as candidates for new maps in 2028.

Officials in GOP-led Mississippi have held hearings this year on redistricting, which could target Democratic Rep. Bennie Thompson. Republicans are also aiming to redraw the state’s legislative lines ahead of next year’s off-year elections.

It’s not clear whether states that were unsuccessful in redrawing their district lines for 2026 will try again when their legislatures convene next year. Republicans in both South Carolina and Indiana fell short in their push to pass new maps and could decide to revisit the issue. But Democrats flipped a House seat in each state last week, and some Republican incumbents won reelection by narrower margins than usual. Still, Republicans maintained their legislative majorities in both states, though Democrats broke their supermajorities in the South Carolina and Indiana state houses.

An analysis by DecisionDeskHQ offers a potential warning sign for Republicans in the Palmetto and Hoosier states: Under the GOP-drawn maps that were not adopted for 2026, Democrats could have flipped even more seats last week.

Redistricting appears off the table in a handful of states where new maps for 2028 had once been considered possible.

Georgia’s outgoing Republican governor, Brian Kemp, said last week that he would not call a special session to address redistricting before the end of the year, after Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms was elected to succeed him.

There were no House flips in the Peach State in the midterm elections, though several Republicans won by closer-than-anticipated margins.

In New Jersey, Democratic Gov. Mikie Sherrill told the New Jersey Globe that she also did not “see a path forward for redistricting right now.”

Democrats flipped two House seats in the Garden State last week. Navy veteran Rebecca Bennett defeated Republican Rep. Thomas H. Kean Jr., while Cape May Mayor Zack Mullock scored a surprise win over GOP Rep. Jeff Van Drew.

With their new majorities in Washington, Democrats could propose legislation to ban partisan gerrymandering.

That’s something John Bisognano, the president of the National Democratic Redistricting Committee, anticipates happening, but he said Democrat-led states should be prepared to respond to new maps drawn in Republican-controlled ones.

“If they are going to continue to take those actions, Democrats in states across the country need to be prepared to respond, and we, of course, now have significantly more opportunities than we did before Tuesday to respond to those states,” he said.

We've found the stargazing deals worth your money this Black Friday at Amazon, including some of our favorite models that we've personally tried and tested.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Black Friday is here once again, and if you've been waiting for the prices to drop before buying your next telescope, smart telescope, binoculars or star projector — this could be the time to pull the trigger.

But as we all know by now, retailers use these sales as a sneaky way to inflate their prices before the sale starts, so in many instances, their "sale" price is actually the same as it was before they put the price up. So how can you be sure that the price you're seeing is truly a deal?

Well, we keep track of prices throughout the year, and use tools to check when they fluctuate. We know whether something is a genuine deal, and, crucially, whether the product is actually worth buying in the first place.

We've searched the web for the best genuine deals on the telescopes, smart telescopes, binoculars and star projectors that we have actually tested ourselves, so you can be confident you're actually saving money and not getting played by capitalism.

All prices correct as of Friday, November 27, 2026, 17:13 GMT

Telescopes give you breathtaking views of the moon and planets.

A great beginner telescope that the whole family can enjoy. This 4.5-inch Newtonian reflector comes with a 20mm eyepiece for scanning across the sky and a 10mm eyepiece for detailed views of the moon or spotting Saturn's rings.

The EQ mount requires a bit of tinkering, but it's a useful skill to have once you've figured it out, as it makes tracking objects across the sky easier than an Alt-Az mount.

This model usually retails for $319.99, so a $40 saving on a telescope of this quality is pretty good.

We've reviewed a smaller telescope in the AstroMaster range, the Celestron AstroMaster LT 70AZ, and our optics writer owns the Celestron AstroMaster 130EQ, which has a slightly larger aperture.

The Celestron StarSense Explorer range is great for anyone who wants to start stargazing but doesn't yet have any knowledge of the night sky, and this model in particular is a good option if you want to invest in something you can grow with.

The setup is a straightforward Alt-Azimuth mount, and you can use the smartphone dock to navigate your way around the sky with the guidance of the StarSense app.

It has a 5.1-inch (130mm) aperture and comes with 25mm and 10mm eyepieces, giving you beautiful views of the moon, Saturn's rings, Jupiter's cloud bands and wide views of some deep-sky objects like the Andromeda Galaxy and the Orion Nebula.

The price tends to fluctuate throughout the year, although on average it sits between $420 and $450. However, it's been the full $499.95 since September, so this price is definitely worth taking advantage of.

Read our full Celestron StarSense Explorer DX 130AZ review

Although it's very close in aperture to the StarSense DX 130AZ we listed above, the differences in optical design and focal length offer a different observing experience.

This model is the better choice if you want higher-magnification observations of the Moon and planets, thanks to its 1,250mm focal length. It also has a much shorter optical tube, so it's more compact and easier to transport. The Schmidt-Cassegrain design is more complex to manufacture than a Newtonian reflector, hence the difference in price between the two.

It was $579.99 throughout most of the year, rising to $589.99 in August, which it has been ever since.

Smart telescopes will locate, track and stack images for you, making astrophotography easier than ever.

Granted, it's not the biggest saving ever, and it isn't listed specifically as a Black Friday deal, but you can save $35 on the ZWO Seestar S30 Pro at Amazon. This is the cheapest we've seen it since its release, and it typically stays at the $699 RRP.

It's an incredible way to get into astrophotography, even for complete beginners. It's an all-in-one system that automatically locates, tracks and stacks images of stunning deep-space objects for you. It's compact and portable, with a quick and easy setup and produces beautiful 4K images.

The smallest and most affordable smart telescope on the market is now even more affordable (but still the same size).

It only produces 2K images, which is still plenty for sharing with friends and family or on social media. In practice, it just means you'll be more limited when it comes to cropping.

It's been $419 since August, and this Black Friday deal is the cheapest we've seen it since its release.

If you're a more advanced user and have been waiting to upgrade, this is one of the best chances you'll get. You can now save a whopping $1,000 on the Unistellar eVscope 2 right now.

It has an aperture of 114mm and a 450mm focal length, making it ideal for deep-sky imaging of even faint and small objects. And the electronic Nikon-produced eyepiece adds an immersive element to the experience, rather than viewing everything on your screen.

Read our full Unistellar eVscope 2 review

Another fantastic saving from Unistellar, and the Odyssey Pro doesn't have as much reach as the eVscope 2, meaning it works better on wider objects.

The Odyssey Pro has an 85mm aperture with a 320mm focal length, which is still plenty to get stunning views of galaxies and nebulas. It also has a Nikon eyepiece that shows you how your image is doing as it's stacking — which is beneficial if you're not connected to the app.

Vaonis describes the Vespera 3 as the "most affordable premium smart telescope on the market," and judging from its specs, we'd be inclined to agree.

It has a new apochromatic quadruplet design that eliminates chromatic aberration and field curvature across the entire frame, excellent clarity even under city skies, a massive 11 hours of battery life and built-in multi-night capture.

It has a 50mm aperture and 245mm focal length, with a native image resolution of 8.3MP, or up to 24MP with covalENS mosaic mode.

If you liked the sound of the Vespera 3 but wanted something a little more powerful, the Vespera Pro 2 is $500 off for Black Friday.

It offers a higher resolution of 12.5MP native and 50MP mosaic, has more internal storage (225GB vs 115GB), and comes with a carbon fiber tripod (as opposed to aluminum) and a hard case, which are perhaps more suited for traveling to dark skies.

We've been testing it out over the past few weeks and are incredibly impressed. The images we've taken of the moon, for example, are breathtaking. The Vespera Pro 2 is currently the highest resolution smart telescope on the market.

Big astronomy binoculars are more portable than a telescope, making them ideal for camping trips and spontaneous stargazing outings.

If you're looking for a pair of binoculars you can take anywhere, with excellent optical quality and edge-to-edge sharpness, the Celestron Regal ED 10x42 is an excellent investment.

The ED glass eliminates chromatic aberration, and it has field-flattening lenses to correct curvature, resulting in sharp, bright and detailed images with basically no defects. Perfect for observing the moon and stars with excellent clarity.

We have seen them cheaper at the start of the year, but over the summer they've been $379, so this price is worth taking advantage of.

Read our full Celestron Regal ED 10x42 review

If birdwatching is more your thing, the 8x42 variant is also in the Black Friday sale.

If the Regal ED is a little out of budget, the Nature DX ED range is an excellent, more affordable alternative that still offers great image quality.

This variant in particular is ideal for birdwatching, thanks to the 8x magnification, and the ED glass is ideal for following birds in flight. Plus, you can enjoy views of the moon and get a closer look at the stars.

We have reviewed the Celestron Nature DX ED 10x42 variant, although this model isn't included in the Black Friday deals.

Big astronomy binoculars are a must for any sky-lover, and the Celestron SkyMaster Pro ED 15x70 are perfect for getting detailed views of the moon, stars and even spotting Jupiter's moons.

They typically fluctuate between $279 and $309, and although they aren't currently listed as a Black Friday offer, the $25 you can apply at checkout makes them the same price as the variant without ED glass. Personally, we'd always buy the pair with ED glass.

Read our full Celestron SkyMaster Pro ED 15x70 review

With a massive 20x magnification and 80mm objective lenses, these are serious skywatching binoculars that provide stunning detail in the night sky. They're perfect for close-up views of the moon and stars, and you can also spot Jupiter's moons and some of the brighter deep-sky objects.

This is the cheapest we've seen them since June, and they tend to fluctuate between around $270 and $319.

Read our full Celestron SkyMaster Pro 20x80 review

The Pro ED version is also discounted, although not labelled as a Black Friday deal. There's a $30 coupon you can apply at checkout to get them down to $319.97.

The Pococo Galaxy Projector is one of our favorites, striking a nice balance between good-quality projections, a variety of available discs and a reasonable price — and no awful green laser stars.

It comes in a choice of three colors (white, black and a pink/blue ombre), all of which are now at the same low price. The price tends to fluctuate throughout the year, usually between $79 and $99, but this is the cheapest we've seen it.

It comes with the 'Westerlund2' galaxy disc and 'Diamond Stars' disc, and you can buy additional discs via their website.

Read our full Pococo Galaxy Projector review

If what you're looking for is more in the realm of "a pretty light", then this star projector is a good one to go for.

That said, it's still a pretty decent projector! It comes with 13 different discs, including the solar system, Earth, Moon, a black hole and various nebulas and galaxies. Not sure how relaxed we'd feel staring at a black hole in our bedroom without having some sort of existential crisis, but there are plenty of others to enjoy instead.

We've tried similar models, which we've enjoyed, and the reviews look really positive. Plus, no awful green laser stars.

One for the kids, here. This astronaut star projector doesn't produce realistic projections of the night sky, but it's a great way to get your kids to sleep and there's still a good amount of customization.

There are 8 different nebula effects to choose from, and you can adjust the brightness, rotation speed and breathing rate (this mimics the twinkling effect). It does have the dreaded green laser stars, but at this price, and considering it's for kids — we'll allow it.

In a similar fashion to the Pococo projector, this one works with slides to project realistic imagery into your home.

It comes with a Northern Hemisphere Chrome Star disc and has just three buttons on the unit itself to control it — no messing around with a remote control or app.

We noticed that the motor is almost completely silent, making it an excellent sleep aid, and it's rechargeable, so you aren't limited to keeping it near an outlet.

Black Friday technically starts at 00:00 AM on Friday, November 27, 2026, running all weekend until 23:59 on Monday, November 30, 2026, which is known as Cyber Monday. However, many retailers have been running early Black Friday deals for the past couple of weeks.

Pretty much all of them! We've sourced these deals from our trusted retailers, including Amazon, B&H Photo, Best Buy, Walmart and others.

We've done the legwork for you. We've checked the price history of all these deals to make sure you aren't being fooled, and we have personally tried and tested all the products we have recommended.
