#6202. The Sky Today on Saturday, November 28: Iapetus near Saturn

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

Saturn remains a bright naked-eye object all evening, setting around 2 A.M. local time. Around 8 P.M., you’ll find it high in the south, to the left of the Circlet of Pisces and above the body of Cetus the Whale.

Tonight and for the next few nights, Saturn’s strange, two-faced moon Iapetus is skimming north of the planet, making it easier to find. Now glowing at 11th magnitude, it is heading west toward a late December western elongation, when it will shine about a magnitude brighter but sit far from Saturn. Once you’ve got Saturn in your scope, look about 2’ northeast to land on Iapetus. Over the next few nights, it will move westward, reaching inferior conjunction and standing due north of the ringed world by the 30th.

If you can catch 11th-magnitude Iapetus, you’ll also see four brighter moons: 10th-magnitude Dione, Rhea, and Tethys closer to Saturn; and mid-8th-magnitude Titan, about 3’ to Saturn’s west. The latter is the planet’s largest and brightest moon, easy to spot in any size scope and often even binoculars. If you keep returning each night to track Iapetus, also keep an eye on Titan, which is moving eastward toward the planet and will pass south of Saturn on December 2. Dione, Rhea, and Tethys have smaller orbits and shorter periods, so they move visibly over the course of several hours, frequently swapping places and passing in front of or behind Saturn. For example, Dione disappears behind Saturn’s southwestern limb in an occultation around 12:20 A.M. EST on the 29th (still late on the 28th in time zones farther west).

Sunrise: 7:00 A.M.Sunset: 4:36 P.M.Moonrise: 9:10 P.M.Moonset: 11:09 A.M.Moon Phase: Waning gibbous (73%)*Times for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location.

Have you ever seen your shadow by planetlight? Venus reaches greatest brilliancy at 2 P.M. EST on November 29, shining at magnitude –4.9. Rising nearly three and a half hours before the Sun, Venus will be so bright that it could potentially cast a shadow if you’re in a location with particularly dark skies (Bortle 1 or 2).

Even without perfect viewing conditions, this morning star can’t be missed. By an hour before sunrise, Venus is roughly 25° high in the southeast, blazing just to the lower left of Spica, the brightest star in Virgo. Far to Venus’ lower left, closer to the ground, Mercury stands nearly 5° above the horizon, shining at magnitude –0.7.

Compare the two planets through a telescope. Venus is a 27%-lit crescent, but its disk stretches 40” across. Mercury, by comparison, is much smaller, just 6” across, but its phase is 82%. Now through the first week of December is the best time to catch the solar system’s smallest planet, as it remains bright but appears to sink toward the horizon day by day. By the 5th, Mercury will be less than 2° high an hour before sunrise, making viewing challenging both because of potential obstacles on the horizon as well as the more turbulent layer of air near the ground.

Alison Klesman is senior editor of Astronomy magazine. She holds a Ph.D. in astronomy and has studied a variety of topics, from minor planets to supermassive black holes.

#6201. Australia’s legless geckos evolved like snakes did

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Pygopods are one of the many legless lizard lineages, but they slither a unique evolutionary path

The sharp-snouted delma (Delma nasuta) (shown) lives in Australia’s arid interior. Like many other pygopod gecko species, the snakelike reptile has a tail that makes up most of its length.

Stu’s Images/Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 3.0)

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Australia’s limbless geckos look a lot like snakes. It turns out they’ve evolved like snakes too.

Snakes are technically a highly modified group of legless lizards. Dozens of other lizard lineages have independently lost their legs, too. But the legless pygopod geckos aren’t quite like their slithering nonsnake kin. Pygopods have dietary pickiness and physical diversity patterns that are more reminiscent of those found in snakes than in other legless lizards, researchers report in a preprint posted at bioRxiv.org on October 23.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The 50 recognized species of pygopod geckos are found throughout Australia and New Guinea. Pygopods range from a meter long to the size of half a cooked spaghetti noodle. They have odd tails, which in some species can be fantastically long, exceeding 400 percent of their less-than-1-centimeter-long bodies. Some use their tails like a spring to leap.

“They create a little sine wave and they shoot themselves up in the air, and they can do successive jumps,” says Ian Brennan, an evolutionary biologist at the Queensland Museum Kurilpa in Brisbane, Australia.

But not much else is known about them, Brennan says.

“They’re real oddballs,” he says, noting that geckos are typically thought of as skilled climbers on walls or glass surfaces. “[Pygopods are] a group that’s gone the exact opposite direction.”

As part of a large project tackling the genetics of Australia’s lizards and snakes, Brennan and his colleagues gathered data on pygopods’ genes, diet and physical features. They analyzed DNA from all 50 species of pygopod and generated an evolutionary tree. The team also put together data from the literature on the ratio of their body and tail lengths and compared this with a dataset of similar information on over 3,100 lizard and snake species.

As they evolved, snakes got longer by lengthening their bodies. Limbed lizards tend to get longer by lengthening their tails. The team found that pygopods have done both, an unusual strategy among legless lizards. This dual strategy resulted in some unexpected physical diversity in tail and body ratio.

Next, the team tackled diet, comparing between 1,738 lizard and snake species. Snakes as a group have a broad diet with lots of specialization, which might be partly why they’ve been so successful at diversifying into so many ecological roles in so many habitats, Brennan says. There are pythons that eat only large mammals and sea snakes that eat only fish eggs, for instance.

This pattern is rare in lizards. Most geckos eat insects such as beetles and cockroaches, Brennan says. This is especially true of the legless groups, which mostly gobble down whatever insects they happen to slither past.

But the team found that the wide variety in what pygopods as a group will eat is exceeded among reptiles only by monitor lizards and colubrid snakes, a hyperdiverse group of over 2,000 snake species. Within that broad dietary range, particular pygopods flirt with snakelike pickiness. Some pygopods chiefly hunt spiders and scorpions. Another group targets ants and termites. One predatory pygopod — the Lialis genus — gulps down other lizards snake-style.

Pygopods’ evolutionary history may provide hints about how this heightened diversity developed. The team’s findings suggest they split off from other geckos in Australia 50 million years ago — much more recently than when the first snakes evolved around 160 million years ago, but before any modern snake groups reached Australia. Brennan thinks pygopods filled the roles of small snakes on the continent for millions of years in isolation.

“Pygopods were probably on a trajectory to do something spectacular, like snakes,” says Brennan. “But then all of these [snake] groups showed up in Australia and filled into those niches.”

Sonal Singhal — an evolutionary biologist at California State University, Dominguez Hills in Carson — would like to see this study’s data combined with data on pygopods’ skull shape, their habitat use and how their bodies move.

“For example, Lialis can swallow prey whole because their jaws are so flexible and kinetic and their teeth hinge back and forth, allowing them to trap prey.”

For Brennan, a lesson from the findings is that lacking limbs need not be an evolutionary constraint. Both snakes and pygopods “have diversified to do really interesting things, either due to or in spite of being limbless,” he says.

I.G. Brennan et al. Pygopods are an exceptional radiation of snake-like geckos. bioRxiv. 2026. doi: 10.64898/2026.06.22.733657

#6200. Sexual harassment overhaul at a crossroads in the House

Chair Teresa Leger Fernández, D-N.M., conducts a news conference with members of the Democratic Women’s Caucus during a 2025 retreat in Leesburg, Va. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

The leaders of an effort to overhaul how the House deals with sexual misconduct hope their proposal will see action before the end of the 119th Congress, though they’re split on the odds.

Rep. Kat Cammack, R-Fla., chair of the Republican Women’s Caucus, said legislative text is done and is being looked at by the relevant committees.

“Yes, absolutely,” she said when asked if the package would get a vote this year. “We’re shopping it now with the different committees, House Admin and Ethics, and waiting on their final feedback, which we should have actually this week.”

Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández, chair of the Democratic Women’s Caucus, said she was still optimistic about getting it done, but stopped short of putting full faith in Republican leadership to get it over the finish line. The effort has been underway since May, when Cammack and Leger Fernández’s caucuses announced a partnership to propose changes after two members of the House resigned amid allegations of sexual misconduct.

Asked if she thought Speaker Mike Johnson would put the proposal on the floor during the busy lame-duck session, Leger Fernández laughed.

“Hopefully, that’s something that will happen, because you know the Republican Women’s Caucus had said they were optimistic before we left. I’m still optimistic,” she said.

The two groups have spent months holding dozens of meetings with staff, their own caucuses and male members of Congress, among others. Suggestions have included banning members of Congress from engaging in sexual relationships with any House staffer, not just those who work for them directly, and outlining penalties for violaters. Initially, the groups were expected to unveil their work by August recess, but that got pushed back as the House canceled weeks in session and as they cited a desire to get it right.

Cammack said she thinks Johnson “has been very sincere in his efforts on this.”

“That would be a tremendous disappointment” if he didn’t put it on the floor, she said when asked about the possibility. “I genuinely believe he cares about this issue.”

Leger Fernández said if it doesn’t get done by the end of the 119th Congress, she hopes some changes would be adopted under the rules package for the next Congress that Democrats bring forward in January. Such packages are typically adopted with party-line votes and give incoming majorities the chance to tweak how the House operates to their liking. While certain narrower proposals aimed at curbing sexual harassment could be written into House rules, others would need to pass both chambers and be enacted into law to take effect.

“We are going to move to make sure it is in the rules package, because we will be in charge next year,” Leger Fernández said. “But I would love for it to pass now, because that was a commitment that it be bipartisan.”

#6199. Nov. 28, 1659: Huygens draws Mars

In the fall of 1659, Christiaan Huygens observed the opposition of Mars, drawing what he saw. The result was the first drawings of the recognizable surface features of the Red Planet – an achievement that wouldn’t have been possible without the advances in telescope manufacturing that Huygens himself had undertaken. One drawing of Syrtis Major that Huygens produced on Nov. 28, 1659, was referred to by Percival Lowell in his book Mars as “the first drawing of the planet worthy of the name, for on it is the first identifiable feature ever made out by man on the surface of Mars.” Additionally, by tracking Syrtis Major over a period of weeks, Huygens was able to calculate Mars’ day – slightly longer than Earth’s – and the planet’s rotation around a north-south axis.

Elisa Neckar is senior production editor of Astronomy magazine, and the editor of the Today in the History of Astronomy feature on Astronomy.com.

Microsoft has doubled down on its Majorana 2 quantum computing platform despite pushback from the physics community, with DARPA researchers now set to evaluate the bold claims.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Microsoft scientists have doubled down on their controversial Majorana 2 quantum computing platform after encountering pushback for saying its "topological qubits" were powered by an enigmatic subatomic particle. In August of 2025, they said they would field a scalable, fault-tolerant quantum computer by 2033 — years ahead of schedule.

Now, after opening a new lab at the University of Maryland and partnering with the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA) to conduct hardware validation, Microsoft has moved up this timeline to 2029.

The company's confidence is based on research suggesting that Majorana 2 represents a generational breakthrough in quantum computing. Scientists first announced that they had created this new qubit in a study published in the journal Nature in February 2025. Then, they followed up by announcing the Majorana 2 platform in a preprint study published this past June.

If verified, the prototype quantum processor would give Microsoft a commanding lead in the race to build a fault-tolerant, universal quantum computer, given that scientists said it can maintain a quantum state for much longer than alternative platforms. But some experts in the quantum physics community dispute the company's claims, suggesting that the qubit modality is highly experimental and had never been demonstrated in a working quantum computer prior to Microsoft's 2025 announcement.

Microsoft started its quantum computing program in 2005 after mathematician Michael Freedman convinced company leadership that conventional quantum architectures would eventually hit a brick wall. He advocated for a radical new approach to quantum computing based on a mathematical concept known as topological quantum field theory (TQFT). TQFT is a branch of theoretical physics and mathematics in which physical observables do not depend on local geometry (such as distances, curvature or angles) of space-time but rather on global topology.

Essentially, in TQFT, local geometry can change without disrupting qubits because its topology remains invariant. This feature of the theory is very attractive to hardware developers because it could yield qubits that are extremely resilient to disturbances such as atmospheric noise and perturbation. By contrast, conventional modalities, such as superconducting qubits, are perturbed pretty easily.

Microsoft subsequently built the first Majorana platform, named after theoretical physicist Ettore Majorana —who in 1937 hypothesized the existence of particles that act as their own antiparticles — to explore the use of TQFT in quantum computing.

If Microsoft's internal data holds up against DARPA's scrutiny, Freedman's theoretical bet may finally be paying off. According to internal research, Majorana 2 creates qubits that last between 20 seconds and a minute. By contrast, conventional qubits tend to last only microseconds.

In 2018, a research team that included Microsoft research scientist Roman Lutchyn published a study in the journal Nature Reviews Materials in which they claimed to have observed compelling evidence of Majorana "zero modes" — ostensibly demonstrating the existence of the theoretical Majorana quasiparticle.

However, when the data was released to reviewers in 2019, several noteworthy physicists raised objections centered on allegations of data trimming, confirmation bias and the potential misidentification of trivial electrical noise as exotic physics. That study was retracted in 2021, after the authors conceded that some of their methodology may have been flawed.

In the new study from June, Microsoft's claims were even bolder. The new study’s authors wrote that they observed physics indicating qubits built with the Majorana platform could last "orders of magnitude longer than typical qubit operation times."

The study was received with skepticism by many of the same critics of the 2018 research paper. The most common criticism, based on those that have been published, is that Microsoft researchers didn't operate a working qubit but instead tracked how long an electron state sits undisturbed before a stray charge flips its parity. The critics noted that measuring an electron's parity state isn't analogous to measuring a qubit's reliability.

Alex Khan, vice president of quantum research and development at physics acceleration firm BQP and a fellow at the University of Maryland QLab, dismissed much of the ballyhoo surrounding the Majorana research papers, comparing nascent quantum computing efforts such as Microsoft's to the Wright brothers' early airplane trials: There were only a few people there, and the aircraft went just a short distance. "And you could have had a lot of people sitting there saying, 'You know, this is never going to really do anything’,'" Khan, who wasn't involved in the Majorana 2 research, told Live Science.

When it comes to quantum computing breakthroughs, he took a more utilitarian view. "I've used a lot of quantum computers, but in order for me to use a quantum computer, it needs to be available," he said. "My most important thing is, can I have access to the computer? What kind of algorithms can I run on it? What can I test or what can I benchmark? What kind of capability will this provide? And does it begin to show some of the quantum advantage that's coming out of the quantum computer versus a simulator?"

Determining whether Microsoft or its critics are correct isn't as simple as running the team's experiments on another system. Microsoft is building Majorana 2 from scratch, one engineering feat at a time, Zulfi Alam, corporate vice president of Azure Quantum at Microsoft, told Live Science in an interview.

"The secret sauce is that we build our devices atom by atom, and that reduces disorder dramatically," Alam said.

Despite the back-and-forth between Microsoft and its critics, the question of whether the company has leapfrogged its competitors on the journey to build fault-tolerant, useful machines remains.

But with the topological qubits, they might know how to read the topological state, but then the question is, what are they reading? Also, is it able to store quantum information? Is it able to build a quantum state?

The U.S. government might be able to validate Microsoft's claims. The company will be included in DARPA's Quantum Benchmarking Initiative, which seeks to determine whether it's possible to build an industrially useful quantum computer by 2033. From now until 2029, the government will evaluate Majorana and Microsoft’s timeline to establish a framework for testing quantum computing claims.

In support of this endeavor, Microsoft is building a quantum computing lab at the University of Maryland so DARPA researchers can conduct their own hands-on evaluation of the hardware.

Khan described the partnership as "exciting," adding that he hopes DARPA can help determine the system's capabilities. "The physics is already known now," he said. "But with the topological qubits, they might know how to read the topological state, but then the question is, what are they reading? Also, is it able to store quantum information? Is it able to build a quantum state?"

If DARPA validates the biggest Majorana 2 claims, not only will Microsoft be vindicated, but the QBI team will have demonstrated their capabilities at the furthest frontiers of quantum computing research.

Alam said Microsoft is looking forward to the challenge. He described the shift in focus from theoretical science to "productizing" results as a focusing mechanism. DARPA has a team of about 50 engineers who are looking at the results and operating the machine at the University of Maryland, he noted.

"We have this deliverable for DARPA, and every six months or so, we have these massive deliverable dumps that we are giving to them," Alam said. "They know everything about our program."

Essentially, Microsoft's claims indicate that Majorana 2 solves most of quantum computing's biggest bottlenecks.

Designing reliable qubits is often cited as quantum computing's greatest challenge — and to solve problems at the edges of cryptography, chemistry and physics, we'll need quantum computers capable of fielding millions of qubits.

The first bottleneck is hardware. Scaling current systems such as those developed by IBM, Google and other quantum hardware labs requires scaling infrastructure in lockstep. Superconducting and spin qubits, for example, both need dedicated analog microwave lines for each physical qubit. This equates to millions of physical cables per computer.

If Majorana 2 works as Microsoft scientists claim, the cable problem goes away because its qubits can be controlled digitally via an integrated processor core that needs only a few connecting wires.

The next bottleneck that Majorana 2 solves is the massive qubit counts required to conduct useful calculations. Majorana 2 purportedly produces exponentially more reliable qubits than other platforms do, which promises a dramatic reduction in the number of error-correcting qubits needed to run a stable quantum computing system.

As Alam put it: "Our own internal teams thought we would need 16 million qubits to look at Shor's algorithm.” This is in reference to a commonly used encryption algorithm that it’s believed would take a classical computer years to crack while a sufficiently powerful quantum system is hypothesized to reduce that time to months or even hours.

"Since then," he added, "we have been able to publicly refine our estimates and think that we need more like 600,000 to 400,000 qubits."

Joseph Kearney, chief strategy officer and post-quantum cryptographer at Quantum Future in the U.K. who was not involved in the research, said that, if verified, Microsoft's Majorana 2 would revolutionize the field of quantum computing and shorten the timelines for quantum advantage in complex fields of study by years.

"If Microsoft had genuinely solved error correction, the 2035 deadline would no longer be credible,” he told Live Science in an email. "A breakthrough of this kind would remove our warning period, the clock is already running. Data intercepted today can be decrypted in the future, and Microsoft's claims, if they hold, would bring that future considerably closer than most organizations have planned for."

#6196. Rep. Ken Calvert wins all-Republican race in California

California Rep. Ken Calvert walks down the House steps after votes on Sept. 3. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call)

Rep. Ken Calvert defeated Rep. Young Kim in a redrawn Southern California district that pitted the two Republicans against one another.

Calvert was leading his rival by 7 points Monday night when The Associated Press called the race for California’s 40th District with more than 70 percent of the vote in.

Calvert, who chairs the powerful House Defense Appropriations Subcommittee, is the longest-serving Republican in the California delegation, first winning election to Congress in 1992.

The race was reshaped by the Golden State’s new voter-approved House map, drawn by state Democrats in response to mid-decade redistricting by Texas Republicans. The new map dismantled Calvert’s 41st District in Riverside County, transforming it into a safely blue Democratic seat in the Los Angeles area. That prompted him to run for the redrawn 40th District, which included a sizable percentage of his current constituents.

The rare intraparty general election was possible because Calvert and Kim finished in the top two slots in the state’s June primary. Under the California system, all candidates run on the same primary ballot, with the top two vote-getters, regardless of party, advancing to November.

Calvert had already declared victory last week, saying on social media that there was “no greater honor than serving my neighbors and our communities in Congress.”

Kim’s defeat is the second of her congressional career — she lost her initial bid during the 2018 blue wave before winning election to the House two years later.

In her concession message, Kim singled out California Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom, who led the redistricting effort last year that targeted five Republican-held districts. Democrats flipped all five seats last week.

“It’s unfortunate that Gavin Newsom’s political redistricting scheme forced two Republican members from Congress into this race,’’ she said in a statement.

The race between was marked by rancor, with Calvert alleging that Kim was not a true conservative and supported higher taxes. Kim accused Calvert of growing rich off stock trades over his decades in Washington.

Calvert will serve in a delegation with a dramatically smaller GOP presence next year, with Democrats likely to hold 48 of California’s 52 House seats. Just two other California Republicans – Reps. Vince Fong and Tom McClintock – have been reelected so far, while a third, Rep. Jay Obernolte, narrowly leads his Democratic challenger in an as-yet-uncalled race.

The Calvert-Kim battle was not the only all-party November clash in California, with several districts featuring matchups between two Democrats.

One incumbent has already been unseated, with Rep. Jimmy Gomez losing to fellow Democrat Angela Gonzales-Torres in the Los Angeles-area 34th District, according to The Associated Press.

Two other blue-on-blue contests in Northern California remained uncalled as of Tuesday afternoon: Rep. Mike Thompson was trailing venture capitalist Eric Jones in the 4th District, while Rep. Doris Matsui led Sacramento City Councilmember Mai Vang in the 7th District.

#6195. A cosmically close supernova may spill the stellar explosion’s secrets

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Across the universe, stars explode every day — but this particular one is something special

Gemini South, a telescope in Chile operated by the U.S. National Science Foundation, captured this image of galaxy NGC 1433 and, within it, the new supernova (in bright blue) on November 9, 2026.

International Gemini Observatory/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

When astronomers first spotted the supernova now designated SN 2026ahvu, it was just one of the dozens detected every day. But scientists soon realized this one was something very special, and they’ve been hustling to study it ever since.

“I think almost everyone in the world is trying to trigger a telescope and look at this,” says astrophysicist Sumit Sarbadhicary of Johns Hopkins University.

Soon after scientists spotted the explosion on November 2, they determined it hadn’t yet peaked in brightness, giving scientists an early glimpse at the event. Even more thrilling, within a day of the explosion’s discovery, astronomers had classified it as a type Ia supernova. These particular outbursts are rare, but they’re astronomical superstars: Scientists use their trademark explosion pattern as a “standard candle” to measure distance into the universe — most notably to discover that the universe’s expansion is accelerating. And to round out a trifecta of reasons to be excited, these blasts rarely occur so close to Earth.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Astronomers know type 1a supernovas occur upon the reignition and resulting self-destruction of a white dwarf star, the small cool remnants of a star like the sun that’s too small to become a superdense neutron star or black hole at its demise. Scientists also know that powering back on requires reaching about 1.44 times the mass of the sun, which can occur only if something is giving the white dwarf extra mass.

But scientists aren’t sure what that something is — whether these supernovas are triggered by a second white dwarf or some sort of star that’s still burning. Usually, these explosions occur so far away that astronomers can’t get a good look at where they come from. But SN 2026ahvu is perhaps 50 million light-years or less away from Earth.

“They happen so rarely at this distance that it could hopefully help us figure out why this white dwarf exploded in the first place,” says astronomer Yvette Cendes of the University of Oregon in Eugene, who has been arranging for radio telescopes to observe the outburst.

Sarbadhicary and colleagues have already submitted preliminary findings November 6 at arXiv.org suggesting that the former white dwarf was less than 100 million years old. That’s remarkably young compared with other supernovas of this type, and may help scientists finetune their understanding of these outbursts.

“These explosions have been enduring mysteries for us for decades, and whenever something happens this close, it’s just really exciting,” Sarbadhicary says.

The James Webb Space Telescope has spotted a tiny, extremely red object in the infant universe. It may be one of the earliest black holes, but researchers can't yet rule out a very different explanation.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Astronomers using the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) have spotted a tiny, extremely red object that existed just 450 million years after the Big Bang.

The object, called CW-LRD-z10, may be a "little red dot" — a mysterious class of objects that many researchers think are black holes growing inside dense cocoons of gas. If confirmed, the newfound object would be the earliest known example, potentially offering a window into how these enigmatic objects form.

"Such an object would be one of the most distant accreting black holes known," Roberto Maiolino, professor of experimental astrophysics at the University of Cambridge, who was not involved in the study, told Live Science in an email. The object may provide further evidence that little red dots trace some of the earliest phases of supermassive black hole formation, he added.

The study was published Nov. 24 in the Astrophysical Journal Letters.

Little red dots, or LRDs, are a population of tiny, very red objects in the early universe. The farther away they are, the more their light is stretched to longer, redder wavelengths. (This phenomenon is called redshift).

LRDs were only recently discovered thanks to JWST. The space telescope's near-infrared camera could only capture objects out to a redshift of about 9, corresponding to a lookback time of about 13.1 billion years ago. So in 2025, the team behind the new study also used JWST's mid-infrared instrument (MIRI) to search for even more distant sources.

CW-LRD-z10 was the only candidate that the search turned up, the study’s first author Takumi Tanaka, a doctoral student at the University of Tokyo, told Live Science.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The James Webb telescope's view of the little red dot CW-LRD-z10

In the study, the team measured the redshift of this compact, red object. They found it to be 10.36, suggesting it emitted its light when the universe was just 450 million years old. They measured it using a sharp drop in its light, interpreted as a ‘Lyman-alpha break.’

The result looks solid in one key respect, according to Maiolino. "The continuum drop attributed to a [Lyman-alpha] break appears relatively convincing, so I would say that the redshift determination is reasonably robust," he said.

The strongest clue that this object is a little red dot is its color, which is much redder in the mid-infrared than in the near-infrared band. The spectrum (its signature of emitted light) also shows the "V-shaped" dip typical of little red dots, possible iron emission, and tentatively detected emission lines whose ratios resemble those in other little red dots and active black holes. None of these three factors is conclusive on its own, Tanaka said, but together they support the little red dot interpretation.

However, the spectrum does not show wide hydrogen lines, which are the telltale sign of a little red dot. This is because the region where these hydrogen lines can be found in the spectrum falls outside the wavelengths covered in the new study. Maiolino said that "at this stage, this should only be considered an LRD candidate."

Tanaka agrees that it is more appropriate to continue calling it a very promising little red dot candidate.

The object's spectrum could instead point to a Balmer break, a sharp drop produced by older stars at closer distances. When redshifted, this would suggest that the object is a much closer galaxy at a redshift of about 3, or about 11.4 billion light-years away.

Tanaka said the data doesn't support this interpretation, as the object's color is hard to explain for such a galaxy, and the emission lines expected at that distance were not seen. "The observed break feature is too strong to be explained by a normal Balmer break from a typical stellar population," he said.

The spectrum of the little red dot CW-LRD-z10, showing its likely composition

Alternatively, an ordinary star-forming galaxy at redshift 10.36 could in principle produce the extreme red color, but it would need an unusually strong signature spectral line. That line falls outside the current spectrum, so future observations should help test it.

CW-LRD-z10's light also shows possible emission features from iron, which are thought to be emitted from the gas close to actively feeding black holes such as in quasars, rather than ordinary star-forming galaxies. "If confirmed, this would support the presence of actively accreting black holes and suggest that gas containing heavy elements was already present in the environment of the possible black hole," Tanaka said.

The nature of little red dots is highly debated. One of the leading theories suggests they host accreting black holes wrapped in dense gas, while other theories involve supermassive stars, black hole stars, or dense star clusters. Because the true nature of the little red dots and their position in black hole evolution scenarios are still uncertain, Tanaka stressed they cannot draw firm conclusions about what CW-LRD-z10 could mean for how supermassive black holes first formed.

Maiolino said that if CW-LRD-z10 really hosts an accreting black hole, then its properties could hold important information about how the first supermassive black holes formed. "Hence, studying its properties could shed light on the different black hole seeding scenarios, he said."

JWST's mid-infrared instrument is scheduled to take a spectrum of the object in 2027. The observations are designed to detect hydrogen and oxygen emission lines as well as the underlying continuum, which should let the team separate a genuinely red glow from the effect of strong emission lines. "We’re really looking forward to seeing the data," Tanaka said.

M., Treister, E., Aravena, M., Harikane, Y., Trakhtenbrot, B., Inayoshi, K., Shimasaku, K., Franco, M., Fujimoto, S., Li, M., Umeda, H., Schindler, J., Inoue, A. K., Billand, J., Kakkad, D., Ding, X., . . . Zavala, J. (2026). EMBER: A Little Red Dot Candidate at z spec = 10.36 in the Seed Black Hole Era. #6192. Jim Jordan picked as new minority leader for House GOP

Rep. Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, center, arrives for a House Republican leadership candidate forum for the 120th Congress in the Capitol Visitor Center on Tuesday, with Rep. Celeste Maloy, R-Utah, walking alongside him. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

House Republicans on Tuesday opted for a new face atop their ranks, electing Rep. Jim Jordan as the incoming minority leader for the 120th Congress after Republicans suffered massive losses in last week’s midterm elections.

The Ohio Republican defeated outgoing Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., in a closed-door, secret-ballot election. The final tally was 106-73.

“Over the next two years, House Republicans will fight for American families. Democrats offer more government. We will offer more freedom,” Jordan said after the hourslong process.

The two had been working the phones before making their pitches during a candidates forum in the Capitol Visitor Center’s auditorium on Tuesday morning. Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., announced last week he would not seek a leadership post in the new Congress, which will be seated on Jan. 3.

“Obviously Jim and I know each other, but I’ve got a proven record of how to bring people together,” Scalise said ahead of the vote, trying to play up his experience, including more than a decade on the leadership team that included a stint as whip.

As House Republicans trickled out of the candidates’ forum for breaks or to take phone calls, one member, granted anonymity to discuss a private session, said Scalise and Jordan “both have strong points, but they both have flaws.” Each made an unsuccessful bid for speaker in 2023 after the ouster of Kevin McCarthy, before the gavel ultimately went to Johnson.

Declining to reveal which would get his vote, the member said: “I won’t talk about a secret vote, but I know who I think is best to lead us.”

The incoming minority conference also selected other leaders on Tuesday.

Majority Whip Tom Emmer of Minnesota held off a challenge from Texas Rep. August Pfluger to become minority whip in January, despite some grumbling about how tight votes were handled on the floor this year.

“We’ve got to retool our whip operation,” Texas Rep. Nathaniel Moran said Tuesday morning, pointing to “the number of times we were held up by either discharge petitions or failed rule votes.”

“Those were things that should not have happened in the majority,” said Moran as he publicly backed Pfluger for whip.

But Emmer projected confidence after his whip win, comparing the moment to when Republicans were down and out after their losses in 2018 only to rebound a few years later.

“To our colleagues on the left, enjoy this honeymoon phase, because come Jan. 3, 2027, you will regret ever putting your name on a ballot,” he said at a news conference, adding that Republicans under his watch would expose the “empty promises” that Democrats made to voters and push back on what he called their “radical” agenda.

In the day’s only three-way race, conference Chair Lisa McClain of Michigan defeated Reps. Erin Houchin of Indiana and Greg Steube of Florida to keep her spot.

“We had a spirited leadership election. There were important conversations about the future of our conference, and I listened,” McClain said at the news conference.

In the race to lead House Republicans’ campaign arm, Rep. Brian Jack of Georgia defeated Rep. Rudy Yakym of Indiana, seen as an up-and-coming Ways and Means Committee member. That means Jack will take on a huge share of the uphill task of selecting candidates and raising funds for the 2028 cycle as he helms the National Republican Congressional Committee.

But most of the attention heading into Tuesday’s closed-door proceedings was on the minority leader race.

Johnson, the outgoing speaker, declined to endorse a candidate but had encouraging words for Jordan after his win. “He’s going to do an excellent job. He’s a good, trusted friend and brother,” he said.

Rep. Tom Cole, R-Okla., said it was a “tough choice for the conference to make,” but he wasn’t disappointed in the pick. “He was an exceptionally capable chairman of both Oversight and Judiciary. He’s excellent in an interview,” Cole said of Jordan. “He’s got boundless energy and determination.”

Jordan’s victory means he will form a political and legal tag team with newly installed White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller in pushing back on a number of investigations House Democrats have planned for President Donald Trump, some of his second-term administration officials and his business-minded family members.

Democrats will have more than 250 seats in the chamber, with a number of races still uncalled. Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, expected to become the next House speaker, told reporters last week he predicts Democrats will have at least 255 seats when all the ballots have been counted and verification processes have played out.

“It’s a historic majority in the 21st century,” Jeffries told reporters in Washington, D.C., the day after the midterms. “The American people have chosen the economy over extremism. The American people have chosen hope over hatred. The American people have chosen common sense over corruption, chaos and cruelty. The American people have chosen House Democrats because they want to see a dramatic change in direction.”

Political analysts have predicted an internal battle within the GOP for the direction the party takes over the next two years — and after Trump leaves office in January 2029.

The Institute for Legislative Analysis, a nonprofit organization that advocates to shrink the size and influence of the government, released a vote study assessment on Monday. Its calculations led ILA to endorse Emmer and three fresh faces: Jordan, Steube and Jack.

“It’s clear many Republican voters feel their representatives in Washington aren’t representing them,” Ryan McGowan, the institute’s CEO, said in a statement. “It will be interesting to see whether House Republicans respond by choosing leaders … whose voting records are much more closely aligned with the party’s conservative base.”

Several GOP sources late last week, granted anonymity to be candid, said they were expecting a close outcome between Scalise and Jordan, adding Emmer was working the phones hard to remain whip. One said having either Scalise or Jordan atop the conference, with the expectation of Emmer staying on as whip, “won’t be much of a change at the top.”

The new leadership team will take over Jan. 3, when Democrats are expected to, in part, use their large majority to target all things Trump 2.0. The same GOP source said the majority party will “inevitably be pursuing impeachment by August recess despite their disciplined statements to the media pre-election.”

Trump replied in the affirmative when a “60 Minutes” correspondent asked him in an interview that aired Sunday night if he could work with Democrats, should they also be aggressively investigating his team.

“Well, I did it for four years,” the president said of his first term. “They impeached me twice. And there are those that say that worked out to my advantage.”

Nina Heller, Michael Macagnone and Samantha Freeman contributed to this report.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

My kids say I’m hard to shop for, but I’d be perfectly happy to find a bag full of DeWalt tools under the tree this year. Especially if somebody got $130 off the bag.

Black Friday is here, and the DeWalt deal I’d point a new DIYer toward is already live. For $269, you get a drill for pilot holes, an impact driver for driving fasteners, and an oscillating multitool for the day you need to trim a doorjamb with the casing still on. If you’ve already got the cordless basics covered, DeWalt’s compact jobsite table saw is $100 off. That’s a light, quick stowaway tool I’d grab if I had a set of shelves to cut and still needed room on my workbench to build out the bookcase. Throw in the more-than-$200 discount on DeWalt’s 12-inch sliding miter saw, and you’re well on your way to a pro-level workshop. With the money you saved, it’s like getting free lumber for your next project.

I pulled together some of the best DeWalt deals to shop around Black Friday and Cyber Monday. Pick something up this holiday season, and outfit your workshop with the unmistakable yellow-and-black DeWalt signature.

If your workshop turns back into a garage around dinnertime, this is the table saw I’d look at. It’s compact enough to stash when you’re done, and the rack-and-pinion fence is deadly accurate, making it easy to dial in repeat cuts for shelves or cabinets. DeWalt does a great job storing all of the saw’s accessories on board, and the entire package weighs just over 50 pounds. Make room on the lower shelf of your workbench for this one, since it’s easy to lift and carry.

Have you ever put the full weight of your body into a lug wrench, only to have the lug nuts refuse to budge? I certainly have. And then your brain starts thinking, “I should really buy an impact wrench at some point.”

Now is a great time to do just that. This 1/2-inch impact wrench from DeWalt breaks stubborn lugs and larger fasteners loose, making it an especially solid buy for someone who works on their own vehicles and outdoor equipment. For this deal, you get the wrench, a 5.0 amp-hour battery, and a charger.

If you asked me to pick the ultimate DeWalt Black Friday deal, I’d have to go with this DeWalt cordless jigsaw. A circular saw will get you right up to the point where a cut starts to curve. Then, it’s time to reach for this jigsaw.

The speed dial on this model from DeWalt lets you slow things down as you enter a tight turn, and the blower helps keep sawdust off the line you’re trying to follow. At $129, which represents a 50 percent discount, this is a pickup you can’t pass up.

You can opt for a basic socket and ratchet kit to perform automotive work at home, but with this comprehensive DeWalt set at more than 40 percent off, why would you? This set includes both metric and SAE sockets across three drive sizes. Grab the small ratchet when there’s barely enough room to turn your wrist and the larger one when you have more room to break a stubborn nut free. I also like the hard case, which keeps the tools both protected and organized. One look at an empty socket chamber, and I know exactly which one I left beneath my mower deck.

If someone on your holiday list just picked up keys to their first place, I’d get them this set. Leave a drill bit in one tool and a driver in the other, and you can go from drilling pilot holes to running screws without stopping to swap bits. That doesn’t sound like much until you've got an afternoon of hanging curtain rods and shelves in front of you. And I like that the kit includes both tools, two batteries, a charger, and a bag to keep everything together and ready for transport. At $149, this is a perfect entry point into the DeWalt cordless tool ecosystem.

The first time you need to slip a piece of new flooring under a doorjamb, you’ll understand exactly why this DeWalt oscillating multitool is one of the most coveted tools in any collection. Trim that jamb right where it sits, without removing it. Same idea if you need to notch a little baseboard in place or make a neat opening in drywall for a new electrical outlet.

Where this deal really shines, however, is the accessories you get with the tool. For $99, you’re also taking home a 4.0 Ah battery, charger, and blade.

If you’re ready to take on that crown molding project you’ve wanted to attempt for so long, this 12-inch sliding miter saw from DeWalt will be your new bestie. The sliding head gives you plenty of room to perform crosscuts on wider boards, and the blade’s shadow line shows exactly where the teeth will land on your measurement. At just over $200 off, this saw is a legacy tool that you’ll likely pass down to the next generation of woodworkers and DIYers in your family.

I love this sander. DeWalt has lowered the overall profile of this new XR sander, so you can reach tight spaces when you need to sand something in place, like the inside of a cabinet. The tool feels great in your palm, and the weight is dead-centered on the pad, which keeps it planted on your work surface. Five speed settings allow you to back off when you’re easing an edge or turn it up when you need serious material removal. At $144, I’d put this one on the Black Friday list for anyone already on the DeWalt platform, as both battery and charger are sold separately.

For many people, a big reciprocating saw is probably too much tool. How much demolition will you actually do? But picture yourself under a sink or in a crawl space trying to cut out an old pipe with your elbows jammed up around your ears. That’s where I’d take this compact DeWalt reciprocating saw over one of those larger ones. With the right blade, you’ll tear through that pipe—or cut the nails holding a broken fence picket and leave the neighboring boards alone. At more than 60 percent off, you still have plenty left in the budget for a battery and charger.

If I were putting together a cordless tool kit from scratch, I’d start here. The drill and impact driver are the pair I reach for whenever I’m drilling pilot holes and driving fasteners in tandem. The oscillating multitool handles the awkward cuts, like trimming a door jamb so I can install new flooring underneath it or cutting a fast hole in drywall for a new receptacle. With three batteries and a charger included in the bag, you can leave a battery on each tool while you work or keep one in the charger until it’s needed.

If you’re considering any of the cordless tools I’ve mentioned earlier, this Black Friday deal is an easy add. This 5.0 Ah DeWalt battery two-pack makes perfect sense for tools that spend a lot of time in use, like a cordless sander or miter saw. I’ve always been a fan of DeWalt’s easy-access charge gauge on their batteries, which lets you see how much juice you have before you start. Again, this is a great choice if you’re picking up that cordless XR sander, as these batteries have impressive run times, and because this is a two-pack, you can charge one as you work and sand without much downtime.

#6190. 21 Best Places to Visit in December in the USA

We’ll never forget the first time we visited New York City in December. We’d seen it in movies, but standing there, seeing the Rockefeller Center tree all lit up for the first time, with skaters below and festive music in the air… it was pure magic.

But December travel isn’t just about snow and Santa. We’ve also spent the holidays escaping to the warmth, trading snow boots for flip-flops.

In fact, we’ve been to almost all 50 states and spent a lot of winters trying to find the most fun destinations and best weather. We’ve done so many road trips in the USA and flown almost everywhere, trying to find the best places to either escape the snow or enjoy the winter, you would think we are obsessed. And we want to share all of that knowledge with you.

If you’re looking for the perfect winter getaway, you have a clear choice: either lean into the winter magic or escape it completely. Are you dreaming of a warm-weather escape with sunshine and sand, or a storybook Christmas town that looks like a real-life snow globe?

Based on all those experiences, we’ve put together this list of our favourite places to visit. Whether you’re looking for a festive city, a snowy mountain, or a sunny beach, we’ll help you find the perfect spot.

Here is a quick look at some of the best places for a December getaway in the USA, from festive winter wonderlands to sunny escapes.

December is a month of pure magic and festive energy. It’s the perfect time to use up that last bit of vacation time for the year. The biggest draw is the distinct choice it offers: You can either dive head-first into a winter wonderland, complete with snow and holiday markets, or you can completely escape the cold weather and find yourself on a sunny beach. It’s a month of festive celebrations, incredible decorations, and finding the perfect atmosphere to end the year.

If you’re anything like us, sometimes the best gift in December is a break from the cold. Trust us, we know after living in Toronto, Canada. Those winters are brutal. These are our favourite spots to find sunshine and warm weather, where you can trade your winter coat for a light jacket or even a swimsuit.

We love the laid-back, quirky vibe of Key West, and it’s even more special in December. We have a great memory of biking around the island, seeing the historic inns draped in holiday lights, and then ending the day at Mallory Square for the sunset celebration. It’s a perfect escape from the cold.

Why Visit in December: This is the perfect time to visit. The summer humidity is gone, the weather is sunny and warm (often in the high 70s), and the risk of hurricanes is very low. The whole island is in a festive spirit, with unique events like the “Bight Before Christmas” boat parade.

Where to Stay: We recommend finding a guesthouse or inn in the historic Old Town to be close to the action.

We once went to a holiday luau in Ka’anapali, and it’s an experience we’ll never forget. You’re eating kalua pork and sipping a mai tai, watching a beautiful hula performance… and then Santa Claus arrives on an outrigger canoe. It was the perfect, uniquely Hawaiian way to get into the festive spirit.

Why Visit in December: You get tropical weather, festive holiday luaus, and it’s the official start of the humpback whale watching season. Be aware that this is a popular time, especially around Christmas, so prices can be high and you’ll need to book in advance.

Where to Stay: Look to the resorts in Wailea or Ka’anapali for a classic Maui experience.

We’ll always remember snorkeling the underwater trail at Trunk Bay in St. John. The water was so calm and clear, and seeing all the colourful fish felt a world away from the snow back home. That’s the magic of a Caribbean trip in December, and the USVI makes it so easy for American travelers.

Why Visit in December: It’s the start of the dry season, with fantastic weather and warm, clear water. You get a full-on tropical, warm-weather Christmas experience, all without needing a passport.

Where to Stay: You can choose from large resorts in St. Thomas or more eco-friendly villas and lodges in St. John.

We were not prepared for how magical St. Augustine is in December. We took one of the Old Town trolley tours at night, and seeing the entire historic city, from the old Spanish architecture to the palm trees, draped in millions of white lights… it was breathtaking. It’s a holiday light display unlike any other.

Why Visit in December: The famous “Nights of Lights” festival. The entire city is illuminated, and the mild Florida weather is perfect for walking around and enjoying the atmosphere. It’s one of the most festive and warm places you can visit.

Where to Stay: We recommend a historic inn or bed & breakfast in the downtown district to be within walking distance of all the lights.

While Maui is our go-to for a resort escape, Honolulu is where you go for a vibrant, city-meets-beach holiday. We loved seeing the massive Santa surfing with his reindeer in the fountain at the Iolani Palace. The whole city has this amazing “Mele Kalikimaka” (Merry Christmas) spirit.

Why Visit in December: It’s the perfect blend of warm beach weather, world-class shopping, and festive displays. It’s also a significant month for history, with the memorial events at Pearl Harbor.

Where to Stay: Waikiki has a huge range of hotels, from historic beachfront properties to modern high-rises.

If your idea of a winter getaway is to truly get away from everything, the crowds, the noise, the stress, then South Padre is a perfect choice. We spent a week there, and our days consisted of long, quiet walks on the beach. It was a total reset and the perfect way to escape the winter blues.

Why Visit in December: The weather is mild, and the crowds are gone. It’s one of the warmest places in Texas and offers a simple, relaxing beach vacation without the high prices or holiday chaos of other destinations.

Where to Stay: You’ll find many beachfront condos and hotels offering great off-season rates.

We thought we knew desert holiday lights, but the “Las Noches de las Luminarias” at the Desert Botanical Garden in Phoenix is on another level. Walking the garden paths lit by thousands of hand-lit luminaria bags, with musicians playing, was a top-tier holiday experience.

Why Visit in December: You get two trips in one: perfect, sunny weather for outdoor adventures like hiking during the day, and stunning, sophisticated holiday light displays at night.

Where to Stay: Choose from upscale resorts in Scottsdale or stylish hotels in downtown Phoenix.

Sometimes, the warm weather destinations just won’t cut it, especially if you are looking for that winter wonderland feel. So, this section is for travellers who want to dive head-first into the holiday spirit. These are the cities and towns that go all-out for December, with millions of lights, Christmas markets, and an atmosphere of pure magic.

We’ve visited NYC many times, but there’s a specific energy in December. We grabbed hot chocolates and walked through the Bryant Park Winter Village, watching the ice skaters zip around the rink under the lights of the surrounding skyscrapers. It felt like being in the opening scene of a holiday movie. There is nothing like New York City at Christmas.

Why Visit in December: It is the quintessential American Christmas destination. From the iconic tree to the world-famous window displays, the entire city is on a different level of festive.

Where to Stay: Midtown is convenient for seeing the main holiday sights, but we also love the West Village for its cosy, neighbourhood feel.

We’d heard Leavenworth was a “Christmas Town,” but we weren’t prepared for the reality. We visited during the Village of Lights festival, and walking through the snow-covered Bavarian-style village while every single building was covered in over half a million lights… it’s not an exaggeration. It’s the closest we’ve ever felt to being inside a real-life snow globe.

Why Visit in December: The entire town transforms into a “Hallmark movie” Christmas village. It’s a full-immersion holiday experience with carolers, festive food, and incredible decorations.

Where to Stay: Book a Bavarian-style lodge or inn right in the village. You must book many months in advance for December.

We love Asheville, but visiting in December is all about the Biltmore Estate. We took the candlelight evening tour, and seeing the main banquet hall with its 35-foot tree, fireplaces roaring, and carolers singing… it felt like we’d stepped back in time into a Gilded Age Christmas party.

Why Visit in December: Christmas at Biltmore is one of the most iconic holiday events in the country. The city itself is a cosy mountain retreat, and the Blue Ridge Mountains are just beautiful with a dusting of snow.

Where to Stay: You can stay on the Biltmore Estate for the full experience or choose a boutique hotel downtown.

Here are the remaining destinations for the “Best Christmas Towns & Festive Cities” section, all written with unique, December-focused content.

We’ve visited a lot of Christmas markets, but visiting the one in Bethlehem, known as “Christmas City USA”, just felt right. We sipped hot cider and browsed the stalls in the old quarter, and you can feel the city’s 250+ years of Christmas tradition. The whole place is lit by the glow of a giant Moravian star on the hillside.

Why Visit in December: This is Christmas City USA. It was nicknamed this on Christmas Eve, 1741. It offers one of the most authentic and historic holiday experiences in the country, blending its Moravian heritage with a European-style Christkindlmarkt.

Where to Stay: Look for a hotel or inn in the historic downtown area to be close to the festivities.

Walking into Solvang in December felt like we’d been transported to a Danish village during its Julefest celebration. We spent the day exploring the half-timbered buildings, windmills, and bakeries, all decorated for the holidays. It’s such a unique and charming way to experience a winter getaway in the middle of California.

Why Visit in December: The town’s month-long “Julefest” (Yule-fest) celebration is in full swing. It’s a one-of-a-kind Danish-style Christmas with parades, markets, and, of course, delicious European pastries.

Where to Stay: Choose one of the charming Danish-themed inns right in the village to be in the middle of the Julefest activities.

We had to see the “Christmas Capital of Texas” for ourselves, and it did not disappoint. The entire historic Main Street is transformed. We loved seeing the vintage railroad, which becomes the “North Pole Express” for the month. They take the “Christmas Capital” title seriously; there are over 1,400 events in 40 days.

Why Visit in December: It is the officially designated “Christmas Capital of Texas”. The sheer number of festive events, light displays, and activities is staggering, making it a top-tier destination for families and holiday lovers.

Where to Stay: The Gaylord Texan Resort is an attraction in itself, or you can stay near the Historic Main Street to be close to the events.

A New Orleans Christmas is an experience all its own. We did a “Reveillon Dinner,” a modern take on a Creole holiday tradition, and it was one of the most memorable meals we’ve ever had. Afterwards, we walked to Jackson Square to see the St. Louis Cathedral all lit up while carolers sang.

Why Visit in December: You get to experience unique Creole Christmas traditions you won’t find anywhere else. The weather is mild, the food is incredible, and the city’s lobbies (like at The Roosevelt) have some of the most elegant decorations we’ve seen.

Where to Stay: We recommend a hotel in the French Quarter to be in the middle of the action and see the decorated lobbies.

We went to Natchitoches (pronounced Nak-a-tish) specifically for its Christmas Festival, and it was a total joy. It’s one of the oldest and biggest in the country. The whole city, which is the oldest in Louisiana, lights up with over 300,000 lights along the Cane River, and the weekly fireworks shows are fantastic.

Why Visit in December: It hosts one of the oldest and most celebrated holiday festivals in the US, running for six weeks. It’s a classic, Southern Christmas experience in a beautiful historic district.

Where to Stay: Book a room at a historic bed & breakfast in the downtown area.

Visiting Colonial Williamsburg in December felt like walking through a living history Christmas card. We joined a candlelight tour, and seeing the historic buildings lit by real candles in the windows, with carolers in period costumes and the smell of woodsmoke in the air… it was absolutely magical.

Why Visit in December: You get to experience a traditional, 18th-century “Colonial Christmas”. The decorations are all-natural (no plastic lights), and the atmosphere is incredibly authentic and charming.

Where to Stay: Stay in one of the historic Colonial Houses or a tavern right in the restored area for the full immersive experience.

Here is the final category of destinations. This section is all about embracing the snow and finding that perfect winter wonderland.

For many, holiday season travel is all about finding that perfect, snowy scene. These are the places to go for world-class skiing, cosy lodges, and that magical feeling of a true winter escape.

We’ll always remember our first “après-ski” in Aspen. We had spent the day on the mountain hitting fresh powder whenever we got the chance, and as the sun went down, the sky lit up with this incredible pink and orange light they call “Aspenglow.” Sitting by a fire, enjoying a glass of Christmas cheer, and watching the snow fall on the historic town, it just felt like the peak of a luxury winter trip.

Why Visit in December: It’s one of the world’s most famous upscale ski destinations, and the town is just as much an attraction as the mountains. The festive atmosphere, high-end shops, and restaurants are all decked out for the holidays.

Where to Stay: Aspen is known for its luxury hotels and ski-in/ski-out resorts.

One of our favourite things about Park City is its history. We loved skiing down to the historic Main Street, popping off our skis, and walking straight into a saloon that’s been there since the silver mining days. It feels like a real Western town, not just a ski resort.

Why Visit in December: It’s a historic mountain town with two world-class ski resorts (Park City and Deer Valley). The historic Main Street is incredibly charming, and the “Snow Globe Stroll” features life-sized snow globes you can walk through.

Where to Stay: You can find ski-in/ski-out hotels or stay at an inn on the historic Main Street.

Jackson Hole in December is just dramatic. We took a sleigh ride through the National Elk Refuge, and seeing thousands of elk gathered against the backdrop of the snow-covered Teton mountains… it was a powerful and wild winter experience we’ve never forgotten.

Why Visit in December: It’s the perfect mix of rugged “cowboy Christmas” charm and some of the most challenging ski terrain in North America. The town square, with its famous antler arches, is beautifully lit for the holidays.

Where to Stay: Stay at a slopeside resort in Teton Village or in a hotel in the town of Jackson.

We love Whitefish because it feels like a real, down-to-earth ski town. We spent a day snowshoeing in nearby Glacier National Park, enjoying the total silence and incredible snowy landscapes, and then came back to town for a casual dinner. It’s all the beauty, without the glitz. Just what we were looking for in a winter vacation.

Why Visit in December: It’s a laid-back, charming mountain town with a top-rated ski resort and stunning scenery. It’s also right next to Glacier National Park, which is a spectacular place to explore in the winter.

Where to Stay: You can find lodges on the mountain or stay in one of the friendly inns in downtown Whitefish.

This was a trip purely for the fun of it, and it was 100% worth it. You drive down streets named “Santa Claus Lane” and “St. Nicholas Drive,” the streetlights are shaped like candy canes, and you can visit the Santa Claus House and see his reindeer. It’s a surreal and joyful experience.

Why Visit in December: It’s the ultimate Christmas fantasy come to life. The entire town is Christmas-themed, 365 days a year, but it’s most magical in December with real snow on the ground and the added bonus of possibly seeing the Northern Lights.

Where to Stay: North Pole is very small; most visitors stay in the nearby city of Fairbanks, which has a wide range of hotels.

For the best warm weather, your top choices are Southern Florida (like Key West), Hawaii (like Maui and Honolulu), and the desert Southwest (like Phoenix and Palm Springs). The U.S. Virgin Islands are also a fantastic passport-free tropical option.

Leavenworth, Washington, is often considered the ultimate “Christmas town” as it looks just like a Bavarian snow globe. Other top choices include Bethlehem, PA (known as “Christmas City USA”), Solvang, CA (for a Danish-style Julefest), and Grapevine, TX (the “Christmas Capital of Texas”).

Yes, but it depends on the park. It’s the perfect time to visit desert parks like Death Valley, Everglades, and Big Bend, where summer heat is unbearable. However, many mountain parks like Glacier, Yellowstone, and parts of Yosemite are mostly inaccessible due to heavy snow and road closures.

You are almost guaranteed to find snow in the mountain towns of the Rockies, like Aspen, CO, Park City, UT, and Jackson Hole, WY. You’ll also find snow in the Cascade Mountains (like Leavenworth, WA), Alaska, and the mountains around Lake Tahoe.

December is a magical month to travel. Whether you’re chasing the sun, seeking out that perfect snowy scene, or looking for a town that’s full of holiday magic, the US has the perfect spot for you.

We hope this list, based on our own winter travels, helps you plan your next getaway. Save this on Pinterest for your holiday planning! Where is your favourite place to go in December?

Across thousands of years, Neanderthals and modern humans (Homo sapiens) interbred, leaving traces of Neanderthal DNA in people alive today. But how these encounters happened is a huge unanswered question. Answering it may shed light on what made us different from our close cousins — and why we thrived while Neanderthals died out.

Live Science interviewed researchers deeply invested in human evolution, and in this exclusive video we explore what scientists are uncovering about these relationships from ancient DNA and archaeological evidence unearthed in Eurasia.

#6188. Rep. Darren Soto survives Republican-drawn map in Florida

Florida Rep. Darren Soto, here at a hearing in July, has won a sixth term representing the 9th District. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

Florida Rep. Darren Soto, the most vulnerable House Democrat running for reelection, narrowly won a sixth term Tuesday in a district that state Republicans redrew in their favor.

Soto was leading Republican Navy veteran Dan Green by less than a point when The Associated Press called the race for Central Florida’s 9th District a week after Election Day. His margin of victory was above the 0.5 percent threshold that would trigger a recount under state law.

House Democrats have so far flipped more than 40 seats and appear on track to hold their biggest majority in the chamber in decades. Soto’s win means that no House Democratic incumbent lost to a Republican in the general election this year. And Florida Democrats defended all four seats the GOP had hoped to pick up under the state’s new Republican-drawn map.

Democratic Reps. Kathy Castor and Jared Moskowitz both won reelection from districts that shifted red, while Democrat Pia Dandiya, a former high school principal, defeated Republican Marine Corps veteran Casey Askar for a redrawn open seat in South Florida.

Soto, who declared victory last week, had been seen as the most vulnerable of the targeted Florida Democrats. The new map reduced the Hispanic population of his district as the seat shifted from one that Kamala Harris would have carried in 2024 to one that Donald Trump would have taken by 18 points.

“Despite the Florida Republican legislature’s efforts to redraw me out of this district, my record of delivering for Florida showed voters that I am a reliable fighter for them in Congress,” Soto said in a Nov. 4 statement.

In a Tuesday memo detailing how House Democrats secured their historic majority, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee took aim at Republicans’ mid-decade redistricting efforts, saying their “attempts to steal seats … supremely backfired.”

While Florida Republicans were unsuccessful in flipping the four Democrat-held seats, the party held all of its House seats in the Sunshine State. Republican Rep. María Elvira Salazar narrowly won reelection in the Miami-area 27th District over Democratic challenger Eliott Rodriguez, the AP reported Tuesday. In the 7th District outside Orlando, Republican former TV news anchor Ryan Elijah defeated Democratic Navy veteran Bale Dalton, a former NASA chief of staff who conceded Tuesday.

Mixing chemicals can be harmful to health, with the dangers worsening exposure depending on the chemicals and concentrations involved.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Household cleaning is often a straightforward, if tedious, task. But some particularly tough spots take more effort. When a stubborn mess needs some extra work, tackling it by combining multiple kinds of cleaning products might seem like a good idea.

But is it dangerous to mix cleaning products? According to one common misconception, doing so could create mustard gas, a toxic synthetic chemical weapon notorious for its use in World War I.

Experts told Live Science that it's not possible to produce mustard gas from these products, but mixing certain chemicals can harm your health.

That's because chemical reactions between some cleaning products can produce gases that irritate parts of the body. For example, mixing bleach with products containing ammonia, such as some glass and stovetop cleaners, produces chloramines. When a person breathes in these compounds, they react with water in the body to form hydrochloric acid. That compound causes burning in the eyes, nose and mucous membranes, said Dr. Mike Chary, an emergency physician at Weill Cornell and co-director of webPoisonControl, a digital platform that guides users faced with poison emergencies.

Ammonia is made up of three hydrogen atoms bound to a central nitrogen atom. When it reacts with bleach, chlorine atoms from bleach can replace one or more of the hydrogen atoms to form chloramines, which are harmful or deadly in high enough concentrations, said Delphine Farmer, an atmospheric chemist at Colorado State University.

"Chloramines are certainly present in a lot of environments," Farmer told Live Science. "We often see them indoors if you just clean with bleach, or you'll get them out of pools. But when you actually mix cleaning products, you can make enough chloramines that they can kill you."

Experts advise not to mix bleach with other cleaning products.

Bleach and ammonia aren't the only compounds that should be kept apart. Mixing bleach with an acid can produce chlorine gas, which irritates the eyes. The gas smells like a swimming pool, Chary said.

But it's not possible to produce mustard gas just by mixing these products. Mustard gas contains sulfur, and although some cleaners have sulfur in them, mustard gas typically doesn’t form at room temperature and pressure, Chary told Live Science.

How dangerous an exposure becomes depends on a few factors, Chary added. The concentration of a hazardous byproduct will be smaller in a larger, well-ventilated room than in a smaller room with no airflow. Existing health conditions, such as asthma or lung disease, could also exacerbate the effects of exposure, Chary said.

Household cleaners also tend to have low concentrations of these chemicals so that any accidental reactions don't produce as much of the byproduct.

"Household bleach is below a certain concentration," Chary told Live Science. "That's primarily designed so that if it gets on you, it isn't going to cause as much damage as industrial-strength bleach. What that also means is that there's less of it per unit to undergo chemical reactions."

If someone mixes any of these chemicals, they typically know right away that there's a problem. Within a few minutes, they might start coughing, their eyes might begin to water, or they might notice a strong odor.

"Most of these things will elicit an aversive response," Chary said. "If you feel something's off, pay attention to that premonition."

Both Chary and Farmer recommended opening windows and moving outside to fresh air if you accidentally mix cleaning products and notice these effects. Chary noted that if a person requires medical treatment, an exposure to chloramines is usually treated similarly to an asthma attack: Doctors may give medicines such as albuterol to open up the airways, and they’ll monitor patients’ oxygen saturation for signs of lung injuries.

To avoid accidentally mixing chemicals that can create something hazardous, Farmer recommended storing oxidizing cleaners, such as bleach and hydrogen peroxide, separately from other cleaning products. If you must use different kinds of cleaners to tackle a stubborn stain, wait until you can't smell the first one anymore before using the second, she added .

Sometimes, you don't need to use heavy-hitting products at all. "I'm a big fan of reducing exposure to those strong oxidants," Farmer said. "If you can use a simpler compound, that's better. Simple soap and water is amazing."

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

Skyler Ware is a freelance science journalist covering chemistry, biology, paleontology and Earth science. She was a 2023 AAAS Mass Media Science and Engineering Fellow at Science News. Her work has also appeared in Science News Explores, ZME Science and Chembites, among others. Skyler has a Ph.D. in chemistry from Caltech.
