#6066. British Airways Visa Card Review: Is It Worth The $95 Annual Fee?

The British Airways Visa Signature® Card is one of Chase’s co-branded airline credit cards, and British Airways Club is certainly a popular frequent flyer program, given the overall value of the Avios ecosystem, plus the number of destinations in the United States that British Airways serves.

Who should be applying for the British Airways Visa, and under what circumstances is it worth spending money on it? Let’s take a look at what you need to know about this card, and what the best alternatives are.

Link: Learn more about the British Airways Visa Signature® Card

Before jumping into a closer look at every aspect of the British Airways Visa Card, here’s a high-level view of the card’s key features, perks, and fees:

Here are my thoughts on the biggest British Airways Visa Card pros and cons:

If you’re considering the British Airways Visa Signature Card, its welcome bonus, application rules, and annual fee are all probably top of mind. So let’s start by taking a look at these important details.

The British Airways Visa currently offers the following welcome bonus: Earn 75,000 Avios after you spend $5,000 on purchases within the first three months of account opening.

Based on my current points and miles valuations, which put Avios at 1.2 cents apiece, this current bonus is worth about $900. That’s a pretty solid welcome bonus, especially for a card with a moderate annual fee.

The British Airways Visa has a $95 annual fee. This is not waived for the first year, and there’s no additional fee to add authorized users.

British Airways’ credit card has no foreign transaction fees, so it’s potentially a great card to use for purchases abroad.

The welcome bonus on the British Airways Visa isn’t available to those who currently have the card, or those who have received a new cardmember bonus on the card in the past 24 months. You are eligible for this card if you’ve had the Iberia Visa Signature® Card and/or Aer Lingus Visa Signature® Card, despite the similarities between the cards.

Chase’s other general policies on card approvals apply as well, including the 5/24, whereby you generally won’t be approved for a Chase card if you’ve opened five or more credit cards in the last 24 months.

The British Airways Visa Card has no foreign transaction fees, but does the rewards structure warrant putting spending on the card? It might, but only thanks to additional bonuses offered by the card, which incentivize spending.

The British Airways Visa doesn’t have terribly exciting bonus categories. You earn:

There are lots of great credit cards for airfare purchases and hotel purchases. This isn’t a card I would be putting much spending on unless you’re trying to earn a Travel Together Ticket, in which case it could definitely be worth it. More on that below.

British Airways Club is a transfer partner of Amex Membership Rewards, Bilt Rewards, Capital One, and Chase Ultimate Rewards, so it could make sense to put spending on a card earning one of those currencies if you want to earn Avios at an accelerated rate.

There are lots of great uses of British Airways Avios. British Airways Club has roughly distance based award pricing, and the program offers value in situations where other programs might not. Generally speaking, here’s where I see value with Avios:

British Airways is known for adding large taxes and surcharges to some of its own award flights, so this is worth keeping in mind.

Personally I find Avios to be one of the most useful frequent flyer programs for redeeming points, thanks to the number of redemptions this opens up.

Often one of the big challenges people have with points is figuring out how to pool them since you typically need enough points in a single account for a redemption. A cool feature of the British Airways Club program is that you can form household accounts. This allows you to pool the Avios you earn with up to six other people registered at the same address as you.

This is especially awesome in the context of a credit card welcome bonus, since you can pool a ton of Avios in a single account if you have two people get the card in a household, etc.

There are some benefits to the British Airways Visa Card that could alone justify having this card. For some people, it will be worth spending money on the card to unlock some perks, while for others just having the card and not spending money on it offers sufficient benefits. Let’s look at what those benefits are, and how they work.

One of the best benefits of the British Airways Signature Visa is that it offers a 10% discount on British Airways flights starting in the United States. To take advantage of this, just book through ba.com/chase10, and use your card to pay while using promotion code BACHASE10.

If you fly British Airways with any frequency, this could cover the annual fee over and over. See this post for everything you need to know about the British Airways Visa flight discount.

If you have the British Airways Visa Card and redeem Avios for a reward flight, you can receive up to $600 in statement credits annually. You can earn up to three statement credits, as follows:

There are some basic terms to be aware of:

British Airways now also offers Reward Flight Saver from the United States, allowing you to redeem more Avios and pay lower surcharges. Getting a further statement credit of up to $200 on that is pretty great.

One of the potentially great perks of the British Airways Visa is that you can earn a Travel Together Ticket when you spend $30,000 on the card in a calendar year.

This companion ticket will be deposited in your British Airways Club account four to six weeks after you’ve completed the required spending.

With this certificate, you can book a British Airways award ticket at the full cost of Avios (plus taxes, fees, and surcharges), and then for the second passenger you don’t have to pay any Avios, but rather just have to pay all the fees.

This also offers a lot of flexibility — you can also use the voucher as a solo traveler and get 50% off the Avios required for a ticket. Your ticket can originate anywhere in the world, and you can even travel on Aer Lingus or Iberia.

This can represent a fantastic deal for first and business class travel, given how much those tickets would otherwise cost. This isn’t for everyone, though it has the potential to represent a good value, and I know it’s a feature that many value.

See this post for everything you need to know about the British Airways Visa companion voucher.

As a Visa Signature card, the British Airways Visa comes with the following shopping and travel protection benefits:

You’ll want to review the card’s benefits guide for any exclusions and rules that apply.

The British Airways Visa Card has a solid welcome bonus, and that could be a legitimate motivator for picking up this card. However, personally this isn’t a card I would use for everyday spending, since you can earn British Airways Avios at a better rate with other American Express or Chase cards. It also lacks a few benefits that many other airline credit cards offer, including a free checked bag and priority boarding.

That said, I absolutely think this card is worth holding onto if you fly British Airways with any frequency because:

There are several Avios currencies, with three belonging to International Airlines Group (IAG) airlines — there’s British Airways, Aer Lingus, and Iberia. There are also two other US-based credit cards that directly earn Avios from these airlines. Specifically, we’re talking about the Iberia Visa Card (learn more) and Aer Lingus Visa Card (learn more).

Which of these cards should you select? They have a lot in common:

The differences mainly come in the form of the perks associated with just holding onto the cards, and also the perks associated with spending $30,000 on the cards in a calendar year:

The best card to select comes down to which benefits you value most. Also, remember that you’re eligible for all three of these cards, should you be interested, so you don’t necessarily have to choose between them.

See here for a full comparison of cards earning Avios.

If you want to earn British Airways Avios, I’d recommend getting a card that earns either Amex Membership Rewards, Bilt Rewards, Capital One, or Chase Ultimate Rewards points. Here’s why:

With that in mind, which cards should you consider? Here are some of my favorite Chase Ultimate Rewards-earning cards:

If you’re over 5/24 or simply prefer Amex points or Capital One miles, here are some top choices:

The British Airways Visa is one of the best co-branded airline credit cards out there, in my opinion. The card offers a solid welcome bonus, and it can be worth spending money on the card to earn a companion ticket.

Beyond that, the card can be worth having for the discounts offered on both paid tickets (up to 10% off) or award tickets (up to $200 in statement credits), which can cover the annual fee over and over. That said, the card would be even stronger if it offered a free checked bag and lounge access as benefits — though I’d expect the annual to increase if those were added, especially the latter perk.

When it comes to earning British Airways Avios long term, personally I’d much rather earn Amex, Bilt, Capital One, and Chase points, and transfer them to British Airways. Not only does this allow you to earn points at a much faster rate, but it also gives you a lot more flexibility.

#6064. No more permanent coalitions: What the midterm results reveal

Senate Democratic leader Charles E. Schumer poses in his office on Nov. 9 for a group photo with incoming members of his caucus: from left, Ohio's Sherrod Brown, Texas' James Talarico, Iowa's Josh Turek, Michigan's Abdul El-Sayed, North Carolina's Roy Cooper, Illinois' Juliana Stratton, New Hampshire's Chris Pappas, South Carolina's Annie Andrews, Minnesota's Peggy Flanagan, Maine's Troy Jackson and Kansas' Adam Hamilton. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call)

ANALYSIS -- “Life moves pretty fast,” that famed 20th-century philosopher Ferris Bueller once said. “If you don't stop and look around once in a while, you could miss it.”

In 2024, Democrats were consigned to the political wilderness. Republicans had captured the White House, flipped the Senate and held the House. President Donald Trump had completely altered the party coalitions as he led the ascendant GOP to victory.

Now, just two years later, Democrats are on the rise. A historic midterm tsunami has swept them into such commanding Senate and House majorities that some are questioning whether Republicans will ever be in charge again. And if Texas is blue, how does the GOP have any chance in the Electoral College again?

A big takeaway from the midterm results should be that there’s very little permanence in our politics.

What may have looked like a new GOP coalition was really more of a Trump coalition, and it crumbled in the face of economic frustrations, affordability concerns and the president’s unpopular policies.

With Trump’s negative job approval rating weighing them down, Republican candidates suffered losses among virtually all demographic groups – including by wide margins among constituencies thought to make up the GOP’s core.

Trump or the Republicans finished ahead among male voters by 4 points in 2018, 8 points in 2020, 14 points in 2022 and 12 points in 2024, according to the exit polls. Men went for Democratic candidates by 4 points (51 percent to 47 percent) this cycle. Meanwhile, Republicans lost even more ground among women. While Kamala Harris finished ahead of Trump by 8 points in 2024, that margin grew to 21 points for Democratic candidates this year.

Trump closed the gap among Hispanic voters to just 5 points behind Harris two years ago. This year, Hispanic voters nationwide supported Democratic candidates by 32 points (65 percent to 33 percent). Even white voters shifted significantly. They backed Trump or  Republican candidates by 10 points in 2018, 17 points in 2020, 18 points in 2022 and 15 points in 2024. And yet Democrats edged out Republicans by a point (50 percent to 49 percent) on Nov. 3.

Voters without a college degree were supposed to be a key cog in Republicans’ new populist coalition. But they went from +13 (56 percent to 43 percent) for Trump in 2024 to backing Republican candidates by just 1 point this year. Meanwhile, the gap among voters with a college degree went from 14 points for Harris in 2024 to 30 points for Democrats this cycle.

Republicans had closed the gap among young voters aged 18 to 29 from 35 points in 2018 to just 11 points in 2024. But younger voters supported Democratic candidates this year by 50 points (74 percent to 24 percent). Not to mention Democrats flipped voters aged 45 to 64 for the first time in nearly two decades.

White evangelicals appear to be one of the only groups that didn’t shift toward Democrats. They supported GOP candidates 82 percent to 17 percent. But they only made up 17 percent of the electorate, according to the exit polls, which is down from a very consistent 25 percent for more than a decade. So there was still a problem with that group of voters, but it was more about turnout than persuasion.

While there was an unmistakable leftward shift this year, the results should not be considered a permanent party realignment any more than 2024 was. While Democrats did extremely well in Texas this year, they still haven’t won the Lone Star State in a presidential race in 50 years. So maybe it’s wise for everyone to take a deep breath.

If you take this year’s election results and match them with the Senate seats on the ballot in 2028, there doesn’t appear to be a viable path for Republicans back to the majority. But there wasn’t a particularly viable Democratic path to the Senate majority at this point two years ago. And if the Alaska election goes their way, they will end up winning Senate races in seven states that were initially rated Solid Republican.

If one party starts to get too comfortable, voters have a way of bringing politicians back down to earth. If Democrats come to Congress and push too far to the left or become too defined by their most extreme members, they will squander the opportunity they earned this year.

The dramatic demographic swings should be evidence that many voters are not beholden to either party and are open to switching allegiances, particularly in a time of economic uncertainty.

At the same time, if Republicans don’t go through some time of reflection and instead triple down on the policies that led to the blue wave, they risk cementing some of the shifts that started this cycle. It just won’t be thick cement.

#6063. Norse Atlantic Collapses: Airline Cancels Flights, Strands Passengers

Back in August 2026, all-Boeing 787 airline Norse Atlantic Airways announced it was in a rough financial spot, and was pursuing a sale, merger, or other arrangement. Not a whole lot of progress was made in subsequent months, and just this morning, the airline announced that it was in a “critical” financial situation.

Well, it seems that it didn’t take long for things to get much worse, as the airline has seemingly canceled all flights just hours later, leaving travelers stranded.

Earlier today, Norse Atlantic provided an update on its financial situation and ongoing strategic review. There’s no point in paraphrasing this, so here’s the direct statement from the airline:

The Company’s financial situation is critical. It is dependent on securing financing to meet its short-term liquidity needs and to continue its operations. Norse, supported by its advisors, has explored various strategic alternatives and entertains discussions for a potential takeover. In parallel, the Board and management have diligently considered other available options, including ACMI contracts. Norse is also engaged in discussions with selected parties on short term financing, however, there can be no assurances that such discussions will result in a viable solution.

To state the obvious, this sounded really, really bad. When the company was publicly stating that its “financial situation is critical” and that it needed to secure financing to meet “short-term liquidity needs,” you knew things weren’t good. I expected we’d see something bad happen in the coming weeks, but it didn’t take that long.

Norse Atlantic has canceled its own scheduled flights effective immediately. On top of that, the airline was leasing two jets to Pakistan International Airlines, and those flights were also canceled with very little notice, “due to an unexpected operational suspension” by Norse Atlantic. Travelers were literally checking in at the airport when they realized the airline was grounded.

Due to an unexpected operational suspension by our wet-lease partner Norse Air without prior notice, tonight’s PK786 (London–Islamabad) & PK710 (Manchester–Lahore) are cancelled.We deeply regret the disruption. Efforts have been made to mitigate the impact, and from tomorrow,…

So while the company hasn’t formally announced that it’s liquidating, it’s clear that operations are at least suspended, and we’ll see how this all plays out.

The airline industry can be a funny business, and there’s no clearer example of that than Norse Atlantic Airways. The airline launched in 2022, with the goal of operating long haul, low cost flights, particularly across the Atlantic.

That wasn’t exactly a unique business model, because this was exactly what Norwegian did, before it discontinued long haul flights in 2021. Not only was the idea sort of copied, but Norse Atlantic had some executives from Norwegian, and even picked up the planes that Norwegian previously flew.

But as is all too common in the airline industry, clearly they thought it would be different this time around… it wasn’t. So in 2024 we saw the airline update its business model, making the focus less about operating regularly scheduled commercial flights, and more about leasing out aircraft, all while reducing its fleet.

The company got a lifeline when IndiGo decided to lease some Norse Atlantic 787s to dabble in long haul flying, ahead of the airline taking delivery of its own Airbus A350s. However, between all the airspace closures, high oil costs, and generally declining performance at IndiGo as the airline increasingly moved away from its core strengths, the airline recently decided to scrap that experiment, and stop leasing planes from Norse Atlantic.

Since then, opportunities for Norse Atlantic have been limited. The airline did manage to lease a couple of Dreamliners to the “new” Pakistan International Airlines, but for an airline with 12 planes, that hardly pays the bills.

Norse Atlantic did still operate some of its own flights, but in a very limited capacity. The airline had some flights from Europe to Thailand, South Africa, and the United States, but most were seasonal, and they were a fraction of what they previously were. Clearly they just didn’t have enough money to “keep the lights on” anymore.

I am curious to see what comes next for Norse Atlantic’s 787s. The airline doesn’t own them, but instead, they’ll presumably return to their leasing companies. I can’t help but point out that Southwest Airlines wants to start long haul flights. The airline had been considering a Boeing 787 order, and was possibly even looking at ways to get planes faster than from a direct order (which requires waiting for years).

Could these dozen Norse Atlantic 787s somehow end up at Southwest? The interiors would just need some updates (assuming the airline wants to offer business class), but talk about a quick way to grow a decent sized fleet.

This morning, Norse Atlantic released a statement admitting that its “financial situation is critical,” and that the company’s future is “dependent on securing financing to meet short-term liquidity needs.” That wasn’t exactly a great sign, but little did we know that the company would collapse just hours later, as the airline has now ceased all flying, including on a wet lease basis.

Financial issues at the company started when… well, it launched. Norse Atlantic was just a direct replica of Norwegian, which had failed. When the airline realized that the long haul, low cost business model doesn’t really work, they tried to pivot to wet leasing. And while there’s some demand for that, it’s also not a 100% consistent business in terms of demand.

I feel horribly for all the frontline employees at Norse Atlantic who put their best foot forward. May they find good opportunities at other airlines.

What do you make of Norse Atlantic’s seeming collapse?

Air travelers returning home from Thanksgiving can breathe a sigh of relief.

Flight schedules were close to normal on Friday after a series of storms snarled flights on both coasts during the run-up to Thanksgiving.

And Mother Nature appeared not to have any more major curveballs to throw at travelers between now and Sunday, normally one of the busiest air travel periods of the year as holiday-goers return home.

That came after more than 460 flights were canceled on Thursday, according to data from FlightAware. The bad weather complicated the plans of tens of thousands of travelers with flights on Thanksgiving Day. East Coast airports serving the metro areas of New York City, Washington, D.C., Boston, Philadelphia and Baltimore were the hardest hit, but disruptions rippled across airports in Florida, the Midwest and the West Coast.

The main culprit: A Thanksgiving Day coastal storm on the East Coast that was strong enough to cause the first-ever postponement of the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade in Midtown Manhattan.

This week's flight problems came after a chaotic few weeks for air travel in the U.S., which featured a nationwide ground stop on Nov. 13 — and then tech outages at two of the largest U.S. carriers.

Now, Mother Nature has interfered with holiday travelers' plans.

“The timing couldn’t be worse,” Fox Weather meteorologist Bob Van Dillen had told TPG entering the Thanksgiving rush.

We've often seen how significant East Coast storms can snarl air traffic. With so many key airline hubs, a major weather system can cause cascading flight woes across the country.

Major airlines rolled out weather-related rebooking policies for airports facing poor conditions:

While Thursday could be a messy weather day, Thanksgiving Day itself typically brings much smaller crowds to airports.

According to preliminary data from the Transportation Security Administration, Thursday was the single quietest day at U.S. airports in nearly five years.

The forecast looks favorable through Sunday as travelers return from the holiday. The Sunday after Thanksgiving is typically the single busiest day of the year to fly.

Last year, the post-Thanksgiving rush set the record as the busiest day ever at U.S. airports for passenger traffic.

Entering the holiday rush, the TSA had projected more than 3 million passengers could fly on Nov. 29. That would be the first time U.S. passenger traffic would eclipse that mark in 2026.

Here are some things you should do if you've been affected by bad weather this holiday week, or plan to fly on the upcoming busy Sunday.

Keep an eye out for airline travel advisories (see above) that could allow you more flexibility to change your itinerary.

Take a close look at the forecast in every city you’ll be in — including wherever you might be connecting. That should give you a better sense of when the problem periods could be.

Just keep in mind: As more and more cities are affected by bad weather, disruptions could cascade across airlines’ networks.

Have your airline’s app downloaded, familiarize yourself with it, and opt in to all push notifications. Use it to:

Want to know how the TPG team deals with travel trouble? Check out some of our top strategies.

When it comes to bad weather, airlines typically will not foot the bill for unexpected hotel stays, meals and ride-hailing services.

However, if you booked your flight with a credit card that has built-in travel insurance, you may be able to file a claim and get some reimbursement.

Also, if you previously purchased a travel insurance plan for this trip — or have an existing annual plan — that may cover you, too.

#6061. Why Avelo Airlines Flies Tampa To McKinney & Concord Instead Of Dallas/Fort Worth & Charlotte Douglas

American ultra-low-cost carrier Avelo Airlines recently began new services from Tampa International Airport (TPA) to Dallas and Charlotte. These routes launched earlier in November 2026 using the Boeing 737-800, and the Dallas route operates four times per week, while the route to Charlotte runs twice per week.

Notably, however, Avelo is not connecting TPA to Dallas/Fort Worth International Airport (DFW) or Charlotte Douglas International Airport (CLT), the primary airports serving their respective cities. Instead, Avelo is connecting TPA to McKinney National Airport (DTX) and Concord Regional Airport (USA).

DTX is located about 30 miles (48 kilometers) from downtown Dallas, while USA is located roughly 17.5 miles (28 kilometers) by driving distance from downtown Charlotte. Avelo only operates one route out of DFW, while it doesn't serve CLT at all, as it instead relies on DTX and USA to serve these markets. While these may seem like unusual choices, this tactic is actually an old page out of the budget airline textbook.

Avelo Airlines is one of the US's newest airlines, competing against companies such as Frontier and Allegiant Air in the ULCC space. Generally, budget airlines and ULCCs in the US have taken two different approaches to their network design, with some companies favoring directly taking on the established full-service carriers.

Others, meanwhile, have preferred to operate out of smaller airports and to commence routes with little competition. Avelo has gone for the second path. Its largest operating base is in New Haven, where it is one of only two airlines currently serving the airport (and the larger of the two). In addition, the carrier also has operating bases in Lakeland and Wilmington, as well as at USA and DTX.

Despite the small size of these airports, they're actually major bases for Avelo, which is why the carrier favors them over the larger airports serving those areas. It's the same logic as to why United Airlines operates most of its New York-area routes out of its fortress hub in Newark. Newark, however, is still a major spoke in its own right for other airlines.

The only airline serving Concord apart from Avelo is Allegiant Air, while Avelo is the only airline operating out of McKinney. Avelo Airlines is also the only passenger airline serving Lakeland and Wilmington, while it is the dominant carrier in New Haven. Throughout its network, Avelo has generally avoided busy city pairs and instead focused on connecting secondary spokes to vacation destinations.

The strategy of focusing on small airports with limited air service has actually been around for decades. While airlines such as Frontier, the now-defunct Spirit Airlines, or JetBlue tend to serve major markets with high competition, companies like Ryanair have long avoided these types of routes. Demand between DFW and TPA is much higher than from McKinney.

However, this route also has competition from American Airlines, which means that every ticket sale for Avelo would be a fight. The airline is smaller, has a less thorough schedule, and lacks connecting options, onboard amenities, premium seating, a well-known loyalty program, or general brand recognition.

As such, Avelo would have to compete against American solely on price, which is a difficult battle to win for a smaller contender. The biggest benefit of operating out of small airports like DTX or USA is that they offer significantly lower operating costs, allowing airlines such as Avelo to better compete on price. Another benefit of serving secondary airports is that this can unlock additional demand for those who may prefer flying out of the spoke rather than the city's primary hub.

While airports like DFW or CLT are generally preferred by business travelers, they're not the most convenient option for everyone in the Dallas or Charlotte markets. The North Dallas area in particular, which DTX is well positioned to serve, is rapidly growing, and this means that Avelo is well positioned to take advantage of said growth.

The carrier's 50-route pullback shows how dramatically the airline is consolidating its network.

By operating out of DTX and USA rather than DFW and CLT, Avelo Airlines finds itself as the more convenient option for customers who live closer to these airports. This gives the carrier another advantage over competitors beyond pricing, while the presence of affordable, nonstop flights to popular leisure destinations helps create demand.

This effect is even stronger in markets such as New Haven, which is located much further away from any major airline hub, which creates an opening for companies such as Avelo Airlines. While city pairs such as New York-Miami have limitless demand, competition is intense. The larger full-service carriers are more compelling choices overall when considering product and schedule, while they can easily afford to drop prices and get into a bloodbath.

The pond is big, but the budget airline will remain the little fish. Being a big fish in a small pond, however, is a much more secure position for an airline, so long as costs are kept under control and the carrier operates its flights reliably. Some airlines take this concept a step further and intentionally connect underserved city pairs with seemingly little demand, then use their low fares to induce demand.

In these scenarios, the appeal of the ULCC is both the low price and the presence of a nonstop flight, the combination of which makes demand for the route much higher than before. Brazilian carrier Azul publicly uses this strategy as a core part of its business model, and it's long been a common commercial practice by budget carriers.

Avelo Airlines' business model can be most closely compared to that of Allegiant Air, which operates many underserved routes where the presence of a nonstop flight is a major competitive advantage. Allegiant Air is, of course, a much larger carrier, and it has recently completed its acquisition of Sun Country Airlines in May 2026.

The full merger is set to be completed in 2028, with the Allegiant Air brand being the survivor, and the company is also set to roll out a new first class cabin in 2027. Frontier is the other major ULCC in the US. It has over 150 aircraft, and unlike Allegiant and Avelo, Frontier tends to compete more heavily against larger players, including the US legacy airlines and Southwest Airlines.

This can be difficult for Frontier to manage, given that it mainly competes on price, but the carrier is working to overcome some of its challenges. It's continuously revising its network and cutting unprofitable services, while the airline is also set to introduce a new first class cabin in 2027. In addition to these carriers, the US is also home to Breeze Airways, JetBlue, and Southwest Airlines.

However, these airlines attempt to differentiate themselves by offering a passenger experience more similar to the legacy carriers. They can be more closely described as 'hybrid carriers' rather than as traditionally budget airlines or ULCCs that mainly compete on price. Notably, Breeze and JetBlue also offer premium seating options, while Southwest currently only sells economy and extra-legroom economy seats.

Avelo and Breeze are showing how its possible to find a niche in an industry dominated by legacy airlines.

Avelo Airlines, in its current form, only commenced operations in 2021, and today, the carrier has 15 aircraft in its fleet operating to over 30 destinations. Most of its operations are centered on connecting its bases to major vacation destinations in Florida, and the airline primarily operates out of smaller airports with less competition.

While Avelo has not planned significant growth for 2027, it will begin taking delivery of the first of 50 Embraer E195-E2s in 2028, with the airline also holding options for an additional 50 aircraft. The carrier's long-term goals are ambitious, but its financial performance today is not enviable. While Avelo made profits during some parts of last year, it generally lost money in 2025.

Meanwhile, 2026 saw a massive rise in fuel prices due to the ongoing Iran War that has affected the entire industry. The airline has focused on trimming its fleet by removing older, less economical 737-700s and has also shut down routes that have been unprofitable, including its former operating base in Burbank and ICE deportation flights. Avelo is a privately-held company, which means that its full financial results are not accessible to the public.

Generally, however, the current market environment has been difficult on budget airlines in particular, and Avelo is no exception. It's also notable that the carrier has not announced a new first class cabin like other ULCCs in the US, as well as the fact that Avelo remains committed to its massive Embraer E2 order so far despite its modest size today.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#6060. Not Again: Cargo Jet Overruns Miami Airport Runway (This Time A FedEx MD-11)

Miami International Airport (MIA) is having a bad luck streak when it comes to cargo planes being able to stay on the runway, but at least this time around there were no fatalities. Still, yikes…

At 8:25PM on Wednesday, November 25, 2026, a FedEx McDonnell Douglas MD-11 overran the runway at Miami Airport, leading the airport to be shut down for an extended period of time.

The 34-year-old MD-11 with the registration code N605FE had just performed flight FX910 from Memphis (MEM), and was coming in to land on runway 26R, which is 9,355 feet (2,851 meters) long. That’s a solidly long runway, for what it’s worth.

However, the plane wasn’t able to stop before the end of the runway, and seemed to exit the paved surface at a speed of around 50 knots, and came to a stop around 320 meters (1,000 feet) past the end of the runway, right by the airport perimeter fence.

🚨 USA | FEDEX CARGO PLANE OVERRUNS RUNWAY AT #MIAMI AIRPORT!MD-11 arriving from Memphis skidded into the grass beyond Runway 26R, triggering an FAA ground stop.2 crew members are safe. No deaths or injuries.#FlaPanthers #Survivor51 #ไฟไหม้ pic.twitter.com/kTM48GkeGf

WATCH: FedEx cargo plane in the grass after overshooting runway at Miami International Airport pic.twitter.com/t4DPQwUb0m

Fortunately there were no serious injuries. There’s video footage showing stairs being pulled up to the plane, and the pilots walking off with their bags. There’s always the classic aviation adage that “any landing you can walk away from is a good one,” and if that’s the case, I guess this was a good landing.

Footage showing the FedEx Express MD-11F after it overran the runway at Miami International Airport tonight. As a result of the incident, a ground stop was issued. pic.twitter.com/ldraejGQ4v

This accident ended up causing a ground stop of nearly two hours at the airport. That’s not exactly ideal timing, given what a busy travel day yesterday was, ahead of Thanksgiving. Operations did eventually resume, but with delays averaging over three hours.

🚨 迈阿密国际机场关闭！今晚，一架联邦快递（FedEx）货运飞机在迈阿密国际机场（MIA）冲出跑道，机场目前已实施地面停飞令（Ground Stop）。根据空中交通管制（ATC）的录音，飞机冲出跑道后，管制员通知其他飞行员，机场“刚刚关闭”。这是今年迈阿密国际机场发生的第二起货运飞机冲出跑道事故。…

Of course the concept of a plane overrunning a runway at Miami Airport is fresh on people’s minds, given the September 6 accident we saw with a 21 Air (Amazon Air) Boeing 767-300 that overran runway 30. Tragically that accident claimed five lives, as the plane ran through the perimeter fence, and killed motorists. What we’ve found out about the piloting of that flight since the accident, and just how recklessly the captain was flying the plane, is astounding.

We’ll have to wait for a full investigation to know what happened (the NTSB typically releases a preliminary report within a month), but in terms of circumstances and possible contributing factors, there are a couple of things we know.

First, there’s footage showing the plane’s approach, and it makes it pretty clear that the plane touched down extremely late.

JUST IN: FedEx cargo plane overruns the runway at Miami International Airport. Flights halted pic.twitter.com/PFFH0TNpe1

A recreation of the approach based on flight tracking data shows just how late the plane touched down, and the big question is why the pilots didn’t perform a go around.

🚨 BREAKING: FedEx FDX910, an MD-11F registered N605FE, went off the end of runway 26R landing at Miami International from Memphis at about 8:28 PM local, Nov 25. Tower sent the next arrival around and ground control closed the airport. No injuries reported so far. pic.twitter.com/IhRUGEVR97

It’s also worth pointing out that weather in the region was really bad at the time of the accident. Anna Giaritelli, a reputable aviation journalist with good sources, quotes a Miami air traffic controller, who told her that “this was absolutely the most dangerous operation I’ve seen,” as much of the traffic approaching Miami had run into a “black hole of weather.”

A Miami air traffic controller sent me this chilling text minutes before the FedEx incident in MIA tonight(Controller was not on duty while texting me.) pic.twitter.com/Fvy7vb7xuP

It doesn’t seem like conditions at Miami Airport as such were that awful (compared to reports of severe turbulence in the region), but I imagine the bad weather could’ve contributed to a sense of “get-there-itis” for the pilots.

While this is of course unfortunate, the great news here is the lack of injuries or fatalities. The plane ended up coming to a stop just feet from the airport’s perimeter fence, and if it had crashed through that, the outcome could’ve been completely different, with fatalities among motorists.

It also has to be acknowledged that the pilots seemingly turned the plane a little bit left off the end of the runway, to avoid the localizer antenna. So at least the overrun was handled as well as it could be.

Based on the preliminary information we have so far, DEI does not appear to be a factor in this accident. 😉

A FedEx MD-11 overran the runway at Miami Airport last night, and ended up in the grass just short of the airport perimeter fence. Fortunately there were no major injuries, and the pilots managed to walk off the plane. This had major operational impacts for the airport, as a ground stop was issued, delaying lots of travelers.

Unlike the 21 Air Boeing 767 accident we saw in September, there were no fatalities this time around. Either way, two cargo planes going off Miami runways in under three months is not great.

What do you make of this FedEx MD-11 accident in Miami?

#6059. Beginner’s luck: Freshmen leave it to chance at House office lottery

Rep.-elect Mark Teixeira reacts after drawing the worst chip during Tuesday’s lottery for newly elected members of Congress. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

As far as birthdays go, Rep.-elect Shannon Taylor was having a pretty good one.

Crowded into a room in the Capitol Visitor Center on Tuesday morning with the rest of her freshman class, the Virginia Democrat walked up to a table with a wooden box and reached in.

“This is so nervewracking,” she said, before pulling out a chip with a “1” printed on it.

Her prize was a coveted one — first choice of office space. Every two years, incoming members of the House play a game of chance to see who can land the best real estate and who will be relegated to less desirable corners of the Capitol complex.

The room broke out in raucous applause and a standing ovation. Her new colleagues started singing “Happy Birthday.”

Not everyone was so lucky. Rep.-elect Mark Teixeira, R-Texas, pulled number 105 — the very last one. The former MLB player raised his arms in a mock celebration.

“Lets all hope for the luck of the Taylors,” said Rep.-elect Brent Taylor, R-Tenn., only to emerge with number 81.

The newly-elected members got their turn in a random order, walking up one by one to a table where deputy executive director of House Office Buildings Kornell Rancy kept watch over the box of chips.

Rep.-elect John Cowan, R-Ga., was the first to pick a number. The first neurosurgeon to be elected to Congress, Cowan wore his white doctor’s coat as he pulled number 11 out of the box.

“I wanted to do something where I’m just representing health care providers around the country,” Cowan said.

As returning members lay claim to more desirable offices made available by those who resign, retire or lose elections, the space they’ve abandoned is left for the newcomers, who are on the Hill this week for orientation. Many of them will end up in the Longworth Building, where suites can be awkward or cramped.

Not all offices are created equal, and the calculus has changed over the years. The previously undesirable Cannon Building just underwent a budget-busting renovation that lasted more than a decade, with a spacious courtyard opening earlier this year. But the coveted Rayburn Building still retains its prestige, despite repeated and dire warnings from the Architect of the Capitol about its crumbling infrastructure.

“You’re welcome,” said Rep.-elect Amish Shah, D-Ariz., after pulling a disappointing number 94.

Prior to the lottery, Rep.-elect Trever Nehls, R-Texas, was hoping for the best but had a backup plan in case his number said otherwise.

“If I don’t pick number one, I’m going to offer one of these cigars as a trade to whoever gets it,” he said, pointing to three of them sticking out of his jacket pocket. He’s preparing to take over the seat currently held by his twin brother Troy, who shares a fondness for stogies.

The office space lottery dates back to 1908, when members of the 60th Congress received their first office assignments after the completion of what would be named the Cannon Building. A House page drew names and numbers from a box, and members selected their offices from a chart, according to House Office Buildings executive director of facility operations Joe Yates, who kicked things off Tuesday with a history lesson.

The lottery now is a little more modern, with members poring over virtual office layouts and doing walkthroughs of spaces on laptops.

“If somebody had to get 105, I’m glad it was me because I am here to serve, and I’m serving my freshman class by picking the worst office,” Teixeira said. “This is low on my priority list.”

Some members announced their lucky draws themselves, while others let Yates break the news.

“Come visit me,” said Rep.-elect Chris Gober, R-Texas, after pulling number 2 from the box.

After the lottery itself, members huddled with their staff to strategize about the next steps — how to leverage their numbers and select the best suites left on the list, while also exploring layouts, paint colors and carpeting.

“First and foremost, a good layout, so we can do good work, and people can be comfortable in doing the work, and then a convenient location. Very utilitarian,” said Rep.-elect Scott Wiener, D-Calif., of his priorities.

“We’ll get a decent Longworth office,” said Wiener, who drew pick 43. “Cannon would have been ideal, but I’m happy with any office.”

Rep.-elect Manny Rutinel, D-Colo., was hoping to replicate the good luck of some of his colleagues. “I’m going to do the Shannon Taylor and Sam Forstag. It’s eyes closed, behind the back,” he said of his moves, reaching into the box. But it wasn’t enough, and Rutinel pulled number 69.

“These are not red numbers, these are not blue numbers. These are the remaining numbers, and there ain’t that many,” said Rep.-elect Johnny Garcia, D-Texas, who was among the last few people to pick. He emerged with number 75.

And when Rep.-elect Joe Strada, R-Fla., the last of the incoming members to draw, walked up to the table, the whole room cheered.

“Wouldn’t it be crazy if I picked number 1?” he joked, pulling out the last chip in the box.

#6058. The Park Hyatt Beaver Creek Will Pay You To Redeem Points Over Peak Dates… But Why?

The Park Hyatt Beaver Creek is incentivizing people to redeem points at the property for stays over some pretty peak dates, which you don’t often see, as flagged by View from the Wing. This has the potential to be a good deal, but beyond that, I think the more interesting part of this story is the topic of why the hotel would offer something like this, since this is pretty rare.

The Park Hyatt Beaver Creek is offering 15,000 points back per night when you redeem over some peak dates, for a total of up to 90,000 points back (which you’d get if redeeming for six nights). To cover the basics:

The Park Hyatt Beaver Creek is a ski-in, ski-out property in Colorado, and it’s one I’ve reviewed before. For what it’s worth, the hotel is currently charging 55,000 World of Hyatt points per night over the dates eligible for this promotion.

Based on my valuation of 1.4 cents per World of Hyatt point, that means a redemption will cost you the equivalent of $770 per night. Meanwhile cash rates are running double as much, and that’s before taxes are factored in.

Understandably, I think a lot of people might be confused as to why the Park Hyatt Beaver Creek would be incentivizing award redemptions in this way. If the hotel wants to fill rooms, why only offer bonus points for points stays, and not for cash stays? That’s especially true when you consider redeeming points is already a good value compared to the cash rate.

The explanation here is probably pretty simple, if you understand the economics at play. I’ve written in the past about how hotels are reimbursed for award stays. Keep in mind that the loyalty program centrally (rather than the individual hotel) sets the cost for redemptions, based on their internal costs associated with redemptions. The way it generally works is as follows:

How does this all factor into the Park Hyatt Beaver Creek’s promotion? I suspect a few factors are at play here:

The Park Hyatt Beaver Creek is offering 15,000 points per night for award redemption over peak holiday dates. So while the standard rate is 55,000 points per night, you’d end up paying 40,000 points per night, which is quite the deal compared to the cash rate.

Given that some hotels treat points guests as second class guests who are staying for “free,” I think the goal here is pretty clear. Hotels are reimbursed for award stays based on overall occupancy levels, and presumably the hotel hopes that a promotion like this will get it to the occupancy level needed to trigger the highest reimbursement rate.

What do you make of this Park Hyatt Beaver Creek promotion?

Welcome to “What’s in My Bag,” a new series where TPG staffers open their carry-ons, personal items and dopp kits to share the travel essentials they never leave home without. First up: The Points Guy founder, Brian Kelly.

As a travel expert who’s constantly on the go, I will say some of my favorite things that you’ll find in my bag revolve around staying organized and being comfortable — I always know where my essentials are. At this stage of my life, I’m willing to splurge a bit on handcrafted or well-made products that last. Quality is nonnegotiable.

This travel pouch is so chic, but definitely a splurge. It’s made with Saffiano leather and Re-Nylon, an innovative fabric that’s produced from recycled plastic recovered from the ocean. You can find it at Saks Fifth Avenue. I love it for keeping everything I might need on the go organized — with two top zipper pockets and one each on the front and back, I never run out of room.

Buy: Prada Re-Nylon and Saffiano leather travel pouch, $1,120

These Bose noise-canceling headphones are comfortable and seamlessly connect via Bluetooth. Plus, they are stylish and have great sound quality. The surround sound is awesome.

Buy: Bose QuietComfort Ultra Headphones, from $349 (normally $449)

As a content creator, I needed a good lav microphone with an iPhone receiver for when I’m out and about. The Rode wireless mic is super easy to use, holds a charge all day and slips right into my travel pouch.

Buy: Rode ultra-compact wireless microphone system with USB-C connector, $89 (normally $99)

My go-to quick snack is Quest protein peanut butter cups — indulgent yet packed with protein. I keep Grüns gummies in my bag for a healthy mix of essential vitamins and prebiotics. They keep me feeling energized and are more than just a multivitamin — they’re made with whole fruits and veggies too.

Buy: Grüns sugar-free gummies (pack of 28), $73.32; Quest protein peanut butter cups (pack of 12), $28.49

I firmly believe in investing in pieces that will last, and this handcrafted leather wallet from Aspinal of London is no exception. It holds up to eight cards and can be personalized with your initials.

Buy: Aspinal of London 8-card billfold wallet in black woven leather, $180 (normally $355)

I have a second phone for travel that’s connected to the T-Mobile network as a backup, and, depending on your service plan, T-Mobile also offers free Wi-Fi on U.S. airlines. I keep my main phone on Verizon, but you never want to be stuck without a phone when abroad.

I’m a big tennis fan, whether it’s traveling for a match or catching the U.S. Open when it's in New York. This easy-to-adjust hat is perfect to keep in my bag, so I always have one on me for sun protection.

Buy: Wimbledon Mono-tone Herringbone Cap, $64

Fashionable sun protection is a no-brainer. I love these Tom Ford sunglasses in black.

Buy: Tom Ford Snowdon sunglasses, $284 (normally $316)

This small device is super versatile — not only does it convert 220–240V AC input to 120V AC output, but it also includes five plug adapters so I can use it in nearly every country in the world.

Buy: Insignia international converter and plug adapters, $17.49 (normally $29.99)

This portable power bank gives me peace of mind knowing I can charge my phone on the go. Small and lightweight, it fits on the back of my iPhone without covering the camera and fits easily into my pocket or travel pouch.

Buy: UGreen 10000mAh 22.5W compact power bank, $19.99 (normally $29.99)

I never know when an idea will strike, or when I need to jot down a few meeting notes on the go. The Moleskine XL leather-bound hardcover notebook feels luxurious and has large pages that make writing easier.

Buy: Moleskine classic hardcover XL notebook, $24.75

Dry air on planes can quickly dry out your lips — hydration is key. I love that the Supergoop lip balm moisturizes without feeling sticky, plus it doubles as sun protection.

Buy: Supergoop! Play Lip Balm SPF 30, $9.60 (normally $12)

Maximize your purchases by stacking rewards through online shopping portals on top of any rewards you earn directly through your credit card. I’m a big fan of earning Amex points through Rakuten or Rove miles through Rove (they also have some of the highest earning rates I’ve seen!).

As we head into holiday shopping, keep an eye on the shopping portals for extra bonus-earning rates. Right now, you can earn up to 7 Rove miles per dollar spent at Best Buy. They also recently added personalized shopping offers with earning rates up to 25 Rove miles per dollar. If you aren’t a Rove member yet, you can join for free and earn 1,500 Rove miles instantly when you sign up using my link (that’s three times more than the standard referral offer!).
